en: The Avadānaśataka. Homage to the glorious Omniscient One.
The First Chapter. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Pūrṇabhadra, Yaśomatī, Kusīda, and likewise the merchant.
Soma, Vaḍika, Padmāṅka, Pañcāla, and Dhūpa— having made the King the last, this group is thus proclaimed. [1] Pūrṇabhadra.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)
Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit,
and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples,
dwelt near Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
There, not long after the Blessed One had attained perfect awakening, his fame filled the entire world.

Now, in the region of Dakṣiṇāgiri, there lived a great brahmin householder named Saṃpūrṇa. He was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself. He was faithful, auspicious, and of noble intent; he was devoted to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, and delighted in renunciation and giving, finding joy in bestowing gifts.
Great renunciation exists.
When he had begun to perform a sacrifice for all the various heretics,
at which many hundreds of thousands of non-Buddhist practitioners were feasting,
and when the Blessed One had converted King Bimbisāra along with his retinue,
Through his discipline, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained discipline.
At that time, Pūrṇa’s kinsmen arrived from Rājagṛha and began to speak in Pūrṇa’s presence of the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Then, having heard this proclamation of the Blessed One’s virtues, the great brahmin householder Pūrṇa attained great faith.

Then, having ascended the sacrificial platform and stood facing Rājagṛha, he placed both his knees upon the ground, scattered flowers, and offered incense and water, beginning to entreat the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One come to my sacrificial enclosure to partake in the sacrifice."

Then, through the power of the Buddhas and the power of the deities, those flowers remained suspended above the Blessed One, forming a pavilion of flowers; the incense was like a mass of clouds, and the water was like a rod of beryl.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, from where has this invitation come?
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, in the region of Dakṣiṇāgiri there dwells a great brahmin householder named Saṃpūrṇa;
we must go there."
"Let the monks prepare themselves!

Having traveled on a tour through the southern regions surrounded by a retinue of a thousand monks, the Blessed One stopped near the sacrificial enclosure of the brahmin mahāśāla Pūrṇa and fell into this thought:
"What if I were to win over the brahmin Pūrṇa by means of a miracle of supernatural power?"
Then the Blessed One, having made those thousand monks disappear, stood alone near Pūrṇa, his hand occupied with bowl and robe.
Then Pūrṇa, the great brahmin householder, beheld the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Seeing him, who was like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides, he approached the Blessed One with great haste and said to the Blessed One:
"Welcome, Blessed One!"
"May the Blessed One sit;
let him take a seat for the sake of favoring me.
The Blessed One said:
"If you have renounced it, let it be given into this bowl.

Then Pūrṇa, the Brāhmaṇa Mahāśāla, surrounded by five hundred young students, began to fill the bowl with various kinds of food for the Blessed One—eatables, chewables, hard foods, lickables, drinkables, and suckables;
and the Blessed One, for his part, transferred food from his own bowl into the bowls of the monks.
When the Blessed One knew that the bowls of the thousand monks were full,
he then showed his own bowl to be full as well;
thereupon, he showed the thousand monks with their full bowls arranged in the shape of a crescent moon.
Even the deities stationed in the sky raised their voices, saying:
"The bowls of the Blessed One and of the thousand monks are full!

Then, from witnessing that miracle, Pūrṇa was filled with serene faith; like a tree cut at its root, he was thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, and having become exalted with joy and gladness, he prostrated himself at the feet of the Blessed One.
He began to make this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of things to be given, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide; may I be the deliverer of beings who have not crossed over, and the liberator of those who are not yet liberated."
He is the one who brings comfort to those who have not found comfort,
and he is the one who leads to final nirvana those who have not attained final nirvana.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the succession of causes and the succession of karmic actions of the brahmin mahāśāla Pūrṇa, manifested a smile.

It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those which go downward, having gone to the hells of Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana,
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma,
fall cooled upon those that are hot hells.
Those who are in the cold hells fall there transformed into heat;
by that, the particular tortures of those beings are stilled,
and they think thus:
"Have we, sirs, passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Indeed, sirs, we have not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere; rather,
this is a being such as has never been seen before."
"By its power, our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having developed faith in that emanation, they exhaust the karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans,
where they become vessels for the truths.
Those which go upward [reach] the Cāturmahārājika, Trayastriṃśa,
Yāma, and Tuṣita [heavens].
The Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahman, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, and Puṇyaprasava [devas].
Having gone to the Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and they recite these two verses:
Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket. AVŚ_1.1 //
"For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya, having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering. Thus it was said.
Then those rays of light, having traversed the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wishes to prophesy past karma,
they vanish behind the Blessed One;
if he wishes to prophesy the future, they vanish in front of him.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell,
they disappear into the soles of his feet.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among animals,
they disappear into his heel; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts (preta), they disappear into his big toe.
If he intends to prophesy rebirth among humans,
the light disappears into his knees.
If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful wheel-turning monarch,
they vanish into the palm of his left hand;
if he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a universal wheel-turning monarch, they vanish into the palm of his right hand.
If he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods,
they disappear into his navel.
If he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth; if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they disappear into the crown of his head.
If he intends to prophesy supreme, perfect enlightenment, they disappear into the *ūrṇā*. If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they disappear into the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, disappeared into the uṣṇīṣa of the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with many thousands of different colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the directions were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has departed, who have abandoned wretchedness and pride, are the supreme causes for the world."
The Conquerors, who have vanquished their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

At that time, O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Sages, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors, whose steadfastness is like that of the King of Mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause.
"The multitudes of people desire to hear that for the sake of which the wise manifest a smile. Thus the Blessed One said. (Speyer 7)
"So it is, Ānanda; so it is.
Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly awakened ones do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
This, Ānanda, is Pūrṇa, the eminent brahmin."

"By this root of merit, by this generation of the thought of awakening, and by this relinquishing of gifts, having fully realized the awakening attained through three incalculable eons, and having fulfilled the six perfections permeated by great compassion, he shall become the perfectly awakened Buddha named Pūrṇabhadra."

"By means of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion— this is his gift of dharma, which consists in the clarity of mind toward me."
When the Blessed One had prophesied that the brahmin great householder Pūrṇa would attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
Pūrṇa then entertained the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for three months at his sacrificial enclosure;
furthermore, he planted many diverse roots of merit.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Yaśomatī. (Ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
The renowned and greatly meritorious one, a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
dwelt with his community of disciples near Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake. Then,
having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by a host of monks and preceded by the community of monks, he entered Vaiśālī for alms.
Having wandered for alms through Vaiśālī in due course, he approached the residence of the general Siṃha;
having arrived, he sat down on the seat that had been prepared.
Now, the daughter-in-law of the general Siṃha, named Yaśomatī, was beautiful, lovely to behold, and gracious.
Upon seeing the Blessed One’s body, radiant with its various marks, she conceived an exceeding faith.
She asked her father-in-law:
"Is there some means by which I too might be endowed with such qualities?
Then this thought occurred to the general Siṃha: "Oh, how noble is the inclination of this girl!"
"However, if she were to encounter the necessary conditions, she might form the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having understood this, he said:
"Girl, if you will proceed by undertaking the cause,"
"You too shall become just like this, such as the Blessed One is."

Then, in order to increase Yaśomatī’s favor, the general Siṃha gave her a great quantity of gold, bullion, and jewels. Thereupon, the girl Yaśomatī invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for a meal at her home on the following day.
And the Blessed One consented for the sake of favoring her.

Then the maiden Yaśomatī, having had flowers made of gold, silver, and jewels, and having prepared a great collection of perfumes, garlands, and ointments, as well as food of a hundred flavors, announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger:
"It is time, Venerable Sir."
"The meal is prepared; may the Blessed One now consider it the right time.
Then the Blessed One, surrounded by a multitude of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached the residence of the general Siṃha.
Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.

Then, the maiden Yaśomatī, seeing that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied them with food of a hundred flavors. She then began to scatter flowers over the Blessed One;

those flowers remained suspended above the Blessed One like a jeweled gabled pavilion, a jeweled parasol, and a jeweled canopy—the likes of which could not be fashioned even by a highly skilled master craftsman or his apprentice.
Just as it happens through the power of the Buddhas and the power of the deities.

Then the maiden Yaśomatī, having seen that most wonderful miracle which captivated both gods and men, fell with her entire body at the feet of the Blessed One like a tree cut down at its root, and began to make this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of enlightenment, and by this renunciation of gifts, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide; may I be the savior of sentient beings who have not yet crossed over."
He is the liberator of those not yet liberated,
the consoler of those not yet consoled, and the one who leads to final nirvana those who have not yet attained it.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the succession of causes and the succession of karmic deeds of the maiden Yaśomatī, manifested a smile.

It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those which go downward, having gone to the hells of Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana,
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma;
Those who are in the hot hells find it become cool as they fall into them; those who are in the cold hells find it become warm as they fall into them.
By that, the particular tortures of those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them:
"Sirs, have we passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them: "Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere."
"Moreover, this is a being never seen before;
by its power, our particular causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having gained faith in that manifested form, they exhaust the karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans.
Therein they become vessels for the truths;
those that go upward [reach] the Cāturmahārājika and Trayastriṃśa [heavens].
The Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita,
Mahābrahman, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha [devas].
Having gone to the gods, they proclaim that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, and they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket.
For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya, having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering. (AVŚ 2.2) Thus it was said.
Then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wished to proclaim past karma,
they would vanish into the back of the Blessed One.
If he wishes to prophesy the future,
they disappear from the front;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear from below.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals, they vanish into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a human,
they vanish into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts,
they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among human beings, they disappear into his knee.
If he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch (*balacakravartin*),
they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he intends to prophesy the attainment of the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakravartin), they disappear into the palm of his right hand; if he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they disappear into his right shoulder.
If he wishes to prophesy awakening as a śrāvaka,
they disappear into his mouth.
If he intends to prophesy solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi), they disappear into the circle of hair between his eyebrows (ūrṇā);
if he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi), [they disappear into the crown of his head].
They disappear into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with many kinds of thousands of colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he speaks these verses:
“The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has departed and who have abandoned both dejection and pride, are the supreme causes for the world.”
The Conquerors, who have vanquished their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.
At that time, O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom for the sake of the listeners who long for it,
[speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Munis.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Buddhas, the Protectors, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the wise ones display a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
Those multitudes of people desire to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how this girl Yaśomatī has performed such an act of veneration for me? "I do, Venerable Sir."

Ānanda, this girl Yaśomatī, by means of this root of merit, this generation of the thought of awakening, and this renunciation of gifts, shall realize the awakening accumulated over three incalculable aeons;
having fulfilled the six perfections cultivated through great compassion, she will become the perfectly awakened Buddha named Ratnamati.

"By means of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion— this is my gift of Dharma, which consists in the serene clarity of mind toward me."
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 3:
Kusīda (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with the community of disciples.

In Śrāvastī there lived a certain merchant, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself.
He took a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and dallied with her;
yet as he was playing, taking pleasure, and dallying, neither a son nor a daughter was born to him.
Placing his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth;
yet I have neither son nor daughter.
Upon my passing, since I am childless, my entire estate will become subject to the king's authority."
He was told by the ascetics, brahmins, fortune-tellers, friends, relatives, and kinsmen:
"Perform a supplication to the deities."
There is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of prayers;
but that is not so.
For if it were otherwise, [everyone would have what they desired].
Each one would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Nevertheless, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three?
The mother and father are filled with passion and have come together;
the mother is healthy and in her fertile period;
and a gandharva is present.
Through the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.

Thus, deceived by ascetics, brahmins, fortune-tellers, friends, relatives, and kinsmen, this childless man, longing for a son, made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other specific deities.
That is to say, he entreated the deities of the groves, the deities of the forests, the deities of the crossroads, the deities of the junctions of three roads, and the deities who receive offerings;
he also entreated those deities who are co-nascent, those who share his dharma, and those who are constantly attached to him. And so he remained, intent on such entreaties.
And a certain being, having passed away from one or another class of beings, entered the womb of that Prajāpati. Five unique qualities belong to certain women of wise nature.
What are these five?
He knows a man who is impassioned and he knows a man who is dispassionate;
he knows the time and he knows the season.
She knows that she has conceived a fetus;
she knows from whom the fetus was conceived;
and she knows whether it is a boy.
He knows whether it is a girl:
if it is a boy, he remains resting against the right side of the womb;
if it is a girl, she remains resting against the left side of the womb.
Filled with joy, she announced it to her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, you prosper;
I have become pregnant."
And since he remains resting against my right side, it will certainly be a boy; thus,
he too was exceedingly joyful.
Raising his upper body high and extending his right arm, he uttered this inspired exclamation:
"May I behold the face of a son long desired;
may one be born to me who is not base-born."
He should perform my duties; being supported, he should support me in return;
and he should receive his inheritance.
"May my family lineage endure for a long time;
and when we have passed away, may someone, having given small or great gifts and performed meritorious deeds, dedicate the merit in our names, saying:
'May this follow those two wherever they go and whatever state they have been reborn in.'"
Knowing that she had conceived, he kept her in the upper story of the palace, free from restraint;

he attended to her with cooling appliances in the cold season and warming appliances in the heat, and provided her with food prescribed by physicians— neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent, but entirely devoid of the qualities of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.
Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces; like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, she moved from couch to couch and from seat to seat without ever descending to the ground below,
and she heard nothing unpleasant until the fetus reached full maturity.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born,
handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
At his birth, his family was filled with joy. Having performed the birth festival upon his birth, they established his name,
asking, "What shall be the name of this boy?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since the entire family has rejoiced at his birth, let the name of this boy be Nanda."
The name "Nanda" was established for him.
The boy Nanda was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nourished by these eight nurses with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other most excellent and refined provisions.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
When he had grown up, being five or six years old,
he became lazy and extremely indolent; he did not even wish to rise from his bed or seat.
Because of his sharp and keen intelligence, he studied the treatises even while remaining within the household.
Then this thought occurred to the merchant: "At some time or other, through the propitiation of the deities, even such a son was born to me;
yet he too is lazy, exceedingly lazy."
He does not even rise from his bed or seat. Therefore, what use have I for such a son as this, who, though possessing a healthy body, remains like a beast?
That merchant was devoted to Pūraṇa;
he invited the six heretical teachers to his own home, thinking,
"Perhaps this boy, through seeing them, will develop a sense of reverence and even rise from his bed and seat."
Then, upon seeing those teachers, the lazy boy did not even cast a glance at them with his eyes,
let alone rise to greet them, pay homage,
or invite them to a seat.
Then that householder, seeing that very situation, became even more deeply distressed; placing his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought.
In the meantime, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Indeed, it is the nature of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—who are great compassionate ones, who are engaged in favoring the world, and who are the sole protectors—[to know all things].

They dwell in calm abiding and special insight; they are skilled in the three bases of subduing; they have crossed over the four floods; they are well-established on the soles of their feet through the four bases of miraculous power; they have long practiced the four means of attraction; they are free from the five hindrances; they have transcended the five destinies;

they are endowed with the six limbs; they have fulfilled the six perfections; they are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment; and they are teachers of the eightfold path.

For those who are skilled in the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling, who possess the strength of the ten powers, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods,
there arises a vision of knowledge three times during the night and three times during the day, as they survey the world with the Buddha-eye.

Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity all at once? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms? Who is heading toward the lower realms?
Whom shall I lift up from the lower realms and establish in heaven and liberation?
Whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I provide with a hand to lift him out?
Whom, deprived of the noble wealth, shall I establish in the sovereignty and mastery of the noble wealth?

In Śrāvastī, a certain great caravan leader, having returned from the great ocean with his ship wrecked, made supplication to his personal deity two or three times before setting out again for the great ocean; yet he returned once more with his ship wrecked.
Thereupon, a great weariness arose within him.
He fell into this reflection:
"What means might I use by which I could acquire wealth?
Then it occurred to him:

"This Buddha, the Blessed One, is far more distinguished than all the gods; he is one who has set out for his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, desiring the Great Dharma, and affectionate toward his children.
What if I were now to descend once again into the great ocean in his name?
If I should return with a successful ship, I would perform worship for him with half of my wealth."
Having thus made his resolve, he again set out upon the great ocean.
By the power of the Buddha, he reached the Island of Jewels, gathered a great quantity of precious gems, and returned safely and in well-being to his own home.
Having dispelled his fatigue from the journey, he began to examine his merchandise;
seeing various and diverse jewels, a great profit arose within him,
and he thought:
"I shall have to give half of such jewels as these to the ascetic Gautama. What if I were to take these from my wife, sell them for two kārṣāpaṇas, and offer perfume to the Blessed One?"
Having purchased some agarwood for two kārṣāpaṇas, he went to the Jetavana;
then, feeling ashamed, he stood at the gateway and burned the agarwood as incense.

Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) that the incense rose up into the sky, pervaded the entire city of Śrāvastī, and remained there like a great mass of clouds.
Having seen this most wonderful miracle, which captivated both gods and men, a great faith arose in him.
He reproached his own mind, saying:
"It would not be fitting for me that I should not honor the Blessed One with jewels."
Then that caravan leader invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for a meal within his residence.
Having satisfied him with exquisite food, he scattered great jewels over them.
Thereupon, those jewels rose up into the air above and remained suspended: a jeweled gabled pavilion, a jeweled parasol, and a jeweled canopy over the head of the Blessed One.
That which cannot be accomplished by a well-trained master smith or his apprentice,
even so was it done through the power of the Buddha and the power of the deities.
Then the caravan leader, his faith redoubled by the sight of that miracle, fell at the feet of the Blessed One like a tree cut at its root and began to make this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of gifts, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide— a savior of beings who have not crossed over,

He is the one who brings comfort to those who have not found comfort,
and the one who leads to final nirvana those who have not attained it.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the succession of causes and the succession of karmic actions of that caravan leader, manifested a smile.

In Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder, a merchant, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself. He took a wife from a family of equal status, and he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While that householder was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant. After the passing of nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born who was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
When he was born, his father performed the birth ceremony and gave him the name Vaḍika.
The boy Vaḍika was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nurtured by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various highly refined provisions.
He grew quickly like a lotus in a pond;
when he had become large, at five or six years of age,
he then showed devotion to his teacher and studied all the treatises.
By virtue of his sharp intelligence, he quickly reached the further shore of all the treatises.

Immediately thereafter, due to the ripening of some karma performed in a previous birth, physical suffering fell upon that Vaḍika; thus becoming miserable and lost in thought, he remained there, wondering:
"What sin have I committed, that this physical suffering has arisen in my body?"

Seeing this state of physical suffering in his son, the father was greatly distressed; fearing for his son’s life, with a dejected mind and a face covered in tears of grief, he quickly summoned a physician and showed him his son’s illness, asking: "What is this disease?

"For what reason has this arisen in my son's body?
Then that physician, having observed the symptoms of his disease, began to administer treatment;
nevertheless, there was no alleviation of his illness.
Furthermore, there is an increase [in anxiety]:

Thus he fell to the ground in a swoon.
Seeing him, the father’s anxiety for his son arose once more;

Though that boy was ill and unable to speak, he somehow addressed his father:
"Father, do not act rashly! Take courage and stand up!"
Lest you too become like me through the fear of my passing,
perform worship to the gods and give gifts in my name;
by that, my well-being shall be restored.
Having heard these words of his son, that householder made offerings to all the gods and gave gifts to all the brahmins, heretics, and wandering mendicants;
nevertheless, his illness was not pacified.
Then a great mental anguish arose within him:
"Worship has been performed for all the gods, and gifts have also been given by my father."
Nevertheless, she did not become well.
Then, recollecting the qualities of the Tathāgata, she began to pay homage to the Buddha.

[To those] endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections, who are rich with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, who teach the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments, who possess the strength of the ten powers, whose fame fills the ten directions, who are distinguished as superior to the thousand [gods] who wield power,

If he wishes to prophesy awakening as a śrāvaka,
they disappear into his mouth.
If he wishes to prophesy solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi), they disappear into the circle of hair between the eyebrows (ūrṇā);
if he wishes to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi), [they disappear into the crown of the head].
They disappear into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, disappeared into the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of diverse colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he speaks these verses:
"The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has vanished and who have abandoned both dejection and pride, are the supreme causes for the world."
The Conquerors, who have vanquished all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.
At that time, O steadfast one, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom,
O Śramaṇa, Lord of Jinas, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Sages, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, whose steadfastness is like that of the King of Mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
Those multitudes of people desire to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda; it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see how this householder’s son, Vaḍika, has rendered me such honor?
"I see it so, Venerable Sir."

Ānanda, by this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of gifts, this householder’s son Vaḍika shall, after realizing the awakening accumulated over three incalculable eons, fulfill the six perfections cultivated through great compassion,
and become the perfectly awakened Buddha named Śākyamuni.

"By means of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion— this is the gift to be given by me, namely, the clarity of mind toward me."
The Blessed One said this;
and those monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Padma. The Buddha,
the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
He was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
When the Blessed One had not yet appeared in the world, King Prasenajit used to worship the deities of the non-Buddhist sects with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
but when the Blessed One appeared in the world, [he ceased this practice].
King Prasenajit, having been disciplined by means of the parable of the young son, gained faith in the Blessed One’s teaching;
then, filled with joy and gladness, he approached the Blessed One three times and honored him with lamps, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Then a certain monastery attendant, taking a fresh lotus, was entering Śrāvastī for the sake of King Prasenajit when he was seen by a lay follower of the non-Buddhist sects, who asked him:
"Will you sell this lotus?"
He replied, "Yes.
Desiring to purchase it, he was following behind the householder Anāthapiṇḍada as he approached that place.
He increased the price from that by double;
then, as they continued to outbid each other, they raised it until it reached one hundred thousand.
Then this thought occurred to the park-keeper:
"This householder Anāthapiṇḍada is unshakeable and of steady resolve;
surely there must be a reason for this. Having thus conceived a doubt, he questioned that man who was devoted to the heretics:
"For whose sake are you growing so large?
He replied, "For the sake of the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa."
Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"It is for the sake of the Blessed One, the Buddha.
The monastery attendant said:
"Who is this so-called Buddha?
Thereupon, Anāthapiṇḍada described the qualities of the Buddha in detail.
Then the monastery attendant said to Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, I myself shall pay homage to that Blessed One."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, taking a monastery attendant with him, approached the place where the Blessed One was.

The monastery attendant saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns— a living embodiment of splendor.
It was like a mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides;
and as soon as it was seen, the monastery attendant threw that lotus toward the Blessed One.
As soon as it was thrown, it became the size of a cartwheel and remained suspended above the Blessed One.

Then that monastery attendant, having seen that miracle, fell at the feet of the Blessed One like a tree cut at its root; with palms joined in reverence, he cultivated a resolute intention and began to make this vow:

"By this root of merit, by this generation of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of gifts, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide, to deliver those beings who have not yet crossed over."
He is the liberator of those not yet liberated,
the consoler of those not yet consoled, and the one who leads to final nirvana those who have not yet attained it.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the succession of causes and the succession of karmic actions of that monastery attendant, manifested a smile.

It is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those which go downwards—
namely, Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, and Pratāpana— [go there].
Having gone to the hells— Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma— they descend into those that are hot hells becoming cool,
and into those that are cold hells becoming warm.
By that means, the specific causes of suffering for those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them:
"Have we, sirs, passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?"
In order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, they think:
"Indeed, sirs, we have not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere."
"Moreover, this is a being who has never been seen before;
it is through his power that our particular causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having developed faith in the mind toward that emanation, they exhaust that karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans.
Therein they become vessels for the truths;
those that go upward [reach] the realms of the Four Great Kings and the Thirty-three.

[He saw] the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin [devas]; the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahman [devas]; the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara [devas]; the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna [devas];
the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala [devas]; and the Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha [devas].
Having gone to the gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut.
"For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya, having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering. Thus it was said;
then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wishes to prophesy past karma,
they vanish behind the Blessed One;
if he wishes to prophesy future karma, they vanish in front of him.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell,
they disappear into the soles of his feet.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among animals,
they disappear into his heel; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts (preta), [they disappear into his big toe].
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans,
they disappear into his knees.
If he intends to prophesy the kingdom of a powerful wheel-turning monarch,
they disappear into the palm of his left hand; if he intends to prophesy the kingdom of a universal wheel-turning monarch, they disappear into the palm of his right hand.

If he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they vanish into his navel. If he intends to prophesy rebirth in the southern palm of the hand, they vanish into the palm of the right hand. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as a god, they vanish into his navel.

If he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth; if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, [they disappear into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows].

If he wishes to prophesy unexcelled perfect enlightenment, they disappear into the *ūrṇā* [the hair-treasure between the eyebrows]. If he wishes to prophesy unexcelled perfect enlightenment, they disappear into the *uṣṇīṣa* [the crown of the head].
Then those rays of light, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the uṣṇīṣa of the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of different colors..."
A bundle [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he speaks these verses:
"Free from rebirth, having abandoned wretchedness and pride,"
The Buddhas are the supreme causes for the world;
the Jinas, who have conquered their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized that at that very moment through your wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Munis, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose must be revealed].
"Those multitudes of people long to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how this monastery attendant, having conceived faith, has performed such an offering for me?
"Yes, Venerable Sir."

This park-keeper, by means of this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishing of the gift, shall, after having accomplished awakening— which is achieved over three incalculable eons— fulfill the six perfections cultivated by great compassion, and become a perfectly awakened Buddha named Padmottama.

"By means of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion— this is his gift of Dharma, which consists of the clarity of mind toward me."
The Blessed One said this. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 8 Pañcāla (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwells at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with the community of disciples.
At that time, the King of Northern Pañcāla was at variance with the King of Southern Pañcāla.
Then King Prasenajit of Kauśala approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Prasenajit of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is indeed the unsurpassed King of Dharma, the protector of beings who have fallen into calamity,
and the pacifier of enmity among those who harbor mutual hostility."
Furthermore, this King of Northern Pañcāla is at enmity with the King of Southern Pañcāla;
the two of them are inflicting great slaughter upon one another’s people.
For these two, the Blessed One brought about the pacification of a long-standing enmity that had persisted for many nights.
"Thinking, 'I shall show compassion,' the Blessed One consented to King Prasenajit of Kosala by remaining silent."
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, understanding through the Blessed One’s silence that his request had been accepted, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, rose from his seat, and departed.
Then, when that very night had passed, the Blessed One dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and set out on a walking tour toward Vārāṇasī, the city of the Kāśīs.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he reached Vārāṇasī and stayed there at Ṛṣipatana in the Deer Park.
Eventually, it became known to those two that the Blessed One had arrived in their domain.
Then, by means of his supernatural power, the Blessed One manifested a fourfold army and terrified the King of Northern Pañcāla.
Frightened, he mounted a single chariot and approached the presence of the Blessed One.
For him, the Blessed One taught the Dharma in order to pacify their enmity.
Having heard that Dharma and having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One,
he— by applying himself, striving, and exerting himself— realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

The King of Dakṣiṇapañcāla also invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for the three-month rainy season retreat, providing him with food of a hundred flavors and clothing him in garments worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
He then made this aspiration:

By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of enlightenment, and by this relinquishing of gifts, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide; may I be the savior of beings who have not crossed over,
the liberator of those who are unliberated,
and the consoler of those who are unconsoled.
One who brings to final nirvana those who have not yet attained final nirvana.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the succession of causes and the succession of karmic actions of the King of Dakṣiṇapañcāla, manifested a smile.

It is indeed the nature of things that whenever the Buddha-Blessed Ones manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those that go downward,
having gone to the hells of Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana,
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma;
Those who are in the hot hells find it become cool as they fall upon them,
and those who are in the cold hells find it become warm as they fall upon them;
thereby, the particular agonies of those beings are allayed.
It occurs to them:
"Sirs, have we indeed passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To generate faith in them, the Blessed One emits a magical creation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere;
rather, this is a being never seen before."
"By the power of this, our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having developed faith in the mind toward that emanation, they exhaust that karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans,
where they become vessels for the truths.
Those that go upward [reach] the Cāturmahārājika, Trayastriṃśa,
Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, and Brahmapurohita [heavens].

Having gone to the gods of Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
And they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut. (AVŚ 8.1)
"For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, they will make an end to suffering. (AVŚ 8.2)
Then those rays, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wished to proclaim past karma,
they would vanish behind the Blessed One's back.
If he wishes to prophesy the future,
they disappear from the front;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear from below.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals, they disappear into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a human,
they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts,
they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans, they disappear into his knee.
If he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch,
they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he wishes to prophesy the attainment of the sovereignty of a universal monarch, they vanish into the palm of his right hand; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they vanish into his navel.
If he wishes to prophesy awakening as a śrāvaka,
they disappear into his mouth.
If he wishes to prophesy solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi), they disappear into the circle of hair between the eyebrows (ūrṇā);
if he wishes to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi), [they disappear into the crown of his head].
They vanish into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) of the Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of diverse colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he speaks these verses:
"The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has departed, who have abandoned wretchedness and pride, are the supreme causes for the world."
The Conquerors, who have vanquished their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.
At that time, O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom for the sake of those listeners who long for it,
[speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Munis.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the King of Mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
Those multitudes of people long to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how the King of Southern Pañcāla has performed such an act of veneration for me?
"I do, Venerable Sir."

Ānanda, by means of this root of merit, this generation of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishing of gifts, this King of Pañcāla will, after having accomplished awakening— which is achieved over three incalculable aeons—
fulfill the six perfections cultivated by great compassion and become the perfectly awakened Buddha named Vijaya.

By means of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion— this is his gift of dharma, which is the clarity of mind toward me.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of Dhūpa] (ed. Speyer, vol. I)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras,
garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; the Buddha, the Blessed One, was renowned and possessed of great merit.
The recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of disciples, dwells at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
At that time, there were two guild-leaders in Śrāvastī who were at odds with one another;
of these two, one was devoted to Pūraṇa.
The second was toward the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Then, while they were engaged in mutual conversation, discussion, and deliberation, the lay follower Pūraṇa said:
"Pūraṇa is more distinguished than the Buddha."
The Buddhist lay follower said, "The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, is more distinguished.
Thereupon, the two of them were imprisoned after all their property had been confiscated.
When King Prasenajit heard this,
he gave an order to his ministers:
"An investigation must be made of those two."
Then those ministers caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout the entire realm:
"On the seventh day, a debate between a follower of the Buddha and a follower of the Tīrthikas shall take place;
let those who wish to see miraculous wonders come."

Then, on the seventh day, in a vast area of the earth where many hundreds of thousands of living beings had gathered and many thousands of deities had assembled in the sky, and when a circle of cow dung had been prepared and all kinds of perfumes and garlands were offered, the lay follower of the heretics first performed a vow of truth (*satyopayācana*).
"By that truth that the six teachers, beginning with Pūraṇa, are the most excellent in the world—
by this truth, may these flowers, this incense, and this water go to them."
As soon as this had been spoken, those flowers fell upon the ground.
The fire was extinguished, and the water on the earth reached its end, exhaustion, and total depletion.
Then a great multitude of people let out a loud cry of "kilakilā" and a clamorous shout.
Upon seeing him, the lay follower of the heretics became silent, crestfallen, with shoulders drooping, face cast down, and rendered speechless.
Devoted to deep reflection, he sat with his cheek resting on his hand, absorbed in thought.
Then, a disciple of the Blessed One, filled with joy and longing, his eyes blossoming with serene faith, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground,
and made this vow of truth:
"By that truth by which the Blessed One is the foremost of all sentient beings..."
"By this truth, may these flowers, incense, and water go toward the Blessed One.
As soon as this was uttered, those flowers set out through the air toward the Jeta Grove like a flight of swans,
and the incense like a mass of clouds.
The water was like [the reflection of] beryl needles.
Then that great multitude of people, having seen that miracle, raised a loud clamor of shouts, cheers, and cries of joy, following closely behind them as they set out.
Then those flowers remained suspended above the Blessed One, while the incense and water stayed before him.
Thereupon, that great multitude, having gained serene faith, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
To them the Blessed One spoke this sutra: "O brahmins and householders, there are these three supreme designations. Which three?"
The designation of the foremost is in the Buddha; the designation of the foremost is in the Dharma; the designation of the foremost is in the Saṅgha.
What is the designation of the foremost regarding the Buddha?
Whatever beings there may be, whether brahmins or householders—whether footless, two-footed, or many-footed; whether possessing form or formless—[the Buddha is the foremost among them].
Whether they possess perception, lack perception,
or possess neither perception nor non-perception,
the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is declared to be the foremost among them.
Whoever has faith in the Buddha has faith in the foremost;
for those who have faith in the foremost, a foremost ripening is to be expected— either among the gods as gods, or among humans as humans.
This, O brahmins and householders, is called the designation of the foremost regarding the Buddha.
What is the designation of the foremost regarding the Dharma?
Whatever dharmas there may be, whether conditioned or unconditioned—
Dispassion is declared by you to be the foremost of those dharmas;
whoever has faith in the Dharma has faith in the foremost.
For those who have placed their faith in them as supreme, a supreme ripening is to be expected—either among the gods for those who have become gods, or among humans for those who have become humans.
This, O brahmins and householders, is called the designation of the supreme in the Dharma. What is the designation of the supreme in the Saṅghas?
Whatever assemblies, groups, guilds, or congregations there may be,
the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost among them; whoever has faith in that community, [they shall attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment].

Those who have placed their faith in the foremost [of the Sangha] may expect a foremost ripening of that very faith: either among the gods as gods, or among humans as humans. This, O brahmins and householders, is called the designation of the foremost within the Sangha.

While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, among those brahmins and householders, some attained serene confidence in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; some took up the precepts for going for refuge;
and some, having gone forth, understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable.
Having repelled all conditioned states by means of their nature of falling, decaying, dispersing,
and being utterly destroyed, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Consequently, that lay follower of the non-Buddhist sect attained serene confidence in the presence of the Tathāgata.
Then, like a tree cut down at its root, he fell at the feet of the Blessed One and began to make this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this relinquishing of the gift, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide; may I be the deliverer of beings who have not crossed over, and the liberator of those who are not yet liberated."
He is the one who provides consolation to those who have not yet found consolation, and he is the one who leads to final nirvana those who have not yet attained it.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the succession of causes and the succession of karmic actions of that lay follower of the non-Buddhist sect, manifested a smile.

It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those that go downward,
having gone to the hells of Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana,
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma—
Those who are in the hot hells find cooling relief as [the light] falls upon them, and those who are in the cold hells find warming relief;
thereby, the specific tortures of those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them:

Because I performed such worship for the Perfectly Awakened One, Brahmā..."
Through the ripening of that karma, I experienced great happiness throughout endless saṃsāra;
even now, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, such is the worship [I receive].
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"In that we shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher;
and having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him"—
thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 13: The Bathing (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a community of disciples.
At that time, in Śrāvastī, about five hundred merchants had set out upon a desolate road through the wilderness.

Fallen away from the path, they reached a desert expanse of sand. Oppressed by the exhaustion of their journey and having consumed their provisions, at the time of midday they were scorched by the rays of the fierce sun;
like fish pulled out of water, they rolled upon the ground, experiencing suffering that was sharp, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable.
Experiencing these sensations,
those thousands of deities made entreaties,
such as Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava, and others.
And no one at all is capable of rescuing them.
Thereupon, a certain lay devotee who was well-versed in the Buddha’s teaching said to those merchants:
"Sirs, go for refuge to the Buddha."
Then, with one voice, they all went for refuge to the Buddha.

In this interval, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. It is indeed the nature of things that for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are great compassionate ones, who are engaged in favoring the world, who are protectors of the one [Dharma], who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, and who have crossed over the four floods and are well-established on the soles of their feet through the four bases of psychic power— [there is nothing hidden].

Those who have long practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), who are free from the five factors (*pañcāṅga*), who have transcended the five destinies (*pañcagati*), who are endowed with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), who have fulfilled the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), and who are teachers of the eightfold path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*).

For those who are skilled in the nine successive attainments, who possess the power of the ten strengths, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods, three times during the night and three times during the day, they survey the world with the Buddha-eye, and their knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms?"
Who is leaning toward the states of woe?
Whom might I lift up from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation? To whom, sunk in the mire of sensual desires, might I extend a helping hand?
Whom, being destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, might I establish in the sovereign mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?
Whose eyes, veiled by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance, might I purify with the medicinal probe of the ointment of knowledge?
For whom, whose roots of virtue have not yet been planted, might I plant them?
"Whose [roots of merit] already planted should I bring to maturity?
Whose [roots of merit] already matured should I liberate? And it is said:
"The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might even exceed its tide-line;"
But the Buddha would not let the time pass by for those who are like calves to be tamed.
When the Blessed One saw that many merchants had fallen into a state of calamity, distress, and confinement,
he vanished from Jeta’s Grove by the mere casting of his gaze and, surrounded by a multitude of monks, arrived at that place.
Those merchants beheld the Blessed One together with the community of monks.
Having seen this, they let out a loud cry.
Then the Blessed One generated a worldly thought:
"O, would that Śakra, the lord of the gods, were to release the great rain of Indra!"
"May cool breezes blow!
As soon as this thought arose in the Blessed One's mind, Śakra released a great rain from the realm of Māhendra,
and cool breezes were sent forth.
When the thirst of those merchants had vanished and their burning fever was stilled,
they then regained consciousness.
And the Blessed One has pointed out the path to them by which they have reached Śrāvastī.
Having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, they approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One delivered to them a teaching on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths;
having heard it, some attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Some attained the fruit of once-returning; some the fruit of non-returning;
and some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka,
some for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and some for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And for the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and gravitating toward the Saṅgha.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, O Blessed One, how these merchants have been rescued by the Blessed One from the path of the wilderness!"
And as soon as that thought arose, a rain from the realm of Mahendra fell and cool breezes blew. The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in former births; their conditions have been met, their causal factors have ripened, they have arrived like a surging flood, and they are inevitable.
These actions were performed and accumulated by me; who else shall experience their results?"
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— do not ripen in the element of wind, but rather ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
for actions do not perish even after hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

In the past, monks, in a time long gone, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Candana appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, is the teacher of gods and men.
Then Candana, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at a certain royal capital.
Thereupon, the consecrated Kṣatriya king approached where Candana, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was staying.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Candana and sat down to one side.
As the consecrated Kṣatriya king sat to one side, the perfectly enlightened Buddha Candana exhorted him with the qualities that bring about awakening.
Then the consecrated Kṣatriya king rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and [extended] his right...
Placing his knees upon the ground and bowing with palms joined toward the perfectly enlightened Candana,
he addressed the perfectly enlightened Candana thus:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, consent to dwell in this royal capital for the three-month rainy season retreat."
The Perfectly Awakened One, Candana, consented to the king by remaining silent.
At that time, a great drought occurred,
by which the rivers and wells became scanty in water.
And the trees were devoid of flowers and fruit.
Then the king began to entreat the Perfectly Enlightened One, Candana: "Blessed One,
in the middle of this city I shall have a lotus pond constructed, filled with scented water, wherein the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, may bathe."
"Perhaps, through the Blessed One’s bathing, the god might send rain upon this my realm.
The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candana, consented to the king by remaining silent.
Then the consecrated Kṣatriya king gave an order to his ministers:
"May you prepare perfumed water and jars made of precious gems,
so that we may bathe the Blessed One together with the community of his disciples."

Then the king, surrounded by his assembly of ministers, had that city cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel; it was adorned with raised banners and flags, strewn with various flowers, sprinkled with scented water, and perfumed with diverse incenses.
Furthermore, he had a lotus pond constructed for him.

Then the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candana, standing alone in a single robe upon a lotus pond for the sake of benefiting all beings, was bathed by the king, surrounded by his assembly of ministers, with water perfumed with various fragrances. Immediately upon that bathing, Śakra, the lord of the gods, released such a rain from the Mahendra-cloud that all the crops were brought to fruition.
And because of that, the great multitude of people gained faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One;
many fragrant stupas were established,
and those who had gone for refuge there to the Perfectly Enlightened One, Candana, [were likewise established].
All of them have attained final nirvāṇa;
I alone remain among them.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
and those monks, with uplifted minds, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 14:
*Ītiḥ* (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples near Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
And in that Nāḍakanthā, a great plague of people arose.
Then the mass of people, afflicted by diseases, supplicated various thousands of deities, such as Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava, and others;
yet that pestilence did not subside.
Now, a certain lay follower was residing in Nāḍakanthā.
He said this to the brahmins and householders of Nāḍakanthā:
"Come, all of you, go for refuge to the Buddha."
"And entreat that Blessed One to come here,
so that perhaps through the Blessed One’s slight effort there might be the pacification of this plague.
Then the brahmins and householders of Nāḍakanthā began to entreat the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One come to liberate us from this calamity and distress."
In this interval, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

It is indeed the nature of things that for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are greatly compassionate, who act for the benefit of the world, who are the sole protectors, who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, and who have crossed over the four floods with their feet firmly established on the bases of psychic power— there is nothing that remains hidden.

Those who have long practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), who are free from the five factors of regression, who have transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), who are teachers of the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), who possess the power of the ten strengths (*daśabala*), whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods.
Three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, his knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms?"
Who is leaning toward the states of woe?
Whom might I lift up from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation? To whom, submerged in the mire of sensual desire, might I extend a helping hand?
Whom, being destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereign mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?
Whose eyes, veiled by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance, shall I purify with the medicinal salve-stick of wisdom?
For whom, whose roots of virtue have not yet been planted, shall I plant them?
"Whose [roots of merit] have been planted that I might bring them to maturity?
Whose [roots of merit] are matured that I might liberate them? And it is said:
"The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might even exceed its tide-line,"
But the Buddha would not let the time pass for those who are like calves to be tamed.
