Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, arrived at Nāḍakanthā. Thereupon, the Blessed One suffused that entire city with loving-kindness from his heart, whereby the Mārakas departed.
The calamity was also pacified.
Then, upon seeing the Buddha, a great faith arose in those brahmins and householders;
and having conceived that faith, they invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, to accept robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Then the Blessed One gave them such a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths,
upon hearing which many brahmins and householders attained the fruit of stream-entry,
while others attained the fruit of once-returning.
Others attained the fruit of non-returning; others, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
And that entire city became inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and tending toward the Saṅgha.
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, how these beings, having fallen into calamity, were liberated from that calamity through their faith in the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causal factors have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
These actions were performed and accumulated by me."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Actions performed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, do not ripen in the fire element nor in the wind element, but rather ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there appeared in the world a perfectly awakened Buddha named Candra— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Then the Perfectly Awakened One, Candra, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, arrived at a certain royal capital.
The anointed Kṣatriya king heard:
"The Perfectly Awakened One, Candra, has arrived within our realm."
Having heard this, the king, endowed with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, approached the place where the Perfectly Awakened One Candra was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, he sat down to one side.
To the consecrated Kṣatriya king seated to one side, the Perfectly Awakened One Candra exhorted him with the qualities that bring about awakening.
Then the anointed Kṣatriya king, having gained confidence, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder,
placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, addressed the Perfectly Awakened One Candra as follows:
“May the Blessed One consent to my invitation to dwell here for the three-month rainy season retreat together with the community of monks;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The Perfectly Awakened One, Candra, consented to the king’s request by remaining silent.
And at that time, in the city of that king, there occurred a great epidemic among the people and a plague,
by which that great multitude of people was exceedingly afflicted.
Then, for the sake of pacifying the disease, the king entreated the Perfectly Awakened One, Candra:
"It would be well, Blessed One, if a means for the cessation of this plague were to be performed.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Candra, said to the king:
"Go, Great King! Fasten this *saṃghāṭī* robe to the top of a banner and, with great honor, circulate it throughout your own realm;
hold a grand festival for it, and cause the entire multitude of people to be inspired to practice the recollection of the Buddha."
"Thus there will be well-being for them.
Then the king did everything exactly as he had been instructed;
and with that as the cause and that as the condition, all calamities were pacified.
Then that multitude of people, having gained faith, as well as the king, the ministers, and the citizens, went for refuge to the Buddha,
and they went for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time, on that occasion, was I myself.
By me, great worship was performed for that perfectly enlightened Buddha, Candra."
Through the ripening of that karma, I experienced great happiness within saṃsāra, reaching the realms of gods and humans; even now, my prosperity is caused by that very same [karma],
such that whatever I think of or whatever I pray for, all of it succeeds exactly as intended.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this;
and those monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
AVŚ_15 The Miracle (prātihārya) (ed.
Speyer, vol. I)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt with the community of disciples at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, instigated by Devadatta, deprived his father— the righteous king of dharma— of life.
And when he himself was established in the kingdom, those who lacked faith became powerful, while those who were faithful became weak.
Meanwhile, a certain senior minister who was faithless and hostile to the teaching of the Blessed One had begun to perform a sacrifice for the brahmins;
there, many hundreds of thousands of brahmins had assembled.
They made a formal agreement:
"No one at all should approach the ascetic Gautama for an audience.
Then those Brahmins, being elderly and assembled together in harmony, began in the middle of the street to invoke Śakra according to the ritual prescribed in the Vedas.
Come, come, you adulterer of Ahalyā!

In this interval, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. It is indeed the nature of things that for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are greatly compassionate, who are engaged in favoring the world, who are guardians of the one [Dharma], who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, who have crossed over the four floods, and whose feet are firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power— [nothing remains hidden].

Those who have long practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), who are free from the five factors [of sensual desire], who have transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with the six limbs,

who have fulfilled the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), who are teachers of the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), who possess the power of the ten strengths (*daśabala*), whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods.
Three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, his knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into hardship, calamity, and distress? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms?"
Who is leaning toward the states of misery? Whom shall I lift up from the states of misery and establish in heaven and liberation?
To whom, sunk in the mire of sensual desire, shall I grant a hand to pull them out?
Whom, being destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereignty and mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?
Whose eyes, veiled by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance, shall I purify with the medicinal salve-stick of knowledge?
For whom, whose roots of virtue have not yet been planted, shall I plant them?
"Whose [roots of merit] planted shall I bring to maturity?
Whose matured [roots of merit] shall I liberate? And it is said:
"The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might even exceed its tide-line,"
But the Buddha would not let the time pass by for those who are like calves ready to be tamed.
The Blessed One saw:

"These brahmins have planted roots of merit in the past, have grasped the path to liberation, and while seeking their own welfare, they are now facing toward *nirvāṇa* and turning away from *saṃsāra*. Yet, due to association with unwholesome friends, they are currently [distant] from my teaching.
What if I were to apply myself with zeal for the sake of their discipline?"
Then the Blessed One, having manifested the form of Śakra and illuminated that sacrificial enclosure with a divine radiance, began to descend. Thereupon,
those brahmins became thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, filled with an exalted sense of rapture and gladness.
Speaking with one voice, they said: "Come, come, Blessed One!
Welcome to the Blessed One!"
Then the Blessed One, wearing the guise of Śakra, sat down on the prepared seat.
This report spread everywhere throughout Rājagṛha:
"Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, has descended at the sacrifice."
Upon hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings assembled.

Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the brahmins were won over, caused his disguise as Śakra to vanish and remained in his own form as a Buddha. He delivered such a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths;
having heard it, sixty thousand brahmins shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity—which rose up with its twenty peaks—and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
And hundreds of thousands of living beings attained faith in the Blessed One.

Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, how these brahmins, having come to the Blessed One, have attained the vision of the Truths, and how many hundreds of thousands of living beings have likewise attained great faith."
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata in former births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
These actions were performed and accumulated by me."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Neither in the fire element nor in the wind element,
but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there appeared in the world a perfectly awakened Buddha named Indradamana—

a Tathāgata, Arhat, perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
While wandering on a tour of the countryside, he arrived at a certain royal capital. That royal capital was occupied by heretics. A certain anointed Kṣatriya king heard:
"Indradamana, the Perfectly Awakened One, has arrived in our realm.
Having heard this, and being endowed with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, he approached where Indradamana, the Perfectly Awakened One, was staying.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, Indradamana, the Perfectly Awakened One, and sat down to one side.
To the consecrated Kṣatriya king seated in private, the Perfectly Awakened One Indradamana exhorted him with the qualities that bring about awakening.
Then that king, having gained confidence, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground,
and bowing with palms joined toward the perfectly enlightened Indradamana, addressed the perfectly enlightened Indradamana as follows:
"May the Blessed One consent to dwell with me for the three-month rainy season retreat;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The Blessed One said:
"Great King, is there in your realm any monastery where visiting and departing monks may take up residence?
The king replied, "There is none, Blessed One; however, let the Blessed One remain."
"I shall have a monastery built where incoming and departing monks may take up residence.

Thereupon, for the sake of the Tathāgata, the king had a monastery constructed, adorned with unperforated walls and gateways, and embellished with windows, balconies, lattices, crescent-moons, and railings.
Provided with coverings, filled with reservoirs of water, surrounded by groves of trees, and endowed with various flowers and fruits,
it was prepared and offered to the Blessed One together with the community of his disciples.
And the Blessed One was requested to perform a great miracle.
Then, at the king’s request, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Indradamana, displayed a great miracle, the playful sport of the Buddha-ornament (*buddhāvataṃsaka-vikrīḍita*).
Upon seeing it, the king, together with his ministers, merchants, countryfolk, and all the city-dwellers, became deeply serene and grew even more devoted to the Teaching.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time, on that occasion, was I myself.
By me was such worship performed for the Perfectly Awakened One Indradamana."
Through the ripening of that karma, I experienced infinite happiness within saṃsāra;
now, as a Tathāgata, I possess this splendor of the teaching.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
and those monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of the Quinquennial Festival] (AVŚ 16)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)
Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit,
and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples,
dwelt near Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
When the deluded man Devadatta had committed thousands of harms against the teaching of the Blessed One, yet was not even able to cause a single hair on the Blessed One’s body to quiver,
he then addressed King Ajātaśatru:
"Let a formal agreement be made in Rājagṛha that no one should approach the ascetic Gautama, nor should anyone provide him with alms-food.
In this way, having failed to obtain gain or honor, he will certainly depart for another country."
The king had it done accordingly.
Thereupon, those lay followers who had seen the Truth began to weep:
"Alas, what a tragedy! Rājagṛha city has become leaderless, for the appearance of one like a blue lotus or an udumbara flower is so rare!"
"Having encountered the Buddha, the Blessed One, whose appearance is as rare as the udumbara flower, it is not possible to fail to gather [his teachings].
This sound was heard by the monks through a succession of oral transmissions.
Then the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One exactly as he had heard it.
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do not be anxious."
"Only the Tathāgatas are the ones who know the proper time in this matter;
however, as long as my teaching endures, there shall be no deficiency of requisites for the disciples, let alone now."
In the meantime, Śakra, the lord of the gods, directed his vision downward;
he beheld such a state of decline within the Blessed One’s teaching.
Upon seeing this, for the sake of inspiring enthusiasm among donors and patrons, and for the sake of generating a sense of the majesty of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, [he acted].
In order to cut through the intoxication and pride of Ajātaśatru and Devadatta, and to generate faith within himself,
he illuminated the entire city of Rājagṛha with a magnificent radiance and proclaimed in a loud voice:
"From this day forward, I shall attend upon the Blessed One together with the community of disciples with divine requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick."
Having said this, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One consent to stay right here in this city of Rājagṛha."
"I shall attend upon the Blessed One with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The Blessed One said:
"Enough, Kauśika; this is sufficient simply by the fact that your mind is so full of serene faith."
"For there are many in the world who desire merit.
Śakra said:
"May the Blessed One consent to stay with me for five years."
"I shall hold a five-year festival for the sake of the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One said:
"Enough, Kauśika; this is sufficient, as long as your mind is full of faith."
"For there are many in the world who desire merit.
Śakra said:
"May the Blessed One consent to stay with me for five days."

Then the Blessed One, in order to manifest the power of his own merit, to show favor to Śakra, the lord of the gods, and for the sake of ensuring a continuous succession of five-year festivals in the future, consented by remaining silent. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, showed him that Bamboo Grove, the Vaijayanta palace, and divine seats.
There were divine lotus-pools and divine food.
Then the Blessed One sat down upon the seat that had been prepared.

Thereupon, Śakra, the lord of the gods, seeing that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, surrounded by many thousands of deities, served and gratified them with his own hands.

In many ways, having personally satisfied and served [the Buddha] with food, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he took a very low seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with his retinue, with a discourse on the Dharma.
And King Ajātaśatru, while situated on the upper terrace of his palace, beheld such a worship being performed for the Blessed One in the Bamboo Grove.
Upon seeing this, he was overcome with remorse and manifested great faith.
Then the citizens dwelling in Rājagṛha, moved by the force of the Dharma, approached the king and spoke thus:
"O Great King, the citizens residing in Rājagṛha are being robbed!
For here, while the gods themselves are heedless and dwelling in negligence, they abandon their divine sensory objects to worship the Blessed One.
It would be well, O King, if the agreement were now broken."
Then King Ajātaśatru, having set aside his formal decree, caused a proclamation by bell to be made in the city of Rājagṛha:
"Let honor be paid to the Blessed One as you please.

Thereupon, the citizens dwelling in Rājagṛha, together with their families, were thrilled, satisfied, and delighted; filled with exalted joy and gladness, they took flowers, perfumes, and garlands and approached the Blessed One to behold him.
Then the Blessed One was honored with great reverence by gods and humans alike,
and the Blessed One performed such a teaching of the Dharma for those gods and humans— which brings about the penetration of the Four Noble Truths—
that upon hearing it, many gods and humans attained the vision of the Truths.
Having seen the worship of the Blessed One, the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that there is such a festival within the teaching of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in previous births; their conditions have been met, their requirements fulfilled, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
Since I performed and accumulated these actions, who else shall experience them?"
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do actions performed ripen in the element of wind, but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, whether they be wholesome or unwholesome.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

In the past, monks, in a time long gone, a Perfectly Awakened One named Ratnaśaila appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

While wandering on a tour through the countryside, he arrived at a certain royal capital. In that capital, a king named Dharmabuddhi was ruling, and in that very capital there was a great plague. Then, for the sake of pacifying the plague, the king invited the Blessed One and his community of disciples to a meal for three months.
After the passing of three months, that plague was pacified.
Then, with their minds won over, the king and the citizens performed a five-year festival for the Tathāgata and his community of disciples. And it is said:
"O Ānanda, when he was a king, [he gave] the great and radiant Jewel Mountain."
Desiring peace, he who was not possessed performed the five-year festival. Thus [it is said].
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Because I performed a quinquennial festival for the Tathāgata Ratnaśaila, I have experienced great happiness throughout saṃsāra."
Since such honor for the Tathāgata is now caused by that very [act],
and there will be many hundreds of five-year festivals within my teaching after I have passed into parinirvāṇa,
therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
and those monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 17:
Praise (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with the community of disciples. At that time, there lived in Śrāvastī about five hundred members of a musical guild who were companions in song.
And at that time, a king of the gandharvas named Supriya arrived;
he possessed such power that he could demonstrate the seven notes upon a single string.
Accompanied by twenty-one musicians,
he arrived at Śrāvastī, proclaiming that the six great cities were no longer functional.
The musicians residing in Śrāvastī then informed the king.
The king said: "Be free from anxiety;
we shall know the proper time for this."
Then, this thought occurred to Supriya, the king of the musicians:
"It is thus reported that King Prasenajit is exceedingly skilled in the art of music."
"What if I were to challenge him to a debate?
Then Supriya, the king of the musicians, approached King Prasenajit of Kośala;
having approached, he spoke thus to King Prasenajit of Kośala:
"I have heard, O King, that you are skilled in the art of music.
If it is not troublesome for you, please examine it."
Then King Prasenajit distracted him and said:
"Good sir, I have a teacher staying in the Jeta Grove, the unsurpassed king of musicians.
Come, let us go to his presence."

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, surrounded by about five hundred musicians led by Supriya, the king of musicians, and accompanied by many hundreds of thousands of living beings, went to the Jeta Grove.
At that moment, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Blessed Buddhas.
Indeed, it is the natural law for the Blessed Buddhas, who are great compassionate ones, who are engaged in favoring the world, and who are protectors of all.

To those who dwell in calm abiding and special insight; who are skilled in the three bases of subduing; who have crossed over the four floods; who are well-established on the soles of their feet through the four bases of psychic power; who have long practiced the four means of attraction; who are free from the five hindrances; who have transcended the five destinies;
who are endowed with the six limbs; who have fulfilled the six perfections; who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment; and who are teachers of the eightfold path.

For those who are skilled in the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling, who possess the strength of the ten powers, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are distinguished from even the thousand-fold lords of the Vasavartin gods,
the vision of knowledge proceeds as they survey the world with the Buddha-eye three times during the night and three times during the day:

Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity all at once? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone to the lower realms? Who is leaning toward the lower realms? Whom shall I pull out from the lower realms and establish in heaven and liberation?
To whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I grant the hand of uplift?
Whom, bereft of the noble wealth, shall I establish in the sovereignty and mastery of the noble wealth?
Whose eyes, veiled by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance, shall I purify with the salve-stick of wisdom?
Whose unplanted roots of merit shall I plant? Whose planted roots shall I bring to maturity?
Whose matured roots shall I liberate? And it is said:
Even the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might exceed its shore; but the Buddha would never let the time for those to be trained pass by.
Then the Blessed One, for the sake of favoring those beings who were ready to be trained, gave rise to a worldly thought:
"O, would that Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, surrounded by seven thousand Gandharvas and taking his lute with its beryl handle, should approach my presence.

Simultaneously with the arising of this thought, Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, surrounded by seven thousand Gandharvas, having honored the Blessed One in the proper manner, presented the Blessed One with his lute with the beryl handle.
Then Supriya, the king of the gandharvas, began to play the lute before the Blessed One;
he began to demonstrate the seven notes and twenty-one melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) upon a single string.
Upon hearing this, King Prasenajit and a great multitude of people were filled with supreme wonder.
Then the Blessed One also played the lute with its beryl staff,
whereby many distinct musical notes and various types of melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) were demonstrated upon each individual string.
And they [the elements] are shown through the very aspect of emptiness; furthermore, he has demonstrated that this body is like a lute,
and the vocal sounds are like the sense organs.

The melodic modulations were like the realm of his mind. Upon hearing them, the Gandharva king Supriya was so captivated that he offered his lute at the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, and by realizing this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and shifting, he [perceived] all conditioned states as being subject to falling, decaying, dispersing, and destruction.

Having struck down [all defilements] through the abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*), he realized arhatship. He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, for whom an axe and sandalwood were the same, who had split the eggshell of ignorance with knowledge, and who had attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the analytical insights (*pratisaṃvid*), and the higher knowledges (*vidyā*).
Turning his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Then the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas were won over, and they began to provide protection, defense, and guardianship for the teaching of the Blessed One.
Among the five hundred musicians, joy and gladness having arisen, this thought occurred to them:
"We are engaged in a lowly occupation and our livelihood is one of hardship."
"What if we were to inform the king and invite the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, to enter the city?
Then, having obtained permission, those musicians invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, to enter the city;
and the Blessed One consented to those musicians by remaining silent.
Then, with the assistance of those musicians, along with the king’s ministers, citizens, and countryfolk, the entire city of Śrāvastī was cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;
it was sprinkled with scented water, strewn with various flowers, perfumed with diverse incenses, and adorned with canopies of blossoms.
And those musicians themselves took up their lutes and provided service with mṛdaṅga drums, flutes, cymbals, and various other musical instruments.
And they fully satisfied the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, with excellent food.
Then the Blessed One smiled.

It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some of them go downward.
Some go upward;
those that go downward [fall into] Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci.
Having gone to the hells— Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma— they fall cooled upon those that are hot hells,
and they fall heated upon those that are cold hells.
By that means, the specific causes of suffering for those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them:
"Have we, sirs, passed away from here?"
"Or have they been reborn elsewhere? In order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Indeed, venerable sirs, we have not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere;
rather, this is a being whom we have never seen before."
"By the power of this [emanation], our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having developed faith in their minds toward the emanation, they exhaust that karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans,
where they become vessels for the truths.
Those that go upward [reach] the Cāturmahārājika, Trayastriṃśa,
Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, and Brahmapurohita [heavens].

Having gone to the gods of Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless."
And they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket! (AVŚ 17.2)
For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.

Then those rays, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One desired to proclaim past karma, [the rays would enter his back].
If he wishes to prophesy past karma, they disappear behind the Blessed One;
if he wishes to prophesy future karma,
they disappear in front of him.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear into the soles of his feet; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts (preta), they disappear into his heel. If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts, they disappear into his big toe.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a human being,
they disappear into his knees;
if he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch (*balacakravartin*), [they disappear into his right hand].
If he intends to prophesy sovereignty as a universal monarch (cakravartin),
they disappear into the palm of his right hand.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the gods,
they disappear into his navel;
if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, [they disappear into his mouth].
If he intends to prophesy individual enlightenment (pratyekabodhi),
they disappear into the circle of hair between his eyebrows (ūrṇā).
If he wishes to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
they vanish into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, disappeared into the ūrṇā-hair between the Blessed One’s eyebrows.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with many kinds of thousands of colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the directions were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has departed, who have abandoned dejection and pride, are the supreme causes for the world."
The Victors, who have conquered their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

At that time, O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Sages, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not manifest a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones manifest a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
"Those multitudes of people desire to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how these musicians have performed such an honor for me?
"I do, Venerable Sir."

Ānanda, by this root of merit, this generation of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishing of gifts, these musicians, having accomplished the individual awakening appropriate to their time, will in a future age become Pratyekabuddhas named Varṇasvara;
they will be compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, devoted to remote lodgings and seats, and will be the sole objects of veneration for the world.
"This gift of theirs is the very fact that they have developed a serene confidence of mind toward me."
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what roots of merit were performed by the Blessed One, the power of which is this?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata in former births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
These actions were performed and accumulated by me."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element,
but rather it is within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there appeared in the world a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Prabodhana— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
While wandering on a journey through the countryside, he arrived at a certain royal capital.
Now, the king’s pleasure grove was endowed with every excellence.
Then the Blessed One, having entered that grove, sat down leaning against a certain tree for the sake of showing favor to the king.
Then, having prepared a seat, he entered the meditative absorption on the fire-element (*tejodhātu*).
Thereupon, the consecrated Kṣatriya king entered the garden while music consisting of women was being played.
As the king was wandering through that garden, he saw the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Prabhodhana.
Seeing him— gracious, inspiring confidence, tranquil in mind, endowed with the highest self-control and serenity of heart, and blazing with splendor like a golden sacrificial pillar—
the king, filled with faith, together with his harem, awakened the Blessed One from that meditative absorption by playing various kinds of musical instruments.
He provided him with exquisite food and established him in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Because I performed an act of worship for the Perfectly Awakened One Prabhodhana, it is by that very cause that such honor has now been shown to me by the musicians."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 18: The Giver of Boons. (Ed. Speyer, Vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with the community of disciples. Now, in Śrāvastī, there was a certain adulterer who engaged in impure deeds.
He was seized by the king’s men and brought before the king;
then, the king, deeming him a criminal, ordered him to be executed.

With a garland of *karavīra* flowers bound around his neck, he was led out through the southern city gate by royal officers dressed in blue garments and bearing raised weapons, while his crimes were proclaimed at the thoroughfares, streets, crossroads, and junctions.

In this interval, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. It is indeed the nature of things that for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are great compassionate ones, who are engaged in favoring the world, who are guardians of the one [Dharma], who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, and who have crossed over the four floods with their feet firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power— [nothing remains hidden].
Those who have long practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), who are free from the five factors, who have transcended the five destinies,

who are endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), who are teachers of the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), who possess the power of the ten strengths (*daśabala*), whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand [gods] who wield mastery (*vaśavartin*).
Three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, his knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into hardship, calamity, and distress? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms?"
Who is leaning toward the states of woe?
Whom might I lift up from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation? To whom, sunk in the mire of sensual desires, might I extend a helping hand?
Whom, being destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereign mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?
Whose eyes, veiled by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance, shall I purify with the medicinal probe of the ointment of knowledge?
For whom, whose roots of virtue have not yet been planted, shall I plant them?
"Whose [roots of merit] planted shall I bring to maturity?
Whose matured [roots of merit] shall I liberate? And it is said:
"The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might indeed exceed its tide-line,"
But the Buddha would never let the time pass for those who are like calves to be tamed.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms. That man saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns— as if he were a walking mountain of gold.
Seeing him, who was like a mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides, he fell at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"I am a boar, O Blessed One."
"Grant me my desired life!
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, to King Prasenajit."
"Speak! Give this man back to me; I am going to ordain him.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached King Prasenajit of Kośala.
Having approached King Prasenajit of Kośala, he spoke in the name of the Blessed One: "Please grant permission;
the Blessed One wishes to ordain this man.
Recognizing that he was of a suitable disposition, King Prasenajit of Kośala gave his consent.
He was ordained and received full admission by the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states as being subject to decay, falling away, scattering, and destruction, [he realized the truth].

Through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to the axe or sandalwood, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings,
and turned away from existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indra.
The monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that everything intended by the Blessed One is accomplished merely by his thinking it.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very deeds were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births; their conditions have been fulfilled, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable."
"These actions were performed and accumulated by me;
who else shall experience them?
"Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element."
not in the water element, not in the fire element, and not in the wind element;
Furthermore, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-fields that actions performed— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen;
actions do not perish even after hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there appeared in the world a Truly Enlightened One named Indradhvaja—
a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One.
While wandering on a journey through the countryside, he arrived at a certain royal capital.
In that capital lived a brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and held the king’s seat of honor.
Then the Perfectly Awakened One, Indradhvaja, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered that royal capital for alms.

That brahmin saw the Perfectly Awakened One, Indradhvaja, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
And having seen him, like a tree cut down at its root, he fell at the feet of the Blessed One and said:
"I am a boar, O Sugata;
let the Blessed One sit upon this foremost seat."
Then the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Indradhvaja, sat upon the preeminent seat for the sake of favoring him.
Seated upon the preeminent seat, the Perfectly Awakened One Indradhvaja was praised with a hundred verses by that brahmin and provided with excellent food.
And he made a vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
because of that cause, the king, the ministers, and the citizens were all won over.
What do you think, monks? He who was that brahmin at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Because I performed worship for the Tathāgata Indradhvaja, as a result of that cause, I have experienced infinite happiness within saṃsāra.
Whatever I think of and whatever I pray for, all that comes to fulfillment.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We will honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Teacher, we will dwell in dependence upon him."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One spoke this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of the Kāśika Cloth] (AVŚ_19)
(Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.)
Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit,
and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples,
was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in dependence upon the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
When King Bimbisāra, accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of living beings, had perceived the Truths,

he then invited the Blessed One for the purpose of demonstrating his gratitude, for the purpose of performing worship to the Buddha, for the purpose of displaying the extent of his palace, and for the purpose of generating great reverence for the arising of a Buddha.
The Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, was invited to a meal at the royal palace;
and an order was issued to the citizens of Māgadha:
"Upon the Blessed One's entry into the city, worship must be performed with flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments."
The entire city of Rājagṛha should be cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;

it should be strewn with various flowers and adorned with raised banners and flags, extending from the Bamboo Grove as far as Rājagṛha, and all the roads in between should be covered with variegated cloths.
The ministers carried out everything accordingly.
Then King Bimbisāra himself held a hundred-ribbed parasol over the head of the Blessed One, while the remaining citizens held them over the thousand bhikṣus.

Then the Blessed One—tamed, with a tamed retinue; peaceful, with a peaceful retinue; liberated, with a liberated retinue; comforted, with a comforted retinue; disciplined, with a disciplined retinue; an Arhat, with a retinue of Arhats; free from passion, with a retinue free from passion;
gracious, with a gracious retinue—was like a bull surrounded by a herd of cattle, or like an elephant surrounded by a troop of young elephants.

Like a lion surrounded by a pack of fanged beasts, like a swan surrounded by a flock of swans, like Garuḍa surrounded by a host of birds, like a learned brahmin surrounded by a group of disciples, like a noble steed surrounded by a herd of horses, like a hero surrounded by a body of warriors,
like a guide surrounded by a multitude of travelers, and like a caravan leader surrounded by a company of merchants, he was like a guild-president surrounded by the citizens.

Surrounded by his assembly of ministers like a provincial king; surrounded by a thousand sons like a universal monarch; surrounded by the host of constellations like the moon; surrounded by a thousand rays like the sun; surrounded by the host of *gandharvas* like Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
surrounded by the host of *kumbhāṇḍas* like Virūḍhaka; surrounded by the host of *nāgas* like Virūpākṣa; and surrounded by the host of *yakṣas* like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Surrounded by the host of Vemacitrī asuras like Śakra surrounded by the hosts of the Thirty-three gods, like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahmakāyika gods,

like a tranquil ocean, like a rain-cloud filled with water, like a lordly elephant free from rut, with his senses perfectly subdued and his deportment unshaken, the Blessed One entered that city, attended by many unique qualities of a Buddha.
And when the Blessed One set his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s pillar, this great earth shook in six ways;
such wonders as these, and others besides, occurred at the Blessed One’s entry into the city.
Namely: narrow places became spacious;
elephants trumpeted, horses neighed, and bulls bellowed; various musical instruments within the houses sounded of their own accord;
and the blind regained their sight.
The deaf regain their hearing, the mute become capable of speech, those with impaired sense faculties obtain complete and perfect senses,
and those intoxicated by liquor become sobered.
Those who have drunk poison become free from poison;
those who are mutual enemies attain loving-kindness;
and pregnant women give birth safely.
Those bound in fetters are liberated; those without wealth obtain riches;
and the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas dwelling in the atmosphere scatter divine flowers.
Then the Blessed One began to enter the royal palace with such splendor.
King Bimbisāra himself, standing at the outer gatehouse, took water scented with gośīrṣa sandalwood for washing the feet and washed the feet of the Blessed One and the community of monks.
Perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, he served them a meal consisting of a hundred flavors.
When he had finished eating, he clothed him in garments from Kāśī;
and because of that, the citizens of Māgadha were won over.
Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Blessed One, where were these roots of merit performed by the Blessed One, such that there is such worship for the Blessed One and for the community of monks?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births; their causal conditions have been gathered, they have reached maturity, they have arrived like a surging flood, and they are inevitable."
"These actions were performed and accumulated by me;
who else shall experience them?
"Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element."
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-fields that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— reach their maturation.
Actions do not perish even after hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, a perfectly awakened Buddha named Kṣemaṃkara appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
While wandering on a tour of the countryside, he arrived at a certain royal capital.
The anointed Kṣatriya king heard that the Perfectly Awakened One, Kṣemaṃkara, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, had arrived at their royal capital.
Having heard this, endowed with great royal splendor and great royal majesty,
he approached the Blessed One, Kṣemaṃkara, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṃkara, he sat down to one side.
When the consecrated Kṣatriya king was seated to one side, the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṃkara exhorted him with the qualities that bring about awakening.
Then the king, having gained faith, invited the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṃkara to his palace and served him food of a hundred flavors,
and clothed him in garments worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
And after he had attained final nirvana, he caused a stupa to be built measuring one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height.
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Because I performed such worship for the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṃkara, I have experienced infinite happiness throughout cyclic existence."
Now, for that very same reason, King Bimbisāra has also performed such worship of me, the Tathāgata.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher."
"Having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of] Divine Food (Divyabhojana) [Avadānaśataka 20]

(Buddha the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with his community of disciples, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
In that place, there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, of great fortune, and of great enjoyment; his possessions were vast and extensive, he had accumulated wealth equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa,
he rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, and he was devoted to the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas).
He was won over by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and introduced to the teaching; he became exceedingly devoted to the Blessed One.
That householder was one of noble aspirations, and he said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Be my companion;
I wish to perform an offering to the Blessed One.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to that householder by remaining silent.
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, taking that householder with him, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this householder desires to feed the Blessed One together with the community of disciples.
May the Blessed One, out of compassion, grant him his consent.
The Blessed One gave his consent to that householder by remaining silent.
Then that householder, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, prepared food of a hundred flavors,
as well as flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana also requested Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Let the preparation for this householder be made.
Thereupon, Śakra, the lord of the gods, manifested the Bamboo Grove as the Nandana Grove,
and thousands of elephants resembling Airāvaṇa and Supratiṣṭhita.
They fanned him with yak-tail whisks;
and many thousands of gandharvas, such as Supriya, Pañcaśikha, Tumburu, and others, were brought forth, who played music with various kinds of exquisite instruments.
And there was divine food of ambrosia.
Then that householder, having attended upon the Blessed One with divine and human requisites, prostrated himself before the Blessed One’s feet with his whole body and began to make this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of things to be given, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide, in order to ferry across those beings who have not crossed over."
He is the liberator of those not yet liberated,
the consoler of those not yet consoled, and the one who leads to final nirvana those who have not yet attained it.
Then the Blessed One, having understood that householder’s succession of causes and succession of karma, manifested a smile.

It is indeed the nature of things that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some go downward and some go upward.
Those that go downward,
having gone to the hells of Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana,
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma;
Those who are in the hot hells fall into them cooled,
and those who are in the cold hells fall into them warmed;
thereby, the particular tortures of those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them:
"Have we, sirs, passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere;
rather, this is a being never seen before."
"By the power of this [emanation], our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having gained faith in the mind of that emanation, they exhaust the karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans,
where they become vessels for the truths.
Those that go upward [reach] the Cāturmahārājika, Trayastriṃśa,
Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika [heavens].
The Brahmapurohitas, Mahābrahmans, Parīttābhas, Apramāṇābhas, Ābhāsvaras, Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas,
Śubhakṛtsnas, Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Abṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, and Sudarśanas.
Having gone to the Akaniṣṭha gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
Shake off the army of death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut.
"For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya, having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering. Thus it was said;
then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wishes to prophesy past karma,
they disappear behind the Blessed One; if he wishes to prophesy future karma, they disappear in front of him.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell,
they disappear into the soles of his feet.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among animals,
they vanish into his heel; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts (preta), they vanish into his big toe.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans,
they disappear into his knees.
If he wishes to prophesy the kingdom of a powerful universal monarch (*balacakravartin*),
they disappear into the palm of his left hand;
if he wishes to prophesy the kingdom of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), [they disappear into the palm of his right hand].
If he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods,
they disappear into his navel.
If he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, they disappear into his mouth; if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they disappear into the crown of his head.
If he intends to prophesy unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they disappear into the *ūrṇā*. If he intends to prophesy unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they disappear into the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Then those rays of light, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the uṣṇīṣa of the Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of different colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the directions were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has departed and who have abandoned both dejection and pride, are the supreme causes for the world."
The Victors, who have conquered all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

At that time, O Hero, O Lord of Śramaṇas, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Sages, for the sake of the listeners who are filled with longing.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause.
"The multitudes of people desire to hear that for which the wise display a smile. Thus the Blessed One said.
"So it is, Ānanda; so it is.
Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how this householder has performed such an act of veneration for me?"
"So be it, Venerable One.

Ānanda, by this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishing of gifts, this householder shall realize the awakening that was fully accomplished over three incalculable eons; having fulfilled the six perfections cultivated through great compassion, he shall be known as Divyānnada."
They will become perfectly awakened Buddhas, endowed with the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion.
This is his gift of merit: the clarity of mind he has directed toward me.
When King Bimbisāra and the attendants of Magadha heard this account, they were filled with supreme wonder.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Blessed One, how this householder has honored the Blessed One together with the community of disciples with divine and human miraculous powers."
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
These actions were performed and accumulated by me."
Who else will experience [the result]?
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the air element,
but rather it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there appeared in the world a Perfectly Awakened One named Pūrṇa— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Then the Perfectly Enlightened One Pūrṇa, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, arrived at a certain royal capital.
The consecrated Kṣatriya king heard:
"The Perfectly Enlightened One Pūrṇa, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, has arrived at our royal capital."
Having heard this, the king, endowed with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, approached the Blessed One, Pūrṇa, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of Pūrṇa, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, he sat down to one side.
As the consecrated Kṣatriya king sat to one side, Pūrṇa, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, exhorted him with the dharmas that bring about awakening.

Then the anointed Kṣatriya king invited the Perfectly Awakened One Pūrṇa, together with the community of disciples, for three months to provide robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
And the Perfectly Awakened One Pūrṇa accepted the king's invitation by remaining silent.

Then the consecrated Kṣatriya king, understanding through his silence that the Perfectly Awakened One Pūrṇa had accepted [the invitation], attended upon him for three months with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
having caused a statue of the Blessed One made of jewels to be fashioned, he brought about the Buddha’s joy.
There, hundreds of thousands of living beings attained great faith;
and with that as their condition, they passed into final nirvana.
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Because I performed such worship for the Perfectly Awakened One, Pūrṇa,"
By that [merit], infinite happiness was experienced by me in saṃsāra;
and for that very reason, such worship as this was performed for the Tathāgata and for me by the guild-leader and Śakra.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The third chapter. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Candana, Padma, Cakra, Daśaśiras, Sūkṣmatvak, Śītadīpta, Nāvikā, Gandhamādana, Nirmala, and Valgusvara— this is the most excellent group.
AVŚ_21 Candana. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit,
and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples,
while wandering on a tour through the Magadha country, arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Now at that time, not far from the bank of the Ganges, there was a stūpa that had collapsed and was completely decayed by wind and sun.
When the monks saw it, they asked the Blessed One, "Blessed One, whose stūpa is this?
The Blessed One said:
"There was a Pratyekabuddha named Candana; [the Buddha spoke] regarding him.
The monks asked: "Lord, from where did the birth and the manifestation of the name of the Pratyekabuddha Candana arise?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, do you wish to hear how the Pratyekabuddha Candana was born and how his name came to be?"—
"Yes, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, monks, listen; attend well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, riots, and disturbances, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo.
The righteous King Dharmarāja governed his kingdom according to the Dharma.
Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other distinguished deities, such as:
the deities of groves, the deities of forests, the deities of crossroads, the deities of street corners, and the deities who receive sacrificial offerings.
He even supplicates the deities who are born together with him, who share his religious practice, and who are constantly attached to him;
for there is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of supplication,
but that is not so.
If it were so, each person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin). Rather, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three?
The mother and father are filled with passion and have come together;
the mother is healthy and in her fertile period;
and the gandharva is present.
Through the presence of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.
While he remained thus intent on his prayers,
there was a great lotus pond in his park.
There, a lotus of extraordinary size grew;
it increased day by day, yet it did not bloom.
Then the park-keeper informed the king.
The king said, "Let this lotus be examined.
Then, at another time, at sunrise, that lotus blossomed;
and upon the pericarp of that lotus, a boy sat remaining in the cross-legged posture.
He was handsome, beautiful to behold,
gracious, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, and a resonant voice.
He had well-knit eyebrows and a prominent nose; his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and his form was radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics.
From his mouth issued the fragrance of a lotus, and from his body the fragrance of sandalwood. Thereupon, the park-keeper informed the king.
Then the king, together with his ministers and his harem, went to that park. Upon seeing him, the boy addressed the king: "Come, father; I am the son for you who have no son."
Then the king, thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, said: "It is exactly so, my son, just as you say.
Thereupon the king, having plunged into the lotus pond, took the boy by his hand from the pericarp of a lotus and placed him upon the palm of his own hand.
Wherever that boy set his feet, there lotuses appeared;
therefore, he was given the name Candana.
When the boy Candana had gradually grown up and reached adulthood, the citizens petitioned the king: "O Lord, our city festival has arrived."
Therefore, Your Majesty ought to release Prince Candana;
he shall enjoy the festivals together with us,
and he will adorn the entire city with lotuses.
The king said, "So be it.

Thereupon Candana, adorned with all his ornaments and surrounded by the sons of ministers, went out from the royal palace to enjoy the city festival, accompanied by various musical instruments being played.
As he walked there, at every step he took, beautiful and delightful lotuses appeared beneath the placement of his feet.
As soon as they are touched by the rays of the sun, they wither and dry up.
Then, upon seeing that, there arose in that pure being of virtuous intention, who had planted roots of merit under previous Buddhas, a thorough mental attention (*yoniśo manasikāra*):
"Just as these lotuses shine when they have first appeared,
yet wither and dry up when scorched by the rays of the sun."
"This body, too, is just like that.
As he reflected, weighed, and examined this, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment became manifest before him.
While standing in the midst of that very assembly of people, he realized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.
When the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm offered him saffron robes,
he put them on and flew up into the expanse of the sky,
whereupon he began to perform various miraculous feats.
"Because of seeing him, the king, together with his ministers and merchants, attained great faith and planted various roots of merit.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, this is the origin and the manifestation of the name of the Pratyekabuddha Candana."
The monks asked the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by the Pratyekabuddha Candana, as a result of which his body is fragrant and his faculties are sharp?
The Blessed One said:
During the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he went forth as a monk;
there, he offered a sprinkling of perfumes and scattered flowers at the stūpa of hair and nails.
And by him the path to solitary awakening (pratyekabodhi) has been cultivated.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher."
"Having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
AVŚ 22: Padma.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with the community of his disciples.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
It was the custom in the Middle Country for monastery attendants to take lotuses and go to the marketplace to sell them.
Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Śrāvastī for alms.
A certain woman, having taken a young boy in her arms, entered the street; and that boy beheld the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns.

Seeing him, who was like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides, he was filled with faith; suddenly extending his arm, he took a lotus from the attendant and threw it upon the head of the Blessed One. Then that lotus became as large as a wagon-wheel.
Having become as large as a cartwheel,
it remained suspended in the sky above and followed after the Blessed One as he went.
While he was standing, [the light] remained.
Then the Blessed One emitted a radiance like ruby, which illuminated the entirety of Śrāvastī; and because of that, the king, the ministers, and the citizens were won over.
Then the Blessed One displayed a smile.
It is the natural law that whenever the Blessed Ones manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from his mouth; some go downward, and some go upward.
Those that go downward,
having gone to the hells of Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana,
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
In those hot hells, they fall as coolness;
in those cold hells, they fall as heat.
By that, the particular tortures of those beings are stilled.
It occurs to them:
"Sirs, have we indeed passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere."
"However, this is a being who has never been seen before; by his power, our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having developed serene faith in that emanation, they exhaust the karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans.
Therein they become vessels for the truths;
