those that go upward [reach] the realms of the Four Great Kings and the Thirty-three.
the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita,
Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha [heavenly realms].
Having gone to the gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
Shake off the army of death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thatched hut.
For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.

Then those rays, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One wished to proclaim past karma, [the rays would enter his back].
If he intends to prophesy the future, they disappear from behind the Blessed One. If he intends to prophesy the future, they disappear from the front.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear into the soles of his feet; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts, they disappear into his heel; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts,
they disappear into his big toe.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a human,
they disappear into his knees;
if he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch (*balacakravartin*), [they disappear into his right hand].
If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakravartin),
they disappear into the palm of his right hand.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the gods,
they disappear into his navel;
if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, [they disappear into his mouth].
If he intends to prophesy solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi),
they disappear into the circle of hair between his eyebrows (ūrṇā).
If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
they disappear into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, disappeared into the *ūrṇā* between the Blessed One’s eyebrows.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of different colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the directions were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he speaks these verses:
Free from rebirth, having abandoned dejection and pride,
the Buddhas are the supreme causes for the world.
The Victors, who have conquered all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.
O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized that at that very moment through your wisdom for the sake of the listeners who long for it,
[speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Sages.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose should be explained].
Those multitudes of people longed to hear it. // AVŚ_22.6 // Thus [it is said].
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is.
Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition."

"Ānanda, do you see this boy who, having conceived a sense of faith, threw a lotus at the Tathāgata? "I do, Venerable Sir. "Ānanda, by this root of merit, this arousal of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of the gift, this boy shall not go to a state of ruin for fifteen kalpas."
"Having experienced divine and human happiness, he will become a Pratyekabuddha named Padmottara.
This gift of his is the clarity of mind that arose toward me;
therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:"
"Whatever services we shall perform for the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas"—
thus, O monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
AVŚ_23 Cakram. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
At that time, a certain caravan leader in Rājagṛha had set out upon the great ocean;
his wife was in the prime of her youth.
She yearned and suffered for the sake of her husband,
yet her husband did not come.
She prostrated before Nārāyaṇa and made this vow:
"If he returns quickly to me,
I shall give you a golden wheel.
Then her husband returned swiftly from the great ocean with safety and well-being.
She had a golden wheel made;
surrounded by a group of female servants and taking the wheel along with perfumes, incense, and flowers, she set out for the temple.

In this interval, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. It is indeed the nature of things that for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are great compassionate ones, who are engaged in favoring the world, who are protectors of the one [Dharma], who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, who have crossed over the four floods, and whose feet are firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power— there is nothing hidden.
They had long cultivated the four bases of sympathy; they were free from the five hindrances; they had transcended the five destinies;

they were endowed with the six limbs; they had fulfilled the six perfections; they were richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment; they were teachers of the eightfold path; they were skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments; they were powerful with the ten powers; their fame filled the ten directions; and they were far superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods.
Three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, his knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone to the lower realms?"
Who is leaning toward the states of woe? Whom might I lift up from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation?
To whom, submerged in the mire of sensual desires, might I extend a hand to pull them out?
Whom, being destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereignty and mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?
Whose eyes, veiled by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance, shall I purify with the medicinal salve-stick of knowledge?
For whom, whose roots of virtue have not yet been planted, shall I plant them?
"Whose [roots of merit] planted shall I bring to maturity?
Whose matured [roots of merit] shall I liberate? And it is said:
"The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might even exceed its tide-line,"
But the Buddha would not let the time pass by for those who are like calves to be tamed.
The Blessed One perceived:
"Upon seeing me, this girl will plant the roots of merit for the awakening of a Pratyekabuddha.
Thereupon, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, he entered Rājagṛha for alms.
Then that girl saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body resplendent with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a radiance exceeding a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Upon seeing him, she gained faith and began to throw a golden wheel.

Then she was restrained by her maidservant, who said, "This is not Nārāyaṇa. Although being restrained, her intense faith caused her mind to be won over; she cast the golden wheel above the Blessed Buddha and offered perfumes and garlands.
Then the Blessed One displayed a smile.
It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, [light rays issue forth from their mouths...]
At that time, rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issued forth from his mouth; some went downward, and some went upward.
Those which went downward...
Having gone to the hells of Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana,
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma, they fall as a cooling balm upon those that are hot hells.
Those who are in the cold hells fall there transformed into heat;
by that, the particular tortures of those beings are stilled,
and they think to themselves:
"Have we, venerable sirs, passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
As soon as they see that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Indeed, sirs, we have not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere."
"However, this is a being who has never been seen before; by his power, our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having gained faith in their minds toward that emanation, they exhaust the karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans.
Wherein they become vessels for the truths;
those which go upwards [reach] the Cāturmahārājika and Trayastriṃśa [heavens].
[He saw] the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita,
Mahābrahman, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha [devas].
Having gone to the gods, they proclaim that "it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket.
For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Then those rays, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wished to declare past karma,
they would vanish behind the Blessed One's back.
If he wishes to prophesy future karma,
they disappear from the front;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear from below.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals, they disappear into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a human,
they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts,
they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans, they disappear into his knee.
If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch (*balacakravartin*),
they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he intends to prophesy the attainment of the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakravartin), they vanish into the palm of his right hand; if he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods, [they vanish into his navel].
If he wishes to prophesy awakening as a śrāvaka,
they disappear into his mouth.
If he wishes to prophesy solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi), they disappear into the circle of hair between the eyebrows (ūrṇā);
if he wishes to prophesy unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi), [they disappear into the crown of his head].
They disappear into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays of light, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, disappeared into the circle of hair between the Blessed One’s eyebrows.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of different colors..."
A bundle [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he speaks these verses:
"Free from rebirth, having abandoned wretchedness and pride,"
The Buddhas are the supreme causes for the world;
the Conquerors, who have vanquished their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a reason.

At that time, O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Munis, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
"Those multitudes of people long to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how this girl has thrown a golden wheel at the Tathāgata? "I see it, Venerable Sir."
"Ānanda, by this root of merit, this generation of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of the gift, this girl shall not go to a state of ruin for fifteen kalpas;
having experienced divine and human happiness, she will become a pratyekabuddha named Cakrāntara.
This is her gift: the clarity of mind she has felt toward me."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall perform services for the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 24: Daśaśiras (The Ten-Headed One) [Ed. Speyer, vol. I]

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples and the community of monks,
while wandering on tour through the Magadha countryside, arrived at the bank of the Ganges. From afar, those monks saw an ancient stūpa that had been broken down and shattered by wind, sun, and rain.
Having seen him, they asked the Blessed One again:
"Venerable Sir, whose stūpa is this?
The Blessed One said:
"Regarding this Pratyekabuddha Daśaśiras," the monks asked:
"Venerable sir, from where did the birth and the manifestation of the name of the Pratyekabuddha Daśaśiras arise?"
The Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, do you wish to hear it? They replied: "So be it, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, monks, listen and attend closely and well; I shall speak.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, and free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and violence.
Free from thieves and disease, and abundant with rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo,
that righteous King of Dharma ruled his kingdom according to the Dharma.
That king, being childless and longing for a son, made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other distinguished deities.
Namely: he entreats the deities of groves, the deities of forests, the deities of crossroads, the deities of triple junctions, and the deities who receive offerings;
he also entreats those deities who are innate, those who share his religious path, and those who are constantly attached to him.
And thus he remains intent on such entreaties.
In his park there was a great lotus pond, covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses, and adorned with birds such as swans, ruddy geese, and ducks.
Therein grew a lotus of immense size, free of thorns, which had arisen spontaneously;
it increased day by day, yet did not bloom.
Then the park-keeper informed the king, and the king said:
"Let this lotus be protected."
Then, at another time, at sunrise, that lotus blossomed;
upon the pericarp of that lotus sat a boy in the cross-legged posture,
handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, golden-hued, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, and a broad forehead.

He had a loud voice, spoke with a resonant tone, and possessed a prominent nose; he was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and his body was radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics.
Upon seeing him, the park-keeper informed the king.
Having heard this, the king went to that garden accompanied by his ministers and his harem.
The king saw him shining thus upon the pericarp of a lotus.

Having seen him, he was thrilled, satisfied, and delighted; filled with exultation, joy, and gladness, he plunged into the lotus pond, seized him, and having brought him to his own home with great honor, he presented him to the ascetics, brahmins, and fortune-tellers.
Having celebrated the birth festival for twenty-one days—three times seven—he gave him the name Daśaśiras.

The ten-headed boy was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him. He was raised and nurtured by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and various other most excellent and refined provisions.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.

And that prince was faithful, auspicious, of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, desirous of the Dharma, and affectionate toward his subjects.
He saw his father established in the duties of kingship, yet committing blameworthy deeds.
And having seen this, the prince was deeply moved and addressed his father:
"Father, grant me permission;
I shall go forth into homelessness in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
When he was permitted by his father, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith went forth from the home to the homeless life.
Without any instruction, he brought the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to manifestation and realized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.
He flew up into the sky and performed various miraculous feats in the presence of his father.
Then he was invited by the king for alms for three months;
exhausted by the burden of carrying his body, he displayed various miracles and, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted, attained final nirvāṇa.
This is his stūpa.
Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Daśaśiras such that he was not conceived in a mother's womb?"
"Born from a lotus."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Daśaśiras; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
Who else shall experience the results of the actions performed and accumulated by Daśaśiras?"
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind; rather, both auspicious and inauspicious actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one eons ago, a Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī.

Then, in the forenoon, the perfectly enlightened Vipaśyin dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, entered the royal capital of Bandhumatī for alms.
At that time, a certain caravan leader, carrying a lotus, set out along the street.
Then he beheld the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,

his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, he threw that lotus toward him.
As soon as it was thrown, it became as large as a cartwheel above the Blessed One; as the Blessed One walked, it followed him, and as he stood still, it remained stationary.
When the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin had prophesied that the caravan leader would attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha,
he returned to his own home with a heart thrilled, satisfied, and gladdened;
at that time, his wife Prajāpatī, who was in the process of giving birth, cried out with a loud voice.
He asked his attendant,
"What is this?
and she explained it to him.
Then the caravan leader, filled with agitation, began to make a formal vow:
"May I never again be born within the womb of a mother in saṃsāra."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the caravan leader, he is this ten-headed Pratyekabuddha."
By that root of merit, for twenty-one eons he was never again born from a mother’s womb;
and in his final existence, this was his splendor.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall perform services for the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas"—
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 25:
Sūkṣmatvak (The Subtle-Barked One)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now at that time, in Śrāvastī, there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with abundant assets and provisions, and possessing great wealth and property; he had many friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations.
That householder was faithful, noble, of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma.
It occurred to him:

"These enjoyments have the nature of the moon reflected in water; they are like a mirage, impermanent, unstable, unreliable, subject to change, and common to those who wield the five fierce punishments.
What if I were to extract the essence from these pithless enjoyments?
Thinking thus, he invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for a meal.
And the house was cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;
it was sprinkled with sandalwood water, perfumed with the fragrant smoke of various incense burners, and strewn with diverse flowers.
Flower-seats were prepared;
then, having made ready delicious, cool drinks and various kinds of food and edibles, he informed the Blessed One of the time by means of a messenger: "It is time, Venerable Sir."
"The meal is ready; may the Blessed One now consider it the proper time.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached the residence of that householder.
Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.

Then that householder, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent food. Having personally satisfied and served them, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he took a lower seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the householder with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he became silent.
Then that householder, having gained faith, prostrated at his feet and cultivated a resolute intention.
Then the Blessed One displayed a smile.
It is the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some of them go downward.

they disappear into the palm of his left hand.

If he intends to prophesy the attainment of the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartirājya*), they disappear into the palm of his right hand; if he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they disappear into his right shoulder.
If he wishes to prophesy awakening as a disciple (śrāvakabodhi),
they disappear into his mouth.
If he intends to prophesy solitary enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*),
they disappear into the *ūrṇā*;
if he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*), [they disappear into the uṣṇīṣa].
They disappear into the uṣṇīṣa.
Then those rays of light, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, disappeared into the ūrṇā-hair between the Blessed One's eyebrows.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with many thousands of colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he speaks these verses:
"The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has departed, who have abandoned wretchedness and pride, are the supreme causes for the world."
The Conquerors, who have vanquished all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized that at that very moment through your wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Sages, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
Those multitudes of people long to hear it. Thus [spoke] the Blessed One:
"So it is, Ānanda; so it is.
Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how this girl has performed such an act of veneration for me?"
"So be it, Venerable One.

Ānanda, by virtue of this root of merit, this resolve of mind, and this renunciation of the gift, this girl shall become a Pratyekabuddha named Gandhamādana. This is her gift: the clarity of faith she has placed in me."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall perform services for the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 29 Nirmala (edited by Speyer, Vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas—thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with the community of disciples. At that time, there was a certain monastery attendant in Śrāvastī.
Taking his tooth-stick, he enters Śrāvastī,
while a fortune-teller stands at the gate and says:
"Whoever shall eat this tooth-stick shall eat food of a hundred flavors.
That speech was heard by the monastery attendant.
Having heard this, he thought:
"To whom should I give this tooth-stick,
so that I might receive great honor?"
This thought occurred to him:
"This Buddha, the Blessed One, is the moving field of merit in this world with its mobile and immobile beings, yielding great fruit that is never barren.
What if I were to give this to the Buddha, the Blessed One?"
Then that monastery attendant, taking a tooth-stick, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that monastery attendant said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, please accept this tooth-stick from me out of compassion.
Then the Blessed One, for the sake of favoring the monastery attendant, extended his gold-colored arm, which resembled the trunk of an elephant, and took it;
having taken it, he ate it.
Having chewed it, he discarded it before the park-keeper;
having discarded that tooth-stick, he buried it in the ground.
As soon as it was buried, at that very moment, a great banyan tree—abounding in branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, and perfectly circular—came into existence right there.
Sitting in whose shadow the Blessed One taught the Dharma to many gods and humans;
thereupon, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada provided the Blessed One with food of a hundred flavors.
Then that monastery attendant, his mind won over by the service rendered to the Blessed One and by the miracle, fell at the feet [of the Buddha] like a tree cut at its root and began to make a vow:
"By this root of merit, may I realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
Then the Blessed One displayed a smile.

It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some [of these rays] go downward.
Some go downward, and some go upward; those that go downward, [proceed as follows].

Having gone to the hells— Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma— they descend into those that are hot hells as a cooling rain.
Those who are in the cold hells fall there transformed into heat;
thereby, the particular tortures of those beings are allayed.
It occurs to them thus:
"Have we, venerable sirs, passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?
To inspire faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Sirs, we have certainly not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere."
"Moreover, this is a being who has never been seen before; by his power, our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having developed faith in the mind toward that emanation, they exhaust that karma which was to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans.
Therein they become vessels for the truths;
those that go upward [reach] the realms of the Four Great Kings and the Thirty-three.

[He saw] the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin [devas]; the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahman [devas]; the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara [devas]; the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna [devas];
the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala [devas]; and the Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha [devas].
Having gone to the gods, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," and they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!"
Shake off the army of death, as an elephant shakes down a hut of reeds.
For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wished to proclaim past karma, they would vanish behind his back.
If he wishes to prophesy future karma,
they disappear from the front;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear from below.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals, they disappear into the sole of his foot;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a hungry ghost,
they disappear into his heel.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts,
they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among humans, they disappear into his knee.
If he wishes to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch,
they disappear into his left palm.

If he intends to prophesy the attainment of the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakravartin), they vanish into the palm of his right hand; if he intends to prophesy rebirth among the gods, they vanish into his navel.
If he intends to prophesy awakening as a disciple (śrāvakabodhi),
they disappear into his mouth.
If he wishes to prophesy solitary enlightenment (pratyekabodhi),
they vanish into the circle of hair between the eyebrows;
if he wishes to prophesy unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi), [they vanish into the uṣṇīṣa].
They disappear into the crown of the head.
Then those rays, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the ūrṇā-hair between the Blessed One’s eyebrows.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with thousands of diverse colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the quarters were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he spoke these verses:
"Free from rebirth, having abandoned wretchedness and pride..."
The Buddhas are the supreme causes for the world;
the Jinas, who have conquered their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a reason.

At that time, O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized it through your own wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Sages, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
Those multitudes of people long to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how this monastery attendant has performed such an act of honor for me? "I do, Venerable Sir."
"Ānanda, by this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of the gift, this park-keeper shall not go to a state of ruin for thirteen aeons.
In his final existence, his final dwelling, his final physical support, and his final acquisition of a self-body, he will become a pratyekabuddha named Nirmala.
This is his gift: the clarity of mind toward me."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. (AVŚ 30) Valgusvarāḥ.
(Buddha, the Blessed One,) was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.

At that time, many members of a social club, intoxicated by liquor, were dancing and singing while various musical instruments—lutes, drums, and small kettledrums—were being played; they had garlands of noble flowers, such as blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and vārṣika jasmine, draped around their necks.
Dressed in exquisite garments, they were departing from Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Blessed One entered Śrāvastī for alms.

Those members of the guild saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, and graced by a fathom-wide halo of light.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides;
at the mere sight of him, their intoxication from liquor vanished.
Then, free from intoxication and pride, with minds inclined toward serene faith, they performed services for the Blessed One with dance, song, and instrumental music,
and they scattered blue lotuses over the Blessed One.
Once scattered over the Blessed One, they remained like a blue gabled pavilion, a blue parasol, and a blue canopy.
And they followed the Blessed One as he went, and remained still as he stood;
and a blue radiance was emitted by the Blessed One.
By which Śrāvastī was established with a radiance resembling that of sapphire gems.
Then those members of the assembly, having gained faith, cultivated the thought: "By this root of merit, may we realize individual enlightenment."
Then the Blessed One displayed a smile.

It is indeed the natural law that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile, at that moment rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue forth from their mouths; some of them go downward.
Some go upward;
those that go downward [fall into] Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci.
Having gone to the hells— Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma— they fall cooled upon those that are hot hells,
and they fall heated upon those that are cold hells.
By that means, the specific causes of suffering for those beings are stilled;
it occurs to them:
"Have we, sirs, passed away from here?"
"Or have they been reborn elsewhere? In order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation.
Upon seeing that emanation, it occurs to them:
"Indeed, venerable sirs, we have not passed away from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere;
rather, this is a being whom we have never seen before."
"By the power of this [emanation], our specific causes of suffering have been stilled.
Having gained faith in the mind toward that emanation, they exhaust the karma to be experienced in hell and take rebirth among gods and humans,
where they become vessels for the truths.
Those that go upward [reach] the Cāturmahārājika, Trayastriṃśa,
Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, and Brahmapurohita [heavens].

Having gone to the gods of Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
And they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut! (AVŚ 30.1)
For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Then those rays of light, having circled the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One wished to proclaim past karma, they would vanish behind his back.
If he wishes to prophesy future karma,
they disappear from the front;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth in hell, they disappear from below.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the animals, they disappear into the soles of his feet;
if he wishes to prophesy rebirth as a hungry ghost,
they disappear into his heels.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the hungry ghosts,
they disappear into his big toe; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among human beings, they disappear into his knee.
If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch (*balacakravartin*),
they disappear into his left palm.
If he intends to prophesy a universal monarch’s sovereignty,
they disappear into the palm of his right hand.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among the gods,
they disappear into his navel;
if he wishes to prophesy the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, [they disappear into his mouth].

they disappear into the circle of hair between his eyebrows (ūrṇā).

Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, asked the Blessed One:
"Variegated with many thousands of colors..."
A mass [of light] issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the directions were illuminated on all sides,
just like the sun as it rises.
And he spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, from whom rebirth has departed and who have abandoned both dejection and pride, are the supreme causes for the world."
The Victors, who have conquered all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

O Hero, O Śramaṇa, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized that at that very moment through your wisdom, [speak] with firm and supreme words, O Bull among Munis, for the sake of the listeners who long for it.
Dispel the doubt that has arisen with auspicious words.
The Lords, the Fully Awakened Ones, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
for whatever purpose the Wise Ones display a smile, [that purpose must be explained].
"Those multitudes of people long to hear it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so."
"Ānanda, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Do you see, Ānanda, how these village elders have performed such an act of honor for me? "I see it, Venerable Sir."

"Ānanda, by this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of gifts, these members of the assembly shall not fall into the lower realms for twenty intermediate kalpas.
In their final existence, their final dwelling, their final physical support, and their final acquisition of a body, they will become Pratyekabuddhas named Valgusvara.
This is their gift: the clarity of mind toward me."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall perform services for the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Fourth Chapter. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Padmaka, Kavaḍa, Dharmapāla, and likewise Śibi; Surūpa, Maitrakanyaka, Śaśa, and Dharmagaveṣin;
Anāthapiṇḍada and Subhadra—this is the group that has been proclaimed.

AVŚ 31: Padmaka. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
At the time of autumn, monks were afflicted by disease; they were pale-yellow, emaciated in body, and weak of limb.
The Blessed One, however, was free from affliction, free from illness, healthy, and strong.
Upon seeing him, the monks questioned the Blessed One:
"Behold, venerable sir, these monks are afflicted by an autumnal disease; they are jaundiced, their bodies are emaciated, and their limbs are weak.
But the Blessed One has few ailments, little discomfort, is strong, and is of a healthy constitution."
And he is endowed with a digestive faculty that ripens food evenly.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very deeds were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
These deeds were performed and accumulated by me."
Who else will experience [the result]?
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the air element,
but rather it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Padmaka reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, free from strife, quarrels, riots,
and disturbances, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo— entire and without thorns.
He ruled the kingdom as if it were his only son, free from thorns.

That king was faithful, noble, and of virtuous intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of all, and one who renounced everything without attachment.
And she was engaged in great generosity.
At that time, in Vārāṇasī, a disease arose due to an imbalance of the seasons or an imbalance of the bodily humors;
for the most part, the beings there were afflicted with jaundice.
Then, upon seeing them, compassion arose in the king:
"I must provide protection for these beings and medical treatment.
Thereupon, that king assembled all the physicians residing throughout his realm and, having observed the underlying causes, dispositions, and latent tendencies of those beings, [proceeded].
He himself undertook medical treatment and the gathering of all necessary medicines. Then, as those beings were being treated, a great deal of time passed.
And even though they were provided with physicians, medicinal substances, and attendants, they could not be cured.
Thereupon, the king summoned all the physicians and, filled with respect, asked them again: "What is the reason that I am so difficult for you to treat?"

The physicians, having deliberated upon the various merits and defects, spoke with one mind: "Your Majesty, we perceive that this condition arises from an imbalance of the seasons and an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
Nevertheless, Your Majesty, there is a single remedy: a fish named Rohita."
"If there were someone who had obtained it, they could be cured.
Thereupon, the king began to search for the Rohita fish.
Although he was sought by many spies, he was not found;
thereupon, they informed the king.
Then, at another time, the king went out for a journey abroad.
And those afflicted by disease, standing together in a single group, said to the king:
"Protect us, O Great King, from this disease!"
"Give me my life!

Then the king, being addressed with words that were piteous, distressed, and faltering, and having heard those words of the sick man, his heart trembled with compassion; with a face clouded by tears, he reflected:
"Of what use to me is such a life as this, or such sovereignty, power, and dominion?"
Thinking, "I am not able to bring peace to others who are afflicted by suffering," the king,

having reflected thus, made a great distribution of wealth, established his eldest son in the sovereignty and lordship of the kingdom, asked his kinsmen for forgiveness, asked the citizens and ministers for forgiveness, comforted the distressed, and [undertook] the eightfold [path].
Having undertaken the vow and ascended to the upper terrace of the palace, he scattered incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
and began to make a formal aspiration facing the east:
"By that truth, by that word of truth, through which, having seen beings fallen into great calamity and oppressed by disease, I renounce my own dear life."
"By this truth, by these words of truth, may I appear here in this river as a great rohita fish!
Having said this, he threw himself from the palace roof.
As soon as he fell, he passed away and was reborn as a great rohita fish in the river sand.
Then the deities raised a cry throughout the entire realm:
"This great rohita fish has appeared in the river sand; he is like nectar for those tormented by the great disease of long-standing suffering."
As soon as they heard this, a great multitude of people emerged with weapons in their hands and baskets, and began to carve out my flesh while I was still alive using various sharp instruments.
While his body was being cut apart, that Bodhisattva, pervading them all with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), his face bathed in tears, reflected:
"It is a great gain for me, truly well-attained, that these beings shall find happiness through my own flesh and blood."
Thus, by this means, for twelve years he sustained sentient beings with his own flesh and blood,
yet his mind did not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
When that disease of those beings had subsided, then that Rohita fish uttered a voice:
"Listen, O beings!
I am that King Padmaka."
For your sake, I have taken up this kind of physical existence by means of sacrificing my own life;
therefore, arouse a mind of serene faith toward me.
When I [attain] unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment...
"I shall attain perfect awakening; then, having completely liberated you from ultimate illness, I will establish you in the final, ultimate nirvana."

Upon hearing this, that multitude of people—the king, the ministers, and the citizens—attained faith; they honored him with flowers, incense, garlands, and ointments, and began to make this aspiration:
"O performer of what is exceedingly difficult, when you have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment..."
"Then we would have been those disciples.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Padmaka—was he someone else? It was I."
Because such acts of renunciation were performed by me, I have experienced infinite happiness within saṃsāra;
even now, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [I continue to experience it].
I am endowed with a digestive faculty that cooks evenly,
by which what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly and comfortably digested; I have few afflictions and am free from disease.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall cultivate compassion toward all sentient beings.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 32 Kavaḍa (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with the community of disciples.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

Monks, if beings knew the fruit and the ripening of giving and the sharing of gifts as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of sharing gifts, then even one who has only the very last morsel, the final mouthful, would not consume it without first giving it away and sharing it, provided they find a worthy recipient.

And may the thought of stinginess that has arisen in them not remain, taking hold of their minds. For it is because sentient beings do not know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts,
as I know the fruit of giving and the ripening of the fruit of the distribution of gifts.
Therefore, they consume without having given or shared, with a mind possessed by grasping;
and the state of stinginess that has arisen in them persists, completely taking hold of their minds.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having spoken this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
"If only beings would understand in the manner proclaimed by the Great Seer!"
So that the ripening of this sharing may become of great benefit.
They should not consume [food] without having given it away, nor should they be stingy; nor should a mind of attachment ever arise in them. (AVŚ 32.2)
But because fools, shrouded by the darkness of delusion, do not understand this,
sentient beings therefore consume [food] with a mind of grasping.
And the stinginess that has arisen in them persists, completely taking possession of their minds.
When this sutra had been spoken by the Blessed One, the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that the Blessed One speaks in praise of giving and describes the ripening of the fruit of giving and sharing.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, what is the wonder here that the Tathāgata speaks in praise of giving and describes the fruit and ripening of the distribution of gifts? It is because in the past, for the sake of a beggar who had come to my door, I renounced my own mouthful of food."
Listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly;
I shall speak.

In the past, monks, in a time long gone by, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people. It was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest;
it was devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo—entire and without thorns.
[He ruled] without thorns;
he governed the kingdom as if it were his only son.

That king was faithful, auspicious, and of virtuous intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of everything, and one who renounced without attachment.
And "great" refers to her generosity;
at another time, a great famine arose, resembling the famine at the end of an eon.

Then those masses of people, terrified by the fear of famine and the calamitous time, their throats and cheeks withered by hunger, resembling the abodes of hungry ghosts, gathered together in a single body, approached the king and said: "Victory and long life to Your Majesty!
Protect us from this fear of famine;
grant us our lives!"
Then the king addressed the steward:
"O man, is there food and drink in the storehouse that would suffice for both us and this multitude of people?
Having heard this, the steward replied:
"Your Majesty, having counted the crops, I shall inform you.

Then, after those skilled in calculation had performed the reckoning, they declared: "For all the inhabitants of the realm, there will be one morsel of food per day, and for the king, two morsels, for such a length of time.
Thereupon, the king summoned the masses of people and said:
"Therefore, sirs, come day after day to the royal palace, eat a morsel of food, and then depart.
Thereupon, they came every day, each ate one morsel of food, and departed as they pleased.
Now, a certain brahmin was not present at that accounting;
having heard [the news] from others, he said to the king:
"Your Majesty, I have heard the account from those who have traveled through the countryside."
"Let a morsel be given to me as well. Thereupon, the king gave one of his two morsels to the brahmin and proceeded to consume the other morsel, which was common to all people.
The knowledge and vision of Śakra, lord of the gods, was directed downward,
and this thought occurred to him:
"Alas, the King of Vārāṇasī is performing a most difficult task!"
"What if I were to test him?
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having transformed himself into the guise of a brahmin, approached the king at mealtime; after greeting him with wishes for victory and long life, he said:
"Being hungry, show me favor with a morsel of your own food.

Thereupon, out of compassion for his resolve, the king, having abandoned his own life, gave his own morsel to the brahmin and undertook fasting. By this means, he underwent the deprivation of six meals.
Seeing that great multitude of people eating, he attained supreme joy.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing the king’s exceedingly difficult resolve, caused his disguise as a brahmin to vanish; standing there in his own form, he congratulated the king:
"Excellent, excellent, Great King! You have won over [the world]."
"By this difficult undertaking of yours, we have found a protector, and this body of people has found a guardian such as you."
"Let no harm come to the seeds in your realm; let all seeds be sown.
On the seventh day, I shall release such a rain from the realm of Indra that all crops will come to fruition."
The king acted accordingly;
and Śakra likewise released such a great rain that the famine was averted and abundance appeared.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Brahmadatta, I am he.
While such a famine was occurring, I gave such gifts as these solely by means of relinquishing my own life."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall give gifts; we shall perform meritorious deeds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. [The Story of Dharmapāla] (AVŚ 33)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
When the deluded man Devadatta, for the purpose of killing the Blessed One, released the noble elephant Dhanapālaka,
scattered poison-dust over the well,
and dispatched assassins;
For a long time he has been the Blessed One’s murderer, adversary, and enemy;
yet the Blessed One has not responded to him with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, or a mind of compassion.
Then the monks asked the Blessed One:
Behold, Blessed One, how far this Devadatta has gone in striving for the Blessed One's death,
while the Blessed One remains toward him with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of compassion.

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what is the wonder here that now the Tathāgata is free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, and is omniscient?"
He is the knower of all aspects, who has attained mastery over all knowledge and its objects.

Listen to this: in the past, when I was still subject to passion, hatred, and delusion, and while remaining in the state of a young boy, I strove to kill him; yet even then, my mind was not at all corrupted toward him.
Listen to that.
Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, a king named Brahmadatta reigned in the city of Vārāṇasī. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo—entirely without thorns or obstacles.
He protects his kingdom as if it were an only son.

That king is faithful, auspicious, and of noble intention; he is dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma. He is affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of everything, and one who renounces without attachment, abiding in great generosity.
That king had a queen named Durmati, who was fierce, wrathful, and impulsive.
He had an only son named Dharmapāla, born from that very same Durmati;
and that Dharmapāla was compassionate, faithful, noble, and of virtuous intent.
He was one who had set out for his own welfare and the welfare of others; he was compassionate, magnanimous, desirous of the Dharma, and affectionate toward his subjects.
He was beloved, dear, cherished, and pleasing to behold by all the brahmins and householders of Vārāṇasī.
And he, having gone into the presence of his preceptor, studied writing together with the other boys.

Then, at another time during the spring season, when the trees were in full bloom and the forest groves resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvaka birds, the king went out to the pleasure gardens accompanied by his queen and surrounded by the women of the harem.
While the king was sporting there in the garden with the ladies of the harem, Queen Durmati became angry, overcome by jealousy and resentment.
And the king set aside for her half of the yellow [portion]. Enraged, she sent a message to the king:
"I would drink the blood of my son."
"If I were to drink half of what you have drunk," he said,
"for one who indulges in sensual pleasures, there is indeed no evil deed that cannot be committed.
Thereupon, although King Brahmadatta was righteous, because his passion for sensual desire had not subsided, he blazed with the fire of anger even while being consoled by the women of the harem.
Then, his anger having increased, he gave the command:
"Go, cut Dharmapāla's throat and make him drink this blood!"
Then, having heard this, Prince Dharmapāla, who was staying in the boys' quarters, began to weep and said:
"Fie upon the commonality of sentient beings in saṃsāra,
wherein, under the sway of anger, they abandon even their own son who has issued from their very limbs!"
Then Dharmapāla, adorned with all his ornaments, fell at his father's feet and said:
"Please, father, be gracious!
Do not abandon me, who am without fault."
"Moreover, sons are beloved by all their fathers.
The king said:
"My son, if your mother consents,"
"I too forgive you.
Thereupon Dharmapāla, weeping, approached his mother, prostrated at her feet with palms joined in reverence, and said:
"Mother, please forgive me."
"Do not deprive me of my life!
Though she spoke these words with syllables full of compassion, distress, and faltering, she was not granted mercy.
Then, the executioners cut Prince Dharmapāla’s throat with a sharp weapon, and the wicked queen was made to drink his blood.
And Durmati did not experience remorse;
the prince Dharmapāla, too, having developed a mind of faith toward those who had killed his parents, passed away.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the prince named Dharmapāla, I was he. And she was Queen Durmati."
This is Devadatta.
Even then, when he had fallen into the hands of my executioners, I gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward him;
even now, as he is intent on killing me, I possess a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of compassion for him.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. ****** AVŚ 34 Śibi (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed great merit.
Receiving robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, [the Blessed One],
together with the community of disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Now at that time, there were two assemblies of monks in Śrāvastī:
one on the full moon of Āṣāḍhā at the commencement of the rainy season retreat, and the second on the full moon of Kārttikī.
There, the monks would bake their alms-bowls.
They were washing robes and sewing rag-robes.
At that time, a certain monk who wished to sew a robe was unable to thread the needle through its eye.
With words faltering, piteous, and drawn out by compassion, he said:
"Who in the world desires merit?
And the Blessed One was walking back and forth on a walkway not far from him.
Then the Blessed One, whose voice was as deep, sweet, clear, and pleasing as that of a kalaviṅka bird or a drum, extended his arm—which resembled the trunk of an elephant—and said:
"Monk, I am one who desires merit in the world.

Thereupon, having heard the Blessed One’s voice endowed with the five qualities, that monk became agitated; he very hurriedly took the Blessed One’s hand, placed it upon his own head, and said: "Blessed One,"
"With this hand of yours, the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom have been accumulated for three incalculable eons.
Then the Blessed One said to him: "O monk, I am not yet satiated with merits."
"O monk, I have obtained the essence through my merits;
therefore, I am not yet satiated."
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that the Blessed One is never satiated by formations consisting of merit."

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what is the wonder here that now the Tathāgata— free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, and fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair— is omniscient?"

He is the one who possesses the knowledge of all modes, having attained mastery over all forms of knowledge and the objects of knowledge. As for me, in the past, I was possessed by passion, possessed by hatred, possessed by delusion; I was not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; and I was insatiable with regard to formations consisting of merit.
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly,
and I shall speak.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, a king named Śibi reigned in the capital city of Śibighoṣā. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo—entirely without blemish and free from thorns.
He protected the kingdom as if it were his only son.

And that King Śibi was faithful, auspicious, and of virtuous intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of everything, and one who renounced without attachment.
She was devoted to great generosity;
rising very early in the morning, she would enter the sacrificial enclosure and distribute food to those seeking food.
He gives clothing to those who seek clothing;
he practices the relinquishment of wealth, grain, silver, gold, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, and so forth.
And he does not reach satiety with those conditioned factors consisting of merit. Having entered the inner apartments, he provides food and clothing for the people of the inner apartments,
as well as for the princes, the ministers, the army commanders, and the merchants and country folk.
Then this thought occurred to King Śibi:
"By him, those who have become human beings have been fully satisfied; only the small creatures remain."
"By what means am I to satisfy them?
Having surrendered all his wealth and possessions, clad in a single garment, and with nothing remaining but his own body, he fell into deep reflection.
This thought occurred to him:
"I offer my own body to the small creatures.
Having thus carved his own body with a weapon, he casts his body down where the gadflies and mosquitoes are and stands there;
he satiates them with his blood as if they were his only beloved son.

The knowledge and vision of Śakra, lord of the gods, extends downward; he thought to himself: "This King Śibi is performing such deeds for the sake of sentient beings—what could be the reason for this?"
Or out of compassion?
"What if I were to find out about him?
Then [he saw one] with eyes like crushed collyrium and the color of a sword.
Having transformed himself into the form of a vulture, he approached King Śibi and proceeded to pluck out his eyes with his beak;
yet the king did not fall into terror.
However, looking at the vulture with eyes wide with loving-kindness, he said: "Child,
let there be affection for that which you take from my body."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, being thus won over, manifested himself in the guise of a brahmin and, standing before King Śibi, said:
"Excellent, O king!
Let these two eyes be given."
The king said: "Great Brahmin, let whatever you desire be taken;
there shall be no obstacle for me in this matter.
Thereupon, Śakra, lord of the gods, being even more deeply pleased, caused his brahmin disguise to vanish, stood in his own form, and, encouraging the king, spoke:
Excellent, excellent, O King! Your intellect is well-settled,
and your resolve is unshakable.
Great compassion has followed you toward sentient beings, since you are indeed fearless regarding those things that cause terror;
before long, by means of this resolve, you shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Śibi, I am he.
Even then, there was no satiety with formations consisting of merit."
It was even so in the past;
therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"Whatever gifts we shall give," [we shall give with a pure mind].
"We shall perform meritorious deeds.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One spoke thus.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 35: Surūpa (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, the wealthy, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, receiving robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
When the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion, taught the Dharma most sweetly to the fourfold assembly,
Like honey free from bees,
the assembly of many hundreds listened to the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with unwavering minds.
When [he had spoken] thus with his senses, the monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how these beings have become vessels for the jewel of the Dharma and consider it necessary to listen to it with reverence.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, listen to how the Dharma was heard and mastered by the Tathāgata with a sense of reverence; pay close and careful attention, and I shall speak."

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Surūpa reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo—entirely without thorns or obstacles.
He protected the kingdom as if it were his only son.

That king was faithful, auspicious, and of virtuous intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of all things, and one who renounced everything without attachment.
She was devoted to great renunciation.
And that king had a queen named Sundarikā, who was beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing.
He had an only son named Sundaraka, who was endowed with all major and minor limbs, beloved, handsome, dear, pleasing, patient, and not contrary [to his father's will].
Then, at another time, a desire for the Dharma arose in King Surūpa.
He summoned all his ministers and said to them:
"O village chiefs, seek out the Dharma for me;
the Dharma pleases me."
Then those ministers, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the king:
"O Great King, the Dharma is difficult to encounter.
It is heard, O Great King, that through the arising of the Buddhas in the world, the arising of the Dharma occurs."
Then the king, having fastened a golden basket to the top of his banner, caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout the entire realm:
"To whoever shall preach the Dharma to me, I shall give this golden basket."
"I shall honor him with great hospitality.
Then, a long time passed,
yet no teacher of the Dharma was found.
Then that king, for the sake of dharma, yearned and was consumed with grief.
And Śakra, the lord of the gods, directed his vision downward;
he saw the king being tormented for the sake of the Dharma.
This thought occurred to him:
"What if I were to test King Surūpa?
Then, having manifested himself in the form of a yakṣa with deformed hands, feet, and eyes, he stood in the midst of the great assembly and said this to the king:
"Are you not indeed a seeker of the Dharma?"
"I shall speak the Dharma to you.
Then, having given rise to joy and gladness from hearing the Dharma, the king said this to the yakṣa:
"Speak, Guhyaka; I shall listen to the Dharmas."
The Guhyaka said:
"O Great King, indeed, the dharmas favor one who is happy.
I am hungry; please give me food first."
Having heard that, the king addressed his attendants:
"Let various kinds of food and drink be brought for him.
The yakṣa said: "I am one who eats the blood and flesh of those recently slaughtered."
"Give me this beautiful only son," he said.
Upon hearing this, the king fell into great despair:
"At long last, today, the sound of the Dharma has been encountered by me."
"He too [demands] an incalculable price.
Then, having heard this, Prince Sundara fell at his father's feet and addressed the king: "Forgive me, Your Majesty!"
"May the intention of the god be fulfilled;
give me to the Guhyaka for the sake of food.
Then the king gave away that only son—beloved, charming, dear, pleasing, patient, and non-opposed—for the sake of the Dharma, to the Yakṣa.

Then, through the exertion of his supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), the yakṣa displayed himself to the king and his assembly in such a way that he was seen tearing off the major and minor limbs one by one and devouring them,
while drinking the blood. Upon seeing this, the king, who longed for the Dharma, did not fall into despair.
That Guhyaka said to the king:
"O King, I am not yet satiated; give me more."
Then the king gave him his beloved wife; she too was presented by him in that very same manner. Thereupon, he spoke again to the king:
"O King,
even now satisfaction has not been attained.
Thereupon the king said to the yakṣa:
"My child, you have given me my only son and my beloved wife;
what more do you ask for?
The Guhyaka replied:
"Give me your own body;
by this I shall attain satisfaction.
The king said: "If I give my own body to you,"
"But how shall I hear the Dharma? First, speak the Dharma to me;
once I have grasped the Dharma, I shall thereafter cast off my body."
Then the Guhyaka, having established the king in his vow, taught the Dharma before an assembly of many hundreds.
From the beloved arises sorrow; from the beloved arises fear.
For those who are completely liberated from the beloved, there is no sorrow—how then could there be fear? (AVŚ 35.1)
Then, upon hearing this verse, the king’s mind was gladdened; with a sense of joy and mental well-being arising within his faculties, he said to the yakṣa:
"O Guhyaka, let this body be done with as you wish."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving that the king was as unshakable as Mount Meru in his resolve for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
caused his yakṣa form to vanish and stood before him in his own form. With eyes blossoming with faith, he took his son with one hand and his wife with the other, and, encouraging the king, spoke:
Excellent, excellent, O noble person!
You are one who has donned firm armor;
before long, by means of this resolve, you shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
