"And this is your reunion with beloved ones.
Then the king said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"
"Our aspiration for the Dharma has been fulfilled."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Surūpa, was I.
The prince Sundara was Ānanda."
This Sundarikā is none other than Yaśodharā.
Monks, even then I made a renunciation of beloved kinsmen and a renunciation of my own life for the sake of the Dharma; how much more so now!
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Dharma;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Dharma, we shall dwell in dependence upon it."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 36:
Maitrakanyaka.

(The Buddha, the Blessed One,) was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, those families among which mother and father are properly honored and properly revered are families that include Brahmā."
They are properly cared for with happiness.
Why is that?
Because, noble son, the parents of a clansman are, in accordance with the Dharma, like Brahmā.
Those families are accompanied by teachers in which the mother and father are properly honored, properly venerated, and properly maintained in comfort.
For what reason?
Because, noble son, parents act as teachers toward their child in accordance with the Dharma;
those families in which parents are properly honored are families worthy of offerings.
They are properly honored and properly maintained with comfort.
For what reason?
For the mother and father of a son of good family are indeed his two *āhavanīya* fires according to the Dharma.
Those families are possessed of the sacred fires in which the mother and father are properly honored, properly revered, and properly maintained in comfort.
For what reason?
Because, noble son, parents are like fire through their rightful dharma;
those families in which parents are properly honored are as if they possessed the gods.
They are properly honored and properly maintained with ease.
For what reason is that?
"For the mother and father of a son of good family are indeed like gods in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then further said this:
For Brahmā, as well as the mother and father and the former teachers, are the two fires to be offered to by a son, as are the deities. AVŚ 36.1.
Therefore, a wise person should pay homage to these two and honor them with ointments, baths, and the washing of their feet;
or else with food and drink, clothing, beds, and seats. (AVŚ 36.2)
By such service toward his parents, the wise man becomes blameless in this world and rejoices in heaven after death. AVŚ_36.3 //

When this sutra had been spoken by the Blessed One, the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that the Blessed One speaks in praise of service to one's mother, father, and teacher."

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what is the wonder here that now the Tathāgata is free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, and is omniscient and all-knowing?"

Having attained mastery over all knowledge and all that is to be known, he was a speaker in praise of service to one's mother, father, and teachers. As for me, in the past, while still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, I experienced great suffering after having committed even a slight offense against my mother.
Listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a caravan leader named Mitra.
He was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-reaching possessions; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself.
He took a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took delight, and amused himself with her;
as he was thus playing, taking delight, and amusing himself, sons were born to him and also died.
Placing his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth,
yet I have neither son nor daughter.
Upon my passing, since I am childless, my entire estate will become subject to the king."
A friend instructed him:
"If sons are born to you, you must give a daughter's name to one of them."
Thinking, "In this way he will become long-lived," he—
being childless and longing for a son— supplicated Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā,
and other specific deities; namely, the deities of gardens, the deities of groves, the deities of crossroads, the deities of junctions, and the deities who receive offerings.
He even supplicates the deities who are born together with him, who share his religious path, and who are constantly attached to him;
furthermore, there is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of such supplication,
but that is not the case.
If it were so, each person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
However, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three conditions?
The mother and father are filled with passion and come together;
and the mother is healthy and in her fertile period.
And a gandharva is present;
through the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.
Yet he remains intent on his prayers.
And a certain being, having passed away from one class of beings or another, entered the womb of that Prajāpatī. There are five unique qualities present in certain women of wise nature.
What are these five?
He knows the person who is attached,
he knows the person who is detached;
he knows the proper time.
She knows the season; she knows when the embryo has entered the womb;
and she knows from whom the embryo has descended.
He knows it is a male child;
he knows it is a female child.
If it is a male child, it remains resting against the right side of the womb.
If it is a girl, she remains resting against the left side of the womb;
then, being exceedingly joyful, she announces it to her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, you are prospering!"

"I have become pregnant; and since he remains resting against my right side, it will certainly be a boy. Overjoyed and filled with delight, he raised his upper body, extended his right arm, and uttered this inspired utterance:
"May I indeed behold the face of a son long desired for a long time;
may one be born to me who is not base-born;
may he perform my duties."
One who has been supported should support [the teacher] in return; one should bestow what is inherited [upon him], thinking:
"May my family lineage endure for a long time."
And for us who have passed away, having given gifts, whether small or great, and having performed meritorious deeds, he will dedicate the merit in our names, saying:
"May this follow those two wherever they go, whatever their rebirth.
And knowing that she has conceived, he keeps her on the upper terrace of the palace, free from all restraint.
In cold weather with cold-apparel, and in heat with warm-apparel, with foods prescribed by physicians— neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty,

nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent; with foods free from the qualities of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency— he moved from couch to couch like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces.
She did not descend from one couch to another until she reached the ground below,
nor did she hear any unpleasant sound whatsoever until the full maturation of the fetus.
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth.

A boy was born, handsome, beautiful, pleasing, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a resonant voice, well-knit eyebrows, a prominent nose,
and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
Upon his birth, a birth festival was held, and his name was established:
"What shall be the name of the boy?
The kinsmen said,
"This boy belongs to Mitra."
"There is a son and a daughter;
therefore, let the boy's name be Maitrakanyaka."

The boy Maitrakanyaka was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him. He was raised and nourished by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the cream of clarified butter, and other various highly refined articles of sustenance.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond;
meanwhile, his father had gone down to the great ocean and met his death right there.
When Maitrakanyaka had grown up and was well-restrained, he said to his mother:
"Mother, what kind of livelihood did our father subsist upon as a result of his past actions?
After that, I too [shall do the same]."
"I shall do so," he replied.
His mother said,
"My dear son, your father was a cock-fighter."
"Since you desire it, act as a ferryman.
She thought:
"If I tell him that he was once a merchant on the great ocean,"
He too might one day set out upon the great ocean and meet his death right there.
He established a daily fee of one *ukkari* coin;
thus, on the first day, four *kārṣāpaṇas* were earned,
which he also gave to his mother.
"Mother, with these [gifts], provide for the ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars.
Thus it was said; meanwhile, another spoke:
"Your father was a perfumer;
having abandoned his status as a high official, he established a perfume shop,
and it became worth eight kārṣāpaṇas."
They too were handed over by him to his mother;
then another said:
"Your father was a goldsmith."
Therefore, having abandoned that shop, he established a goldsmith’s shop.
On the first day, sixteen kārṣāpaṇas were produced;
those too were delivered by him to his mother.
On the second day, thirty-two kārṣāpaṇas were produced;
those too were handed over by him to his mother.
Eventually, some goldsmiths, being envious by nature, learned of all the transactions of the city and said:
Maitrakanyaka,
what use have you for this unrighteous livelihood?
Your father was a merchant who traveled upon the great ocean.
"Why have you been appointed to this dishonest business?
Urged by the words of the goldsmith, he went to his mother and said:
"Mother, it is thus heard: our father was once a merchant who traveled upon the great ocean."
"Therefore, give me your permission;
I too shall embark upon the great ocean.
His mother said:
"It is so, my son; however, you are a child and my only son. Do not abandon me and set out upon the great ocean."
Deceived by evil friends who were envious by nature, he did not turn back.
Consequently, disregarding his mother’s words as if they were not spoken, he had a proclamation made by bell in the city of Vārāṇasī:
"Listen, you merchants residing in Vārāṇasī!"
"The caravan leader Maitrakanyaka is about to embark upon the great ocean.
Whoever among you is able to embark upon the great ocean together with the caravan leader Maitrakanyaka— free from customs duties, free from tolls, and without having to pay freight charges—
let them gather the merchandise suitable for a voyage to the great ocean."

Having performed the rites of curiosity, auspiciousness, and benediction, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred merchants, he gathered merchandise suitable for the great ocean in carts, loads, bundles, baskets, camels, oxen, and donkeys, and set forth. His mother, her heart overwhelmed with affection, her face clouded with tears, clung to his feet.
"My dear son, do not, do not abandon me and descend into the great ocean! Then, with such words— compassionate, piteous, drawn out, and consisting of few syllables— he spoke.
Though being thus addressed, he remained firm in his resolve; having struck his mother on the head with his foot, he set out accompanied by the caravan.
His mother said to him: "May you not, my dear son, experience the ripening of this deed."
As he proceeded, observing villages, market towns, kingdoms, royal capitals, and ports, he reached the seashore.

Having hired a ship for five hundred *pūrāṇas* and taken five attendants— providing food for them, as well as a sailor, a fisherman, and a helmsman— and having made a proclamation by the ringing of a bell three times, he set out upon the great ocean.
While he was being carried along, he was brought to disaster by a sea monster from among the species of fish.
Then Maitrakanyaka, having reached a plank, arrived at dry land.
Wandering about on the shore, he saw from no great distance a city named Ramaṇaka.
He approached that place,
and thereupon four apsarases emerged from it— beautiful, lovely to behold, and gracious.
They said:
"Come, Maitrakanyaka;
welcome to you."

"This is our house of food, our house of drink, our house of clothing, and our house of beds, filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, and various kinds of gold and silver. Come, let us enjoy ourselves.
Thus he experienced pleasure with them for many years.
Just as when a being who has performed merit and cultivated wholesome deeds is prevented from proceeding along the southern path,
and because he is turned back from that southern path, [he does not go there].
Then, becoming even more intensely longing to go,
as he was traveling again by the southern road, he saw a city named Sadāmatta;
he became its gatekeeper.
Then, from that [place] as well, eight apsarases emerged, who were even more beautiful, more lovely to behold, and more pleasing;
they said:
"Come, Maitrakanyaka!"
"Welcome to you!

Here is our house of food, our house of drink, our house of clothing, and our house of bedding, filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, and various kinds of gold and silver. Come, let us enjoy ourselves."
Together with them, he experienced delight for many years—
just as a being who has performed meritorious deeds and cultivated wholesome roots [would].
Those [women] also block his path toward the south;
yet, the more he is turned away from the southern path, the more intensely he yearns to go.
Then, proceeding again along the southern path, he saw a city named Nandana;
he became its gatekeeper.
From that city as well, sixteen apsarases emerged—more beautiful, more lovely to behold, and more pleasing than before.
They said:
"Come, Maitrakanyaka;
welcome to you."

"This is our house of food, our house of drink, our house of clothing, and our house of beds, filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, and various kinds of gold and silver. Come, let us enjoy ourselves.
Thus he experienced pleasure with them for many years, just as a being who has performed merit and cultivated wholesome deeds would.
They also block his right path;
and from the moment he is turned away from that right path, he becomes even more intensely eager to go.
Furthermore, as he continued along the southern path, he saw a palace named Brahmottara;
he became the gatekeeper there,
until thirty-two apsarases emerged from it— more beautiful, more lovely to behold, and more gracious than before.
They said:
"Come, Maitrakanyaka;
welcome to you."

"This is our house of food, our house of drink, our house of clothing, and our house of beds, filled with jewels, pearls, beryl, shells, crystals, coral, and various kinds of gold and silver. Come, let us enjoy ourselves.
Thus he experienced pleasure with them for many years, like a being who has performed meritorious deeds and cultivated wholesome roots.
Those [women] also block his path to the right;
and from wherever he is turned away from the path to the right, from that very place he becomes even more intensely longing to depart.
Just as he proceeds along the southern path,
his desire increases;
until, proceeding further south as before, he sees an iron city.
He entered there;
as soon as he had entered, the door was closed behind him,
and then he went further inside.
There, his door was closed;
having entered further inside,
he saw a man of immense stature.
And upon his head, an iron wheel— blazing, aflame, fiercely burning, and become a single mass of fire— spins;
the pus and blood that flows from his head is his food.
Then Maitrakanyaka asked that man: "O man, who are you?
He replied:
"I am one who has wronged my mother.
As soon as those words were uttered by that man, Maitrakanyaka’s own past deed became manifest before him:
"I too am one who has wronged my mother; I believe it is by that very same karma that I have been drawn here."
Then, in that interval, a voice issued from the sky:
"Those who are bound are liberated; those who are liberated are bound."
As soon as this was said, the wheel vanished from that man’s head and appeared upon the head of Maitrakanyaka.
Then, seeing Maitrakanyaka afflicted with suffering, that man addressed him in verse:
Having passed beyond Rāmaṇaka, Sadāmatta, and Nandana,
as well as the Brahmottara palace, by what means have you come here?
Maitrakanyaka said:
"Having passed beyond Rāmaṇaka, Sadāmatta, and Nandana,
as well as the Brahmottara palace, I have come here of my own accord."
For karma drags one far away, and from afar karma impels one;
karma carries one to that place where karma ripens.
"By the ripening of that karma, a wheel— blazing, fiercely aflame, and obstructing my life-breath— is borne upon my head. (AVŚ 36.4)
The man said:
"With a corrupted mind, you struck with your foot on the head of your mother, who performed difficult deeds; this is the fruit of that action. (AVŚ 36.5)
Maitrakanyaka said:
"For how many thousands of years shall this wheel remain upon my head—blazing, fiercely burning, and obstructing my life? (AVŚ 36.6)
The man said:
"For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years, an incandescent iron wheel shall revolve upon your head. (AVŚ 36.7)
Maitrakanyaka said:
"O man,
will anyone else also come here?"
The man said:
"He who will be the one to perform such a deed."
Then Maitrakanyaka, overcome by painful sensations, gave rise to compassion toward sentient beings and said to that man:
"O man, I desire to bear this wheel upon my head for the sake of all sentient beings;
let no one else who performs such an act come here."
As soon as these words were spoken, that wheel rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees above the head of the Bodhisattva Maitrakanyaka and remained there;
and he, having passed away, was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was Maitrakanyaka—was I.
Because I was conducting business with him, my mother was provided for with kārṣāpaṇas."
Through the ripening of that karma, I experienced great happiness in four great cities;
however, because a slight harm was done to my mother, through the ripening of the fruit of that very karma, I have experienced such suffering as this.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall perform services for our mothers and fathers, and not acts of harm.
In this way, those faults that befell Maitrakanyaka will not occur.
"O monks, this very multitude of qualities that belonged to him when he was a son of the gods shall belong to this ordinary person as well;
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
And for what reason?"
For, monks, the mother and father of a son are doers of what is difficult; they are his nourishers, sustainers, and rearers; they are the givers of milk and the showmen of the wondrous Jambudvīpa.
Even if a son were to carry his mother on one shoulder and his father on the second for a full hundred years, [he would not repay them].

Or, if one were to establish him in sovereignty and dominion over all such things as exist on this great earth— gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, emerald, musāragalva, ruby, and right-spiraling shells— even by that much,
a son would not have done or rendered service to his parents.
But he who encourages, disciplines, and establishes his faithless mother and father in the perfection of faith—
He establishes one who is immoral in the perfection of morality,
and one who is stingy in the perfection of generosity.
He encourages and disciplines one of poor wisdom in the perfection of wisdom.
He settles [them] and establishes [them];
by this much, a son may have done or rendered service to his parents.
The Blessed One said this;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
AVŚ_37 The Hare.
(ed. Speyer, vol. I) The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—honored by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus revered by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

In Śrāvastī there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, with extensive and vast holdings; he had accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He took a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took delight, and dallied with her.
While he was thus playing, taking delight, and dallying, after some time his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A son was born; he was raised, nurtured, and grew up to be a man. Meanwhile, his father fell into the loss of wealth and the depletion of possessions.
He, who had many extensive circles of friends, relations, and kinsmen, sent that son to his relatives from time to time;
he was so cherished by those relatives that his affection for them grew intense.
Then, at another time, having gone out to Jetavana,
he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body resplendent with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides, he was filled with serene faith;
having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat before him to hear the Dharma.
For him, the Blessed One delivered a teaching on the Dharma intended to produce world-weariness.
Having heard this, perceiving the faults of cyclic existence and the virtues of nirvāṇa, he requested permission from his parents and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.
While thus having gone forth, he lived in close association with his kinsmen;
thereupon, the Blessed One restrained him from such association with householders and directed him toward the forest.
He did not find delight there;
until finally, the Blessed One restrained him from association with householders even three times, saying: "Child, this association with householders is corrupted by many faults."
There are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, dear, pleasing, associated with sensual desire, and provocative of passion;
there are sounds cognizable by the ear,
and odors cognizable by the nose.
Tastes cognizable by the tongue,
tangibles cognizable by the body,
and mental phenomena cognizable by the mind— those which are desirable, lovely, dear, agreeable, connected with sensual pleasure, provocative of passion, and yet acting as thorns.
In many ways, the virtues of the forest have been extolled,
wherein one who dwells finds an increase in wholesome qualities.
Thus, that son of good family, having approached the Blessed One as his spiritual friend, dwelt in the forest and applied himself with diligence.

By striving and exerting himself, having understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra as moving and unstable, and having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and be destroyed, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, for whom an axe and sandalwood were the same, who had split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge, who had attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights,
and who turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor. He became one worthy of worship, respect, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Having recollected his former lives and witnessed the extremely difficult austerities of this Blessed One, he approached the Blessed One and, filled with reverence, praised and honored him.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir!"

When this son of good family had been restrained by the Blessed One from dwelling even as much as three times in the vicinity of villages and directed instead toward the forest, and was finally established in arhatship—
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, what is the wonder here that now, by me— who am free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion,

fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; who am omniscient, possessed of all modes of knowledge, and have attained mastery over all knowledge and its objects— this son of good family [was led] even as far as the outskirts of the village, up to three times?"
Having been restrained and appointed in the forest,

he was eventually established in arhatship. However, in the past, while I was still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair—
This son of good family, having renounced his own life, has been restrained from living in the vicinity of villages and enjoined to dwell in the forest.
Listen to this; attend well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.

Long ago, monks, in the past, there lived in a certain mountain cave a seer who was devoted to rigorous austerities. He subsisted on fruits, roots, and water; he wore garments of bark and maintained the sacred fire-sacrifice.
This seer had a friend, a hare, who could speak the language of humans.
Day after day, he approached the presence of the ṛṣi three times;
having approached and paid his respects, he delighted him with various conversations.
Thus, their affection increased until they remained like a father and son.
After some time, a great drought occurred,
by which the rivers and wells became scantily supplied with water,
and the trees were deprived of flowers and fruit.
Then that seer no longer took delight in the enjoyments and pastimes within that hermitage;
he began to gather up his deerskins, bark garments, and woven robes.
Then the hare, seeing him proceeding in that manner, asked:
"Great Seer, where will you go?
The Seer replied: "I shall go to the edge of the village. (Speyer)
"I shall understand; there I will sustain myself with cooked alms-food.
Then, having heard the words of the seer, he was filled with distress and, feeling as though he were experiencing the separation from his parents, fell at the seer's feet and said to him:
"Do not abandon me!
Furthermore, dwelling at home is beset by many faults, whereas dwelling in the forest is endowed with many virtues.
Even though he was addressed in this way many times, he did not turn back.
Then he was addressed by the hare:
"If you must go, why not wait here for at least today?"
"Tomorrow you shall go wherever you intend.
Then this thought occurred to that seer:
"Surely this man wishes to invite me with a supply of food."
"Since these creatures born as animals are intent on accumulation," he said,
"therefore, that was promised by him."
Then, having completed his daily duties at the time for eating, the hare approached the seer, circumambulated him, and began to ask for forgiveness, saying:
"Forgive me, Great Seer, if anything has been done wrong to you by me, who am born in the animal realm and devoid of the capacity for reflection and discernment.
Having said this, he suddenly leaped up and fell into the fire.
Then that seer, overcome with agitation and his face clouded by tears, embraced him as if he were his own beloved only son and said:
"Child, what is this that you have undertaken?"

The hare said: "O Great Seer, out of my love for the forest, you shall pass day and night on my flesh. Moreover, there are no mung beans, no sesame seeds, and no rice grains for one who has grown up in the forest, such as I am.
Having prepared this body with fire, please consume it today and dwell in the penance grove. Thus [he spoke].
Then that seer, having heard the hare’s words, was moved by a sense of urgency and said:
"If it is so, out of love for you, I shall willingly renounce my life right here."
"And I shall not descend to the edge of the village.
Having heard these words, the hare became joyful in mind;
looking up toward the expanse of the sky, he began to entreat it, saying:
Having come together in the forest, my mind delights in solitude;
by this word of truth, O God, let there be rain from the realm of Indra! AVŚ_37.2 //
As soon as this was said, through the power of the Bodhisattva, the palace of Mahendra trembled,
and a vision of knowledge arose among the deities below:
"What has been done?"

They saw this through the power of the Bodhisattva; indeed, Śakra, the lord of the gods, sent down a "great Indra" rain, by which that hermitage once again became abundant with grass, shrubs, medicinal herbs, flowers, and fruits.
Then, while that sage was dwelling there having approached the hare as a virtuous friend, he realized the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
Thereupon, the sage said to the hare: "O hare, what do you seek by means of this difficult undertaking and your state of compassion?"
He said: "In a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide, may I become a Buddha to ferry across those beings who have not crossed over,
to liberate those who are unliberated,
and to give rest to those who have found no rest."
"May I be one who brings to final nirvāṇa those who have not yet attained it.
Then, having heard these words, that seer said to the hare:
"When you shall become a Buddha..."
"Please turn your attention toward us as well," they said.
The hare replied, "So be it."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was the hare at that time and on that occasion was I;
this noble son was the seer."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall dwell with virtuous friends, with virtuous companions, and in association with the virtuous; we shall not have evil friends, nor evil companions, nor association with the evil."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, while I was here alone, in seclusion, and in retreat, this reflection arose in my mind:
'This is half of the holy life, namely, having a virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and association with the virtuous.'"
"There is no association with evil friends, no companionship with the wicked, and no contact with the unwholesome.
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do not speak thus."
"This is half of the holy life, namely: having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates, and not having evil friends, evil companions, or evil associates.
"Ānanda, this entire holy life—complete, perfect, pure, and cleansed—is precisely this: having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates."
There is no association with evil friends, no companionship with the wicked, and no contact with the depraved.
For what reason?
It is because, Ānanda, by relying on me as a virtuous friend, beings subject to birth are [freed] from the nature of birth.
They are liberated from the nature of birth;
beings who possess the nature of old age, sickness, sorrow, death, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair are liberated from the nature of despair.

Therefore, Ānanda, by this very method it should be understood that this entire holy life—exclusive, complete, pure, and purified—is namely: association with the virtuous, companionship with the virtuous, and contact with the virtuous;
not association with the wicked, not companionship with the wicked, and not contact with the wicked.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
AVŚ_38 Dharmagaveṣī (The Search for the Dharma)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.
The recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of disciples, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
It was the custom of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
Having risen early in the morning, he went to see the Blessed One and began to sweep the Jeta Grove himself.
Then, at another time, a certain distraction arose for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, in order to show a field of merit to sentient beings who desire merit, took up a broom himself and set about sweeping the Jeta Grove.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, even the great śrāvakas—Śāradvatīputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Nanda, Revata, and others—began to sweep.
Then, having swept the Jetavana together with the śrāvakas, he entered the hall of attendance and sat down on the seat prepared in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, there are these five benefits in sweeping.
What are the five?
One's own mind becomes serene."
The mind of another becomes serene;
the minds of the deities become gracious;
and one accumulates roots of merit conducive to [rebirth in] the [heavenly] realms.
And after the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods.
Thus are the five benefits of sweeping.

Then the four assemblies, having heard from the Blessed One these five benefits regarding sweeping, were filled with faith; with hearts full of joy, gladness, and serenity, they rose from their respective seats, joined their palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to him:
“Blessed One, we, the attendants of the Blessed One, wish to sweep the entire Jeta Grove at all times.”
"Please grant us your favor.
Then the Blessed One consented to them by remaining silent.
Thereupon, those four assemblies, understanding the Blessed One's consent, took up brooms and set about sweeping the entire Jeta Grove.
Having swept the entire Jeta Grove as far as the garden paths, they sat down to one side with great reverence to listen to the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada also arrived at that place.
He heard that the Blessed One, together with his great disciples, had personally swept the Jeta Grove himself.
Having heard the five benefits of sweeping taught by the Blessed One, he became remorseful and thought:

For what purpose have I [given] in that monastery of the Blessed One, that field of merit, where the very seed sown this very day bears fruit this very day, and where an infinite result is produced from a tiny cause?

In that place where the Tathāgata was present, which was inhabited by all the śrāvakas, an exceedingly delightful ground, a source of joy for all gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; a place where there was no room for any bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, hell-beings, or malevolent spirits;

a world where there was no place for any Māras or their hosts of gods and humans; and where the power of those beings corrupted by passion, hatred, delusion, stinginess, envy, and pride had been shattered—[he sat].

[This is] for those who have not understood its power; who follow evil conduct; who have failed to attain [the path]; who have fallen into the hands of evil friends; who are born into what is unpleasant; who are devoid of faith; who lack the quality of renunciation; who have not seen nor contemplated the true nature of reality; who are immoral and of wicked behavior; who are disagreeable; who are devoid of compassion;
who are prone to anger and speak harshly; who have found no refuge; who are lacking in vigor and are of indolent character; and who have abandoned their undertakings and lack tranquility.

When [the Buddha] has departed far away, for those whose mindfulness is lost due to falling from meditative absorption, who wander in false views, who have set out upon evil paths, who are shrouded in darkness, who possess poor wisdom,

who have attained a semblance of knowledge through base intellects, and for donors who have not yet reached the state of arrival— [he is] a most heartening abode for those endowed with excellent conduct and who practice patience.

In such a dwelling, the playground of the Buddhas— attained through respectful approach, reached by those who have initiated vigor through constant following, belonging to those who delight in meditation within the secluded realm, and characterized by the field never abandoned by the light of awakening for those who uphold wisdom— an agitation of the mind was produced to sweep it clean.
"However, I shall never again act in such a way.
Having thus resolved, it occurred to him once more:
"In this place where the Blessed One himself performed the sweeping, accompanied by his great disciples..."
"How can I go over him?
Then Anāthapiṇḍada, appearing ashamed and with a heart overcome by modesty, remained standing in that spot.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers and questioners.
The monks were asked by him, "Who is this?
The monks replied,
"Venerable Sir, Anāthapiṇḍada, appearing ashamed and with a heart overcome by modesty, does not wish to approach the Blessed One here above by placing his feet."
When it was reported that the Blessed One himself, accompanied by his great disciples, had personally swept the Jeta Grove,
the Blessed One then said to him:
"Householder, the word of the Buddha..."
Perhaps it should be restored as:
"Having heard [this], one should enter [the city] by means of the Blessed One."
Why? Because the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have reverence for the True Dharma, for the Dharma is the teacher of Arhats.
Thereupon, Anāthapiṇḍada approached the Blessed One, singing with the chanting of verses.
Having approached and prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side in front of him to listen to a discourse on the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One through many methods with a discourse on the Dharma, he departed.
Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that the Blessed One has conceived such reverence and respect for the Dharma, and speaks in praise of the Dharma alone!
Behold, Venerable Sir, how these beings, having become as it were vessels for the jewel of the Dharma, have begun to sweep the entire Jeta Grove with such devotion."
"And they think that the Dharma should be heard.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, what is the wonder here, that now the Tathāgata—who is free from passion, hatred, and delusion, and who is fully liberated—[should teach it]?"
Having developed reverence and respect for the Dharma through birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair, he speaks only in praise of the Dharma.

As for that which was done by me in the past when I was possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and not yet liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair— for the sake of the Dharma, even my own life—
I have made this renunciation; listen to it, attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo—entirely without blemish and free from all thorns.
He protects the kingdom as if it were his only son.

And that king is faithful, noble, and of virtuous intent; he is dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma. Affectionate toward his subjects like a father toward his children, he is a giver of all things, a renouncer of all, and one who renounces without attachment, abiding in great generosity.
At a later time, he played, enjoyed himself, and dallied with his queen.
While he was thus playing, enjoying himself, and dallying, after some time that queen became pregnant, and a longing arose within her.
"I wish to hear a well-spoken word.
She reported this to the king,
and the king summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them.
They said, "O Lord, this is due to the power of this being.
Thereupon, for the sake of a reward, the king had a chest of gold distributed throughout the villages, towns, market towns, provinces, and royal capitals.
He searched everywhere,
yet that well-spoken verse was not found.
Eventually, after nine full months, the queen gave birth.

A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a high voice, well-proportioned eyebrows, a prominent nose, and endowed with all major and minor limbs. Upon his birth, having performed the birth ceremonies, they established his name:
"What shall be the name of this boy?
The ministers replied,
"Since this boy seeks out well-spoken words even before he is born, therefore let the boy's name be Subhāṣitagaveṣin (Seeker of Well-Spoken Words)."
He was given the name Subhāṣitagaveṣin. The boy Subhāṣitagaveṣin was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to play with him, and two to cleanse him.
He was reared and nourished by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent provisions most refined;
he grew quickly like a lotus in a pond.
When he had gradually become a great man, even then he sought out well-spoken words.
And he does not obtain it.
Having been established in the kingdom upon his father’s passing, he issues a command to his ministers:
"Village chiefs, I have need of well-spoken words;
seek out for me even a single well-spoken verse."
Then those ministers displayed chests of gold throughout the entire Jambudvīpa for the sake of obtaining a well-spoken verse, yet they did not find any such verse.
Thereupon, they informed the king.
Thereupon, that king yearned and was consumed with longing for the sake of hearing well-spoken words.
The vision of knowledge of Śakra, the lord of the gods, operates below;
he saw King [Bimbisāra] being distressed for the sake of hearing well-spoken words.
This thought occurred to him:
"What if I were to test the king?
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, assuming the form of a secret agent with deformed hands, feet, and eyes, stood before the king and spoke this verse:
"One should practice the Dharma well; one should not practice what is ill-conducted."
One who practices the Dharma sleeps happily in this world and in the next. Thus [it is said].
Then the king, his eyes wide with astonishment, said to that guhyaka:
"Speak, speak, O Guhyaka! Let me hear this verse.
Then the Guhyaka said to the king:
"If you will do for me whatever I tell you,
then I too shall do whatever you command."
The king said: "What will you command?
The Guhyaka said:
"If, after heating a fire-pit with khadira wood for seven days and nights, you cast yourself therein,"
Then he said, "I shall speak a verse to you once more.
Upon hearing this, the king, with a joyful mind, said to that guhyaka, "So be it."

Then the king, having bound the Guhyaka to his promise, caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout the entire realm: "On the seventh day, for the sake of hearing well-spoken words, the king will cast himself into a pit of fire.
Those who wish to see wonders [should come]."
"Let them come."

Then, when many hundreds of thousands of living beings had assembled and many hundreds of thousands of deities had gathered in the vault of the sky, they remained there to perceive the purity of the Bodhisattva’s resolute intention and to behold his marvelous state.
Then that Guhyaka, having flown up into the air, spoke to the Bodhisattva:
"O Great King, let that which was promised be fulfilled.

Thereupon, the king, having consecrated his eldest son in the kingdom, having asked forgiveness from his ministers, merchants, and countryfolk, and having comforted the multitude of people, approached the vicinity of the fire-pit and spoke this verse:
"This pit of glowing coals, which causes great terror and resembles the red flames of the sun,
I shall enter with a resolute mind, undaunted regarding my life;
and by the power of my merit, this pit of fire shall become auspicious for me."
The lotus pond was cool, its waters scented with sandalwood paste, and filled with lotuses.
Having said this, the Bodhisattva fell into that pit of fire.
As soon as he had fallen, the pit of fire appeared as a lotus pond.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having witnessed that most wonderful miracle which wins over both gods and humans, vanished from his yakṣa form, stood in his own true form, and spoke this verse:
One should practice the Dharma with good conduct; one should not practice evil conduct.
One who practices the Dharma sleeps happily in this world and in the next. Thus it is said.
Then the Bodhisattva, having memorized that verse and inscribed it upon golden leaves, traveled throughout the entire Jambudvīpa—through villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time and on that occasion was I.
Even then, for the sake of hearing well-spoken words, I relinquished my own life, let alone now."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall revere, honor, respect, and worship the Dharma;
having revered, honored, respected, and worshipped the Dharma, we shall dwell in dependence upon it."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 39:
Anāthapiṇḍada.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— worshipped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms. As he proceeded by stages, wandering for alms, he came down onto the royal highway.
And there on the royal highway, a certain brahmin arrived.
Then he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Having seen him and gazed upon him for a long time, he drew a line on the ground and said to the Blessed One:
"O Gautama,"
"You must not cross this line of mine until you have paid me five hundred purāṇas."
Then the Blessed One, in order to demonstrate the non-perishing of karmas and for the sake of abstaining from taking what is not given, stood in that place like a boundary pillar.
And this report spread throughout Śrāvastī:
"It is said that the Blessed One has been challenged by a certain brahmin on the royal road for five hundred purāṇas.
Upon hearing this, King Prasenajit of Kośala, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One go;
I shall provide [the meal]."
"Great King, these must not be given by you; rather, they must be given by another.

In this manner, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā, the two architects Ṛṣidatta and Purāṇa, the gods such as Śakra and Brahmā, and the four world-protectors beginning with Vaiśravaṇa, taking gold and bullion, [approached] the Blessed One...
They approached him, and the Blessed One said to them as well:
"These must not be given by you."
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard this,
he filled a container with gold and bullion, added five hundred purāṇas on top, and approached the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One,
please accept this."
The Blessed One said:
"Householder, these must be given by you;
let them be given to the brahmins."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada gave that golden wreath to the brahmin.
The monks, filled with doubt, along with the assembly including the king, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Blessed One, how this brahmin has detained the Blessed One, while Anāthapiṇḍada has offered kārṣāpaṇas! From what point did the Blessed One begin to accept [the payment] from him?"
The Blessed One said: "Do you wish to hear it, monks?
"Yes, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, monks, listen and attend closely and well; I shall speak.
By the Tathāgata these [were spoken]... (V)
(The passage from *tathāgatenaitāni* up to *khalu dehinām* is out of place here.
Monks, these actions that were necessarily produced and accumulated by you in previous births—
who else would experience them?
Monks, it is not in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element,
nor in the wind element.
Moreover, it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the necessary conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo—entirely without thorns or obstacles.
He protected the kingdom as if it were his only son.
His eldest son was the crown prince.

At another time, during the spring season, when the trees were in full bloom and the forest groves resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvaka birds, he was surrounded by the sons of his ministers.
He played and took his pleasure. Vayasya was the son of Amātyaputra; he played at dice together with another man.
Then the minister’s son was defeated by that man for five hundred *purāṇas*; and the prince stood as his guarantor. (There seems to be a long gap.)
Because of that, I experienced endless calamities regarding wealth throughout saṃsāra;
even now, though I have attained perfect awakening, I am afflicted by this.

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.

Therefore, monks, having abandoned exclusively black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves solely to exclusively white deeds and strive for the abandonment of taking what is not given.
"Monks, you should train yourselves in such a way that these kinds of faults do not occur for you."
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 40: Subhadra (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, was staying at Kuśinagarī in the grove of twin śāla trees belonging to the Mallas, having received robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Then, at that very time of his final nirvana, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, prepare a couch for the Tathāgata between the twin śāla trees, with its head toward the north.
Today, in the middle watch of the night, the Tathāgata will pass into final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having prepared a couch between the twin śāla trees with its head toward the north, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, a couch has been prepared for the Tathāgata between the twin śāla trees, with its head toward the north."

Then the Blessed One approached the couch; having approached, he lay down on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, keeping in mind only the perception of extinction (nirvāṇa).
Now at that time, there lived in Kuśinagarī a wandering mendicant named Subhadra, aged, elderly, and advanced in years.
He was two hundred years old and was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by the Mallas of Kuśinagarī as one regarded as an Arhat.
The wandering mendicant Subhadra heard:
In this regard, during the middle watch of the night, the parinirvāṇa of the śramaṇa Gautama will take place in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of substrate.
There is still uncertainty regarding the teachings,
yet my hope remains steadfast.
And that Blessed One Gautama is capable of dispelling my longing;
having heard this, he departed from Kuśinagarī and approached the Śāla grove of the Yamakas.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was walking back and forth on a walkway in the open air outside the monastery.
The wandering mendicant Subhadra saw the Venerable Ānanda from a distance;
having seen him, he approached the Venerable Ānanda.
Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Venerable Ānanda and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the wanderer Subhadra said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"I have heard, Ānanda, that today, in the middle watch of the night, the ascetic Gautama has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"Parinirvāṇa will come to pass;
yet I still have doubt regarding the teachings."
My hope is established,
and that Blessed One Gautama is capable of dispelling this state of longing in me. If it is not a burden for the Blessed One, Ānanda, [to do so].
Let us enter and ask him about a certain matter, provided he would grant us the opportunity to have our question answered.
Ānanda said: "Enough, Subhadra;
do not trouble the Blessed One. The Blessed One is weary in body."
The Sugata’s body was weary.

For a second and even a third time, the wanderer Subhadra said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "O Ānanda, I have heard that today, during the middle watch of the night, the ascetic Gautama has entered the realm of Nirvana without remainder."
"Parinirvāṇa will occur, yet I have a state of doubt regarding the teachings; nevertheless,
my hope remains firm."
And that Blessed One Gautama is capable of dispelling this doubt of mine. If it is not troublesome for the Blessed One, Ānanda, [please explain].
We would enter and ask him about a certain matter, if he would grant us the opportunity to have our question answered.
A second and even a third time, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the wanderer Subhadra:
"Enough, Subhadra; do not trouble the Tathāgata."
The Blessed One was weary of body; the Sugata was exhausted.
Then again, the wanderer Subhadra said this to the venerable Ānanda:
"O Ānanda, I have heard from the ancient wandering mendicants— those who were aged, venerable Buddhas,
great masters of conduct— that at some time or other, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas arise in the world."
It is just like the flower of the udumbara tree.
And today, during the middle watch of the night, the Blessed One Gautama will pass into final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Yet, I have a state of doubt regarding the teachings.
My hope is fulfilled;
that Blessed One Gautama is capable of dispelling this doubt of mine. If it is not a burden for the Blessed One, Ānanda—
We would enter and ask about a certain matter, if he would grant the opportunity for the answering of our questions.
Again, Ānanda said this to the wanderer Subhadra:
"Enough, Subhadra!
Do not trouble the Tathāgata."
The Blessed One’s body was weary; the Sugata’s body was exhausted.
Furthermore, the Blessed One heard with his purified divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, this conversation between the Venerable Ānanda and the wanderer Subhadra as it was being interrupted;
and having heard it, he said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Enough, Ānanda."
"Do not stop the wanderer Subhadra;
let him enter and ask whatever he desires.
This will be my final conversation with a wanderer of another sect."
"And this shall be my last [disciple] among those who have gone forth by the 'Come, monk' formula, namely the wanderer Subhadra. Then,
having been granted leave by the Blessed One, the wanderer Subhadra— elated, satisfied, joyful, and filled with uplifted rapture and gladness— approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the wanderer Subhadra said this to the Blessed One:
"O Gautama, as for these various non-Buddhist sects in the world..."
Namely: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Māskarin Gośālīputra,
and Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra.
Ajita Keśakambala,
Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
They each made their respective promises to me.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Subhadra, when I went forth at the age of twenty-nine, seeking what is wholesome."
Subhadra, it has been more than fifty years since I went forth into homelessness.
Virtue, concentration, conduct, and knowledge, along with one-pointedness of mind, have been cultivated by me.
Outside of this, there is indeed no other ascetic who can speak even a portion of the noble Dharma.
Subhadra, in whose Dharma and Vinaya the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, there the first ascetic is not found;
there the second, third, and fourth ascetics are not found.
"But, Subhadra, in whatever dharma and discipline the Noble Eightfold Path is found, there the first ascetic is found;
there the second, the third, and the fourth ascetics are found.
And in this dharma and discipline, Subhadra, the Noble Eightfold Path is found."
Here the first ascetic is found,
here the second,
here the third.
In this regard, this is the fourth:
there are no ascetics or brahmins outside of this [teaching];
the doctrines of others are empty of ascetics or brahmins.
Thus, in this assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar.

While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose in the wandering mendicant Subhadra. Then the wandering mendicant Subhadra, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma, crossed over doubt.

Having crossed over doubt, being independent of others and not led by another, having attained confidence in the teachings and dharmas of the Teacher, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Venerable Ānanda, he said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "It is a gain for the Venerable Ānanda, a great gain, that he has been consecrated by the Blessed One, the Great Teacher, with the consecration of a Great Teacher’s disciple."
"Moreover, it would be a gain for us, a great acquisition, if we were to receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, this wanderer Subhadra desires the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the wandering mendicant Subhadra: "Come, monk; lead the holy life.
That itself became for that venerable one the going-forth and the full ordination.
That is the state of being a monk.

Having thus gone forth, that venerable one dwelt alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, he attained that goal for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with right faith go forth from the home to the homeless life.
Having personally realized and attained that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life in this very life through direct higher knowledge, he declares:
"Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this."
The Venerable Subhadra became one who had realized full knowledge, an Arhat, well-liberated.
Then, as the Venerable Subhadra experienced the bliss of liberation upon attaining Arhatship, this thought occurred to him:
"It would not be fitting for me to witness the Teacher entering final Nirvana."
"Suppose I were to attain final nirvana first.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhadra attained final nirvana first, and after him, the Blessed One.
When the Blessed One had retired to his final bed, while he was experiencing sensations obstructive to the Dharma,
while phenomena were being severed, and while the joints [of the body] were being released,
When Subhadra was established in arhatship and many of the Mallas of Kauśinagara were set upon the Dharma,
the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, venerable sir,

that this wanderer Subhadra, while the teachings were being cut away and the joints [of his bonds] were being severed by the Blessed One, was released from the snare of saṃsāra and established in the ultimate, final nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One said: "Monks, what is there to marvel at here, that now, by me who am free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, and fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, the wanderer Subhadra [has been converted]?"
Having released them from the snare of cyclic existence, he established them in the ultimate, final nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, in the past, while I was still possessed by passion, hatred, and delusion; not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair;
and devoid of the capacity for discernment and judgment—having been reborn among the animal realm, I saved Subhadra and the Mallas of Kauśāmbī by sacrificing my own life.
Listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak.
Long ago, monks, in the past, there lived in a mountain valley a leader of a herd of deer, surrounded by many thousands of deer; he was wise, discerning, and intelligent.
That deer herd was tracked down by a hunter and reported to the king.
Thereupon, the king set out with a fourfold army and hemmed in that entire deer herd.
Then this thought occurred to the leader of the herd:
"If I do not protect these now,
they will all cease to exist this very day."
Then the leader of the herd began to look all around, wondering by which direction there might be an escape for this deer community.
He saw a river flowing through that mountain ravine.
That river was swift-flowing and carried away all that it seized,
while those deer were weak;
thereupon the leader of the herd suddenly descended into the river, stood in its midst, and uttered a cry:
"Come, sirs; having leaped from this bank and placed your feet upon my back, establish yourselves on the opposite shore.
By this means, I see that you shall preserve your lives."
"Otherwise, death will result.
Thereupon, those deer did exactly as instructed;
then, by the falling of a razor-sharp blade upon his back, his skin was sliced.
He remained there as a heap of flesh, blood, and bones;
yet his resolve did not turn back, for he felt compassion toward the deer. Then, when all had leaped away, he began to look behind him.
"Let no one here remain untraversed," he thought;
then he saw a single fawn that had not been traversed.
Then, while his vital organs were being torn asunder and his joints were being severed, the leader of the herd, disregarding his own beloved life, crossed the bank,
placed the young fawn upon his back, ferried him across the river, and set him down on the shore. Seeing that the herd of deer had safely crossed,
he began to make a formal vow at the moment of death:

"Just as these deer and this young fawn have been covered with the gift of their desired life and rescued from calamity by me, so too, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in a future time, may I release them from the snare of saṃsāra."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the lord of deer, I am he;
these deer are the Mallas of Kauśinagara."
This very fawn was Subhadra.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what actions were performed by Subhadra such that he was the very last [to attain realization] among the disciples?
The Blessed One said:
Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Subhadra himself in previous births;
they do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Neither in the fire element nor in the wind element,
but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases do performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even after hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, during this very Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years,

there appeared in the world a Truly Enlightened One named Kāśyapa— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
Now, of the Blessed One, Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one—
His nephew, named Aśoka,
having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One seeking liberation,
did not exert himself, thinking that liberation was already within his own grasp.
After Aśoka had dwelt for a long period of time in the countryside,
the Blessed One, the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa, having completed all the work of a Buddha, passed into his final rest like a fire when its fuel is exhausted; and at that time,
the monk Aśoka was absorbed in meditative seclusion beneath an Aśoka tree.

Then, the deity who was dwelling in that Aśoka tree, having heard of the final nirvāṇa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one, began to weep. As she wept, drops of her tears began to fall upon the body of the Aśoka tree.
Then Aśoka, looking upward, said to that weeping deity:
"For what reason, O deity, do you weep?
The deity replied:

"Tonight, during the middle watch, the final nirvāṇa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, will take place. Then Aśoka, having heard the words of the deity, shook as if pierced in a vital organ;
he too began to weep most piteously.
Then he was asked by a deity,
"For what reason do you weep? Aśoka replied:
"Due to separation from my teacher and separation from my kinsmen,
the Perfectly Awakened Kāśyapa was my maternal uncle; thus,
I lived in a state of complacency and did not exert myself."
"That [state] is far away,
and I am a worldling;
because the path is so remote, I shall not be able to attain distinction."
The deity said:
"If, however, I were to lead you into the presence of the Blessed One,
would it be possible [for him to do so]?"
Aśoka said:
"Indeed, my intellect has matured to such an extent that, upon merely seeing the Blessed One, I shall be able to attain distinction."
Then, by means of his supernatural power, a deity led Aśoka into the presence of the Blessed One.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, faith arose within him.
Once faith had been born, the Blessed One Kāśyapa taught him such a Dharma that, upon hearing it, he realized arhatship.
First, the Venerable Aśoka passed into final nirvāṇa, and after him, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one.
Then that deity, seeing the final nirvāṇa of the venerable Aśoka, felt joy and reflected:
"Whatever distinction has been attained by this venerable one,"
Having approached me, everyone [realized this]:
"Even so, in the future time, regarding that young brahmin named Uttara who was prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa—
'Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni'— "

When he has reached his final bed, may I alone be the very last of his disciples to go forth by the "Come, monk" formula, and may I enter parinirvāṇa even before the Blessed One Śākyamuni. Thus [he spoke].
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? That deity was this very Subhadra."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall dwell with virtuous friends, with virtuous companions, and in association with the virtuous;
we shall not have evil friends, nor evil companions, nor association with the evil.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhadanta, while I was alone, in seclusion, and in retreat, this reflection arose in my mind:
'This is half of the holy life, namely, having a virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and association with the virtuous.'"
"There is no state of having evil friends, no state of having evil companions, and no association with the wicked.
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do not speak thus."
"This is half of the holy life, namely: having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates;
not having evil friends, evil companions, or evil associates.
"This is the whole of it, Ānanda."
The holy life that is exclusively complete, pure, and purified is this: namely, friendship with the virtuous, companionship with the virtuous, and association with the virtuous;
it is not friendship with the wicked, nor companionship with the wicked, nor association with the wicked.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, it is by relying on me as a spiritual friend that beings subject to birth are completely liberated from the nature of birth;
beings subject to aging, sickness, sorrow, death, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair are completely liberated from the nature of despair.

Therefore, Ānanda, by this very method it should be understood that this entire, exclusive, complete, pure, and purified holy life consists of this: namely, having virtuous friends, having virtuous companions, and associating with the virtuous;
not having evil companions, not having evil friends, and not associating with the evil.
In this way, Ānanda, you should train yourself.
The Blessed One said this;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
