and Jāmbālaka as the son—this is declared to be the group.
AVŚ 41 Guḍaśālā. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
When the Blessed One had fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana made this vow: "We shall not consume almsfood until— " (Speyer).
"We shall enjoy [the fruits of our merit] as long as we have not liberated even a single sentient being from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Thereafter, those two venerable ones would from time to time occasionally go on an inspection tour of the hells.
Once, while wandering through the realms of animals and hungry ghosts,
the two of them saw there the incoherent lamentations of beings afflicted by various forms of torment; having returned, they reported this to the fourfold assembly,
and they too, upon hearing it, were moved to a sense of spiritual urgency.
Then those two, presiding over that place, delivered such a teaching of the Dharma that many beings attained distinction and became fit vessels for the discourse on hearing the Dharma.

Then, at another time, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while wandering among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), saw a ghost who resembled a mountain peak, whose belly was like the ocean, whose mouth was like the eye of a needle, and who was covered with his own hair; he was burning, fully aflame, become a single mass of fire, brooding and crying out with a piteous voice.
Experiencing painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant sensations,
he wandered here and there toward the places for excrement and urine, reaching them only with great difficulty.
Then the Elder questioned the preta:
"What deed, sir, have you committed by which you experience such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations?
The preta replied: "When the sun has risen, there is no need for a lamp.
Ask the Blessed One about this matter."
"He will explain to you the web of our karma.
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached the place where the Blessed One was.
At that time, the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion, was teaching the Dharma most sweetly to the fourfold assembly,
like pure, unadulterated honey;
and the assembly, numbering many hundreds, listened to the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with their senses undistracted.
Then the Blessed Buddhas, who are the first to speak, who speak with affection, who say "Come,
welcome," and who are preceded by a smile—
There the Blessed One said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Come, Maudgalyāyana; welcome to you. From where have you come just now?"
Maudgalyāyana said:

"I am coming, venerable sir, from my journey among the hungry ghosts (pretas). There I saw a hungry ghost with a mouth like the eye of a needle and a belly like a mountain, covered with its own hair, foul-smelling, exceedingly foul-smelling. And he said:

With his throat and lips parched, he was deeply distressed; his body was like a massive mountain, yet his frame was emaciated; his face was covered by his own hair, he was naked, and his mouth was as thin as a fine needle. AVŚ_41.1.
Naked, covered with his own hair, raised up like a skeleton machine, with a skull in his hand, terrible, and wailing, he runs toward [him]. AVŚ 41.2.

Exhausted by hunger and thirst, tormented by calamity, and crying out with a piteous voice, he experiences painful sensations. What terrible evil was committed by him in the world of mortals? Thus [he asks]. AVŚ_41.3.
The Blessed One said:
"Maudgalyāyana, that preta is an evildoer. Do you wish to hear the account of his course of action?"
"So be it, Venerable One.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, listen and pay close and careful attention; I shall speak."

Long ago, Maudgalyāyana, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a certain guild-president who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he had accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He owned about five hundred sugarcane plantations where the sugarcane was pressed.

And when Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world— those who have compassion for the lowly and the wretched, who frequent remote lodgings and seats, and who are the sole objects of veneration for the world. At one time, a certain Pratyekabuddha, compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched and a dweller of remote lodgings, dressed himself in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
That venerable one was afflicted with a wasting disease;
a physician prescribed sugarcane juice for him,
and so he went to the merchant's workshop.
The merchant saw that Pratyekabuddha, who was serene in body and serene in mind;
having seen him, the merchant asked, "What does the Noble One require?"
The Pratyekabuddha said, "Householder, with sugarcane juice.
Then that householder gave an order to his hired servant: "Give the noble one some sugarcane juice."
And that householder set out for the outside on some business;
then, a sense of stinginess regarding another's property arose in that man: "If I give him this flavor," he thought.
Thinking, "He will come again," he—

leaning toward a fall into the three undesirable destinies, rejecting both of the two desirable destinies, and having moved utterly far away from the noble dharmas— generated an evil thought and said to that pratyekabuddha,
"Bhikṣu, bring me your bowl."
"Give it; I will give you its juice.
For the knowledge and vision of Arhats, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas does not function without focused attention.
Out of compassion for the lowly and the wretched, thinking, "This is a servant; I must show him favor," that bowl was presented to him.
Then that man of evil conduct, cruel-hearted, took it and went to a secluded spot, filled it with urine, covered it over with sugarcane juice, and gave it back to that Pratyekabuddha.
He perceived this and thought:
"Much evil has been committed by this ascetic;
having cast it aside in a secluded spot, he has departed."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Maudgalyāyana? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the hired laborer—"
This is that hungry ghost (preta).
As the ripening (vipāka) of that karma, he has experienced infinite suffering within saṃsāra;
even now, having become a hungry ghost, he experiences even more intense suffering.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should exert yourself for the abandonment of stinginess, so that such faults as those of the hungry ghost (preta) may not occur.
For indeed, Maudgalyāyana, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should set aside actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed, and instead apply yourself to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, Maudgalyāyana, you should train yourself.
The Blessed One spoke thus.

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, with a joyful mind, and the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [Avadānaśataka 42: The Meal] (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-masters, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with the community of disciples. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was seated at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard the voice of a hungry ghost crying out in distress,
experiencing painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant sensations as she searched for food, saying:
"I am hungry, sirs!"
"I am thirsty, O worthy ones. Then, having seen the female preta, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked her:
"What evil deed did you commit, by which you must experience such sufferings as these?"
The female spirit said: "When the sun has risen, there is no need for a lamp.
Ask this matter of the Blessed One;
he will explain to you the web of our karma."
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion, was teaching the Dharma most sweetly to the fourfold assembly,
like honey free from bees;
and the assembly, numbering many hundreds, listened to the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with their senses undistracted.
Then the Blessed Buddhas are those who speak first, who speak kindly, who say "Come" and "Welcome," and who are preceded by a smile.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

"From where have you come now?
Maudgalyāyana replied,

There I saw a female preta with a mouth like the eye of a needle and a belly like a mountain, covered by her own hair, naked, and crying out in a piteous voice, experiencing painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant sensations. And she said:
"With my throat and lips utterly parched, I am deeply afflicted; my body is as massive as a towering mountain."
Her face covered by her own hair, naked, with a mouth as thin as a very fine needle, she was emaciated. (Speyer: ŚcañcitāŚ) AVŚ_42.1 //

Overcome by hunger and thirst,

and crying out with piteous voices, they experience painful sensations.
"What terrible evil was committed by her in the world of mortals,

"Yes, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, listen; pay close and careful attention, and I shall speak.

Long ago, Maudgalyāyana, in a past time when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.

Now, in that city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain householder’s wife who was miserly, a hoarder, and one who clung to her possessions; she did not even resolve to offer a portion of food to a crow, much less to other beggars.
Whenever she saw ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, or beggars, her mind became corrupted.
Once, a certain alms-collecting monk entered her house;
upon seeing him, avarice arose within her.
And having become corrupt in mind, he fell into this thought:
"If I pay him honor,
he will come here once again."
Then that evil-doing woman, disregarding the undesirable fear of the next world, invited the monk, locked the door, and caused him to be deprived of food; having reviled him extensively, she said:
"Monk, this is the hospitality you receive!"
"Do not enter this house again!"

Due to that stinginess— practiced, cultivated, and increased— she has been reborn among the pretas and experiences such sufferings as these. Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, one should exert oneself for the sake of abandoning stinginess.
These faults will not exist for them after they have passed away from that state.
The Blessed One spoke thus.
With joyful minds, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of] Water. (Speyer, Vol. I)

Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples near Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while wandering on a journey among the hungry ghosts, saw a female ghost who resembled a charred pillar and was covered by her own hair.

With a mouth like the eye of a needle and a belly like a mountain, blazing, glowing, aflame, become a single mass of fire, and swelling with heat, she is afflicted by thirst and experiences painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant sensations.
Merely by the sight of her, the rivers and wells dry up;
and when the god rains, then a rain of glowing embers accompanied by sparks falls upon her.
Seeing her, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:

Ask the Blessed One about this matter;
he will explain to you our web of karma,

Pay close and careful attention; I shall speak.

Long ago, Maudgalyāyana, in the past, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He was dwelling in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
There, a certain monk who had set out on a journey,
being afflicted by thirst, approached a well.
There, a certain girl stood having filled a water jar.
She was addressed by the monk: "I am afflicted by thirst, sister."
"Give me some water," he said.
A sense of stinginess arose within her;
clutching her belongings tightly, she said to the monk:
"O monk, if you die,
I will not give you water; my jar will become depleted."
Then that monk, afflicted by thirst and losing hope, departed.
Thereafter, that girl, having practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in that stinginess, passed away and was reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta).
She experiences such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant sensations.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should train yourself thus: "We shall exert ourselves for the abandonment of stinginess.
In this way, Maudgalyāyana, you should train yourself.
The Blessed One said this.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, with a joyful mind, and the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.

and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

Then, in the forenoon, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.

Ask this matter of the Buddha, the Blessed One;
he will explain to you the web of our karma,

There I saw a female ghost who resembled a burnt pillar, naked, covered with her own hair, and having a mouth like the eye of a needle."

Her belly was like a mountain; she was burning, blazing, aflame, and become a single mass of fire, crying out with a piteous voice, experiencing sensations that were painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable.

When the god rains, then upon her falls a rain of glowing embers accompanied by sparks;
she receives as food excrement—foul-smelling, most foul-smelling, and resembling ordure—and even that she obtains only with great difficulty. And it is said:
Naked, covered with her own hair, and rising up like a skeleton frame, she cries out with a piteous voice and experiences painful sensation. (AVŚ 44.1)
For she runs toward the latrines, distressed, thinking:
"I shall drink the excrement and eat it; that is what is obtained with such great suffering. (AVŚ 44.2)
What terrible sin was committed by her in the world of mortals, because of which she experiences such a fearsome suffering? AVŚ_44.3 //
The Blessed One said:
"Maudgalyāyana, that female ghost is an evildoer. Do you wish to hear the narrative of her karma?"
"So be it, Venerable One.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, listen and pay close and careful attention; I shall speak."

Long ago, Maudgalyāyana, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain Pratyekabuddha who was compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, and who frequented remote lodgings and seats. Being afflicted by illness, he entered Vārāṇasī for alms; eventually, a physician prescribed a diet suitable for his condition.
He went to the residence of a certain merchant;
there he was seen by that merchant and asked: "Noble sir, what is your need?"
He replied, "With food that is agreeable to the family.
Thereupon, the merchant gave the command to his daughter-in-law: "Agreeable food must be given to the noble lady."
Then, a sense of stinginess arose in that bride:
"If I give him food today, he will come again with even greater frequency tomorrow."
Having gone aside to a secluded spot, she filled a vessel with excrement, covered it over with cooked food, and gave it to that Pratyekabuddha.
Since the knowledge and vision of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas does not function without deliberate attention,
he accepted it.
Having accepted it, he perceived that it was foul-smelling; "Surely this has been filled with impurity by her," he thought.
Then that Great Being, having discarded it in a secluded spot, departed.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Maudgalyāyana? She who at that time, on that occasion, was the merchant's daughter-in-law, she is this very female ghost."
Because she committed such evil by means of that [action],
from that time forward she was constantly reborn among hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, and she always fed upon excrement.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should strive for the abandonment of stinginess so that those faults which exist after death shall not occur.
In this way, Maudgalyāyana, you should train yourself.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, with a joyful mind, and the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of Maudgalyāyana] (AVŚ 45)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)
Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit,
and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with his community of disciples,
was dwelling near Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

Now at that time, between Rājagṛha and the Bamboo Grove, in that interval, there were five hundred hungry ghosts (pretas) who were like scorched pillars— naked, covered with their own hair, with bellies like mountains and mouths like the eye of a needle;
they were burning, blazing, aflame, and become a single mass of fire, wailing with cries of distress in suffering.
Experiencing intense, harsh, bitter,
and unpleasant sensations, they wander through space like circles of wind.
They find no support anywhere.
Then, in the forenoon, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms;
there he saw those hungry ghosts.
Those pretas also [addressed] the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Then, approaching the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana as a single group, they spoke with a single voice in words that were piteous, distressed, and drawn out:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, we were five hundred guild-leaders in Rājagṛha. We were miserly, stingy, and hoarded our belongings; indeed, we ourselves did not give any gifts or offerings."
Furthermore, obstacles were created when others were giving gifts,
and many who were worthy of offerings were reviled with the word "ghosts," saying: "Like those reborn as ghosts, you constantly wander for alms at the houses of others."
"Having died, we have been reborn as such pretas.

Therefore, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, inform our kinsmen who reside in Rājagṛha of our situation resulting from our past karma; then, having made a request for alms, feed the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and on our behalf, have them perform the dedication of the merit."
"And may there be liberation for us from the realm of hungry ghosts.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to the hungry ghosts by remaining silent.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana made a request for alms from the houses of their kinsmen and invited the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal on the following day.
And it was announced to the pretas:
"Tomorrow the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, has been invited for a meal; you should come there."
It was also announced to the kinsmen:
"You must come there to that meal for the kinsmen;
we shall see those hungry ghosts."
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana himself applied himself to looking after the meal.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn and food had been prepared, at the appointed time for the gaṇḍī, he did not see those hungry ghosts.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana began to search for those hungry ghosts with his divine eye;
yet he did not see them anywhere within the entire region of Magadha.
He proceeded to survey the four-continent world system in succession,
yet even there he did not see it.
Then, as far as his knowledge and vision extended, [he looked].
Then he began to look about;
even there, however, he did not see him.
Thereupon, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, feeling distressed, informed the Blessed One: "Blessed One," he said.
"I do not see my patrons," [Maudgalyāyana said].
The Blessed One said:
"Do not fall into despair, Maudgalyāyana."
Beyond the domain of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there exist immeasurable world-systems;
there they have been cast by the wind of karma.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, behold today the power of the Tathāgata!
"I shall manifest the vision of the knowledge of the omniscient one; I shall display the miraculous transformations of the Tathāgata.
Let the gong be struck!"
Then, when the gong was struck, the entire community of monks assembled;
the relatives of the hungry ghosts and other beings who had come out of curiosity, longing to see the hungry ghosts, also gathered together.
Thereupon, the Blessed One displayed such a feat of supernatural power that the hungry ghosts saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, partaking of the meal.
And they regained their mindfulness, thinking:
"Our kinsmen are feeding the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for our sake.
Then the Blessed One pronounced a dedication of merit with a voice endowed with five qualities:
"Whatever merit arises from this gift, may it follow after the hungry ghosts;
may they quickly rise up from this most dreadful world of pretas. Thus [he said].
When the Blessed One had performed such a discourse on the Dharma through that empowerment,
many hundreds of thousands of living beings, having heard it, abandoned the stain of avarice and realized the vision of the Truths.
And those hungry ghosts, having conceived a serene faith in the Blessed One, passed away and were reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
It is indeed the natural law that when a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods has recently been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?
They see that they have passed away from among the hungry ghosts and have been reborn among the sublime gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
"Having generated a mind of intense faith toward the Blessed One," then this thought occurred to those sons of the gods who had previously been hungry ghosts:
"It would not be fitting for us [to remain here]."
"Should we approach the Blessed One for a visit after our probation has expired,
or should we approach the Blessed One for a visit while our probation is still unexpired?

Then those sons of the gods who had previously been hungry ghosts— wearing shimmering, stainless earrings, their bodies adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and their heads crowned with various jewels and gems— [approached].

With their bodies anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā, and other unguents, they filled their laps with divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, mandārava flowers, and so forth— and having illuminated the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, on all sides with a sublime radiance,
they scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the intentions, latent tendencies, dispositions, and natures of those sons of the gods who had previously been hungry ghosts, delivered such a teaching of the Dharma that upon hearing it, those sons of the gods who had formerly been hungry ghosts attained a great distinction.
Like merchants who have gained their profit, they circumambulated the Blessed One three times and vanished right there.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Excellent, excellent, Mahāmaudgalyāyana! Your service has become fruitful."
Those deceased ones who were established among the gods have approached me this night;
the Dharma has been taught to them by me.
Having attained their rise and secured their gain, they departed.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana informed those kinsmen;
having heard this, they were filled with great wonder, they conceived faith in the presence of the Blessed One, and they performed even greater acts of honor.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should exert yourself for the sake of abandoning stinginess.
These faults do not exist for those who are among the hungry ghosts (pretas).
Thus spoke the Blessed One.

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, with a joyful mind, and the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. [Avadānaśataka 46: Uttara] (ed. Speyer, vol. I)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

In Rājagṛha there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, of great fortune and vast enjoyments, possessing extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status,
and he sported with her.
He took his pleasure and enjoyed himself. While he was thus sporting, taking his pleasure, and enjoying himself, after some time his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A son was born; having performed the birth ceremony upon his birth, they established his name, asking,
"What shall be the name of this boy?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since he was born under the constellation Uttara, let his name be Uttara.
The boy Uttara was reared, grew up, and became a man.
His father passed away,
and Uttara became the master of the household;
he established a shop.
He bought and sold, making his livelihood through buying and selling. Day after day, he approached the presence of the Blessed One.
From seeing the Blessed One and hearing the true Dharma, faith arose in him toward the teaching of the Blessed One.
The thought of going forth arose in him, and he made a request to his mother:
"Mother, give me your permission; I shall go forth in the teachings of the Blessed One."
Then the mother said:
"Son, you are my only child; as long as I live,"
"You must not go forth into homelessness until I have died; you shall perform whatever is required once I am dead.
And whatever Uttara acquired, he gave it all to his mother.
"Mother, give these to the ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars.
But his mother was greedy, avaricious, stingy, and possessive of her belongings; having hidden those kārṣāpaṇa coins, she reviled those ascetics and brahmins who entered her house seeking alms:
"You wander constantly for alms at the houses of others like those reborn as pretas," she said,
while deceiving her son by saying,
"Today I am providing food for this many monks."
When she passed away, she was reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta).
Meanwhile, Uttara, following his mother’s death, gave gifts, performed meritorious deeds, and went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he [penetrated] this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra.

Having understood that all conditioned phenomena are unstable and having struck down their course by means of their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the higher cognitions, and the analytical insights.
Turning his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Having built a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges, he sat in meditation.

Meanwhile, his mother, reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), appeared naked, resembling a charred pillar, covered with her own hair and body-hair, with a mouth like the eye of a needle and a belly like a mountain; blazing, aflame, and become a single mass of fire, she cried out in a piteous voice toward the Venerable One.
They approached Uttara;
when the Venerable Uttara saw that female ghost, he asked her, "Who are you who have become such as this? The female ghost replied:
"I am your affectionate mother, my dear son, by whom you were begotten; I have come here among the pretas who are deprived of food and drink. (AVŚ 46.1)
Since I passed away twenty-five years ago,
I do not recall ever having seen water, much less food.
I go to trees that bear fruit, yet they become fruitless for me; I go to lakes that are full, yet they are dry for me. AVŚ 46.3.

The venerable one’s tree-root is indeed pleasant, and he enjoys cool water from this vessel. Having given rise to compassion for me, who am wretched and afflicted by thirst, please give me water. (AVŚ 46.4)
Then Uttara said to his mother:
"Mother, did you not previously, while I was still a human being, cause me to give gifts and perform meritorious deeds?"
The female spirit said: "My son, overcome by stinginess, I gave no gifts nor performed any meritorious deeds;
all that wealth I buried in a pit of fire with a wicked mind."

Therefore, my son, go now to the house of a kinsman, make a request for sandalwood, and in my name feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha; offer the dedication of merit and cause them to perform a confession of transgressions.
"In this way, may my liberation from the womb of a preta come to pass.
Uttara said: "So be it, mother;
however, you must remain at the Buddha's side."
The female spirit said: "My dear sons, you should feel ashamed, being naked yet possessed of modesty.
Uttara replied: "Mother, when you commit evil deeds,"
"Then you felt no shame;
why do you feel ashamed now, at the time of the fruit?
The female preta replied: "So be it."
"I shall come."
Then, having gone north to the houses of his kinsmen and requested alms of sandalwood, he invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal on the following day.
At the time of the striking of the gong, the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, had assembled;
and that female ghost stood at the edge of the assembly.

Many hundreds of thousands of living beings, desiring to see that female ghost (*pretī*), gathered together. Upon seeing her with such a deformed body, they were overcome with supreme spiritual agitation (*saṃvega*) and developed serene faith (*prasāda*) toward the Blessed One.
Then, the Venerable Uttara, having satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with exquisite food, had the female ghost perform the dedication of merit (*dakṣiṇā-deśanā*) in his own name.
And the Blessed One himself, with a voice endowed with five qualities, pronounced the dedication of the merit:
"Whatever merit arises from this gift, may it follow after the female preta;
may she quickly rise up from this most dreadful world of pretas. (AVŚ 46.5)

Then the Blessed One performed that empowerment for her and for the great multitude of people, giving such a teaching of the Dharma that upon hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings realized the vision of the Truths.
With a mind full of serene faith, she passed away and was reborn among the pretas of great psychic power.
The Venerable Uttara reflected and perceived that she had been reborn among the pretas of great supernatural power.
Then the Venerable Uttara said:
"Mother, do you have the power?"
"Let the distribution of gifts be made," [he said].
The preta of great supernatural power replied:
"Son, I am not able."
"I have no desire for giving.
Then the Venerable Uttara said to the preta of great supernatural power: "Even now that body of yours remains, with its flesh, skin, bones, and hide completely wasted away."
"In the world of the hungry ghosts, you have turned back her whose eyes were shrouded by the darkness of greed. Thus [he spoke].
When the Venerable Uttara had rebuked him extensively, he obtained one *yamalī* coin;
he then gave it to the Saṅgha.
And that monk who had purchased that *yamalī* from within the Saṅgha—
He placed it with that young man;
then, having departed, she came back at night and stole it.
Thereupon, that monk informed the Venerable Uttara.
Having gone to the north and rebuked the preta, he brought her back and gave her [to him].
In this manner, even up to three times, she was snatched away from that monk and brought back and given by the Venerable Uttara.
The monk tore it apart and sewed it into a patch for the fourfold community of monks; thereafter,
she did not steal it again.
Therefore, having seen that stinginess brings about the mockery of sentient beings, one should meditate for the sake of abandoning stinginess;
in this way, such faults as those will not exist after death.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.

With joyful minds, those monks and the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. The Story of the One Born Blind (Jātyandha) (Avś I, ed. Speyer)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with the community of disciples.
Then, in the forenoon, the venerable Nandaka dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Having finished his meal and returned from his alms-round, he put away his bowl and robes and went out on a journey among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

There the Venerable Nandaka saw a female ghost who resembled a scorched pillar, born blind, covered with her own hair and body-hair, with a mouth like the eye of a needle, a belly like a mountain, foul-smelling, resembling a cemetery, and [surrounded] by crows and vultures.
She is assailed by dogs and jackals, which, from all sides, tear away her flesh again and again and devour it.
Stricken by the pain of her vital organs, she cries out with a piteous voice, experiencing sensations that are painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable.
The venerable Nandaka, filled with agitation, asked:
"Sister, what evil deed have you committed that you experience such suffering?
The female ghost replied: "When the sun has risen, there is no need for a lamp."
"Ask the Blessed One about this matter;
he will explain to you our web of karma,
hearing which other beings here also will desist from evil."
Then the venerable Nandaka approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Now at that time, the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion, was teaching the Dharma most sweetly to the fourfold assembly, like honey free from bees;
and the assembly of many hundreds listened to the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with unblinking senses.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are the first to speak, saying "Come," welcoming [others], and preceded by a smile.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Nandaka: "Come, Nandaka;
welcome to you."
"Nandaka, from where do you come now?
Nandaka replied,
"I am coming, venerable sir, from my journey among the hungry ghosts."

There I saw a female preta who resembled a charred pillar, covered with her own hair and body-hair, with a mouth like the eye of a needle and a belly like a mountain; she was foul-smelling and resembled a cemetery,
being pursued by crows, vultures, dogs, and jackals, which tore off her flesh from all sides and devoured it.

Stricken by that agony in her vital organs, she cried out with a piteous voice, experiencing a sensation that was painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable. And she said: "With throat and lips parched, exceedingly miserable, her body crushed like a massive mountain; her face covered with her own hair, naked, her mouth like a very fine needle—she is emaciated. (AVŚ 47.1)
Naked, covered with her own hair, towering like a framework of bones,
with a skull in her hand, the terrible one runs about wailing. (AVŚ 47.2)
Exhausted by hunger and thirst, afflicted by calamity,
and crying out with piteous voices, she experiences painful sensations.
"What terrible sin was committed by her in the world of mortals, because of which she experiences such a fearsome suffering? (AVŚ 47.4) Thus [he asked].
The Blessed One said:
"Nandaka, that female ghost is an evildoer. Do you wish to hear the narrative of her course of action?"
"So be it, Venerable Sir.
In that case, Nandaka, listen and pay close and careful attention; I shall speak."

Long ago, Nandaka, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana.
In Vārāṇasī, there was a certain daughter of a guild-leader;
she was a seeker of the Dharma.
When she had heard the Dharma, she came to perceive the defects of saṃsāra and to perceive the qualities of nirvāṇa.
Having obtained permission from her parents, she went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.
For her sake, her kinsmen had a rainy-season residence for bhikṣuṇīs constructed.
She lived there together with both trainee (śaikṣā) and non-trainee (aśaikṣā) bhikṣuṇīs. Eventually, due to negligence, she became lax in her training;
consequently, the bhikṣuṇīs expelled her, declaring her to be of immoral conduct (duḥśīlā).
Then, from the houses of that patron, the gifts that had been set forth were seized by dogs and jackals.
She spoke dispraise of those in training and those beyond training;
and seeing the monks who were virtuous, she closed her eyes.
"What do you think, Nandaka? That merchant’s daughter was this very same hungry ghost;
it was because she practiced stinginess regarding the rain-garment."
Because of that, she was reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Because she committed the perpetual severance [of the roots of merit], she is pursued by crows, vultures, and dogs.
Because she spoke dispraise of the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* bhikṣuṇīs, [she suffers this].
Because of that, she acquired a foul odor;
and because she closed her eyes upon seeing virtuous monks, she became blind from birth.

Thus, Nandaka, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, Nandaka, you should abandon entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, and apply yourself exclusively to entirely white deeds.
In this way, Nandaka, you should train yourself.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, one hundred thousand living beings attained the vision of the Truths.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Knowing these and other such perils that lie in stinginess and verbal misconduct, you must exert yourselves for the abandonment of stinginess and verbal misconduct."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
with joyful minds, those monks and others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
AVŚ_48 The Guild Master. (ed. Speyer, vol. I) The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with the community of his disciples.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

In Śrāvastī there was a certain guild-president who was wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, with vast and extensive holdings; he had accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
On another occasion, he went out to the Jeta Grove.
Then he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,

his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Having seen him, he again paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One gave him a teaching on the Dharma intended to produce detachment from saṃsāra; having heard it, he came to perceive the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa, and thus went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.
Having gone forth, he became well-known and possessed of great merit, and he obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Having taken up his requisites, he accumulated whatever he obtained,
yet he did not share them with his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Because of that stinginess— practiced, cultivated, and increased— he died while obsessed with his requisites and was reborn among the hungry ghosts in his own cell.
Then his fellow religious practitioners, having struck the wooden gong for the tonsured, performed the removal of his body.
Having performed the funeral rites for his body, they returned to the monastery.
Then, opening the door of the cell, they began to inspect his bowl and robes.
When they saw that hungry ghost, with his hands, feet, and eyes deformed, appearing as the very embodiment of extreme loathsomeness, standing there clutching a bowl and a robe,
the monks were deeply moved by seeing him in such a state and informed the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, for the sake of showing favor to that son of good family, to cause agitation among the assembly of disciples, and to demonstrate the undesirable maturation of stinginess, was surrounded by a multitude of monks and preceded by the community of monks.
Having arrived at that place,
he then beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides,
faith arose in him upon the mere sight of the Blessed One;
he felt a sense of shame.
Then the Blessed One, whose voice was as deep as a thundercloud filled with water and like the sound of a drum, addressed the preta:
"O gentle-faced one, it was you yourself who procured this bowl and robe for the sake of your own destruction, by which you have been reborn in the states of woe."
"It is well; gladden your heart toward me and turn your mind away from these possessions,
lest you, having passed away from here, be reborn in the hells."
Then that hungry ghost, having offered his bowl and robe to the Saṅgha, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and confessed his transgression.
Thereupon, the Blessed One dedicated the merit on behalf of the hungry ghost, saying:
"Whatever merit arises from this gift, may it follow after the hungry ghost."
"May he rise quickly from this most dreadful world of hungry ghosts! Thus [he said].
Then that preta, having developed faith in the Blessed One, passed away and was reborn among the pretas of great psychic power (*maharddhika*).

Thereupon, that preta of great psychic power— wearing shimmering, stainless earrings, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, his head crowned with a diadem variegated with jewels and gems, and his limbs anointed with saffron, *tamāla* leaves, *spṛkkā*, and other fragrant unguents— [approached].

On that very night, having filled his lap with divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, great white lotuses, and mandārava flowers, and having illuminated the entire Jeta Grove with a sublime radiance, he scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat before him to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma that,
upon hearing it, he was filled with faith and departed.
The monks were dwelling devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
They saw a sublime radiance near the Blessed One,
and having seen it, they were filled with doubt and questioned the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a visit this night?
The Blessed One said, “Monks, neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor the four world-protectors have approached me for a visit.”
Furthermore, that preta, having passed away, was reborn among the pretas of great supernatural power;
he approached me this very night,
and the Dharma was taught to him by me.
Having conceived faith, he departed.
Therefore, monks, you should strive for the abandonment of stinginess;
then these faults will not arise.
"Those who [acted] toward that merchant who had become a ghost—
thus, monks, you should train yourselves."
The Blessed One spoke thus.
With uplifted minds, those monks and the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Fifty-ninth Story:
Sons] (Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, the wealthy, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, in the forenoon, the venerable Nālada dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
Having wandered for alms in Rājagṛha and finished his meal, he returned from his alms-round after the meal, put away his bowl and robes, and set out on a journey among the hungry ghosts.

In the vicinity of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, he saw a female preta who resembled a Rākṣasa of Yama, covered in drops of blood and surrounded by fragments of bone, standing as if in the middle of a cemetery.
Having given birth to five sons day and night, she experienced such suffering that, despite her affection for her children, she was devouring them due to the emaciation caused by hunger.
Then the Elder Nālada questioned her:
"What evil deed did you commit such that you experience such suffering?
The female ghost replied: "When the sun has risen, there is no need for a lamp.
Ask the Blessed One about this matter."
"He will explain our web of karma,
so that upon hearing it, other beings here also will desist from evil actions.
Then the Venerable Nālada approached the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion, was teaching the Dharma most sweetly to the fourfold assembly, like pure honey free from bees;
and a multitude of several hundreds [listened] to the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.
He hears with his sense faculties unshaken.
Then the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are the first to speak; they say, "Come," they offer words of welcome, and they are preceded by a smile.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Nālada: "Come, Nālada."
"Welcome to you!
From where have you come now, Nālada?
Nālada replied, "I am coming, Venerable Sir, from my journey among the hungry ghosts."
There I saw a female preta who resembled a Rākṣasa of Yama, covered in drops of blood and surrounded by fragments of bone, standing as if in the middle of a cemetery. She said:
"By night I eat five sons, and likewise five others by day; though I give birth to them and devour them, even so I have no satisfaction. (AVŚ 49.1)
"What terrible evil was committed by her in the world of mortals,
because of which she experiences such a fearsome suffering? Thus the Blessed One said:
"Nālada, this is a female hungry ghost (preta) who committed evil deeds.
Do you wish to hear the narrative of her karma?
"Yes, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, Nālada, listen; pay close and careful attention, and I shall speak.

Long ago, Nālada, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and great enjoyments, with extensive and vast possessions, accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa,
and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her;
yet, as he played, took pleasure, and amused himself, neither a son nor a daughter was born to him. Resting his cheek upon his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth,
yet I have neither son nor daughter.
Upon my passing, since I am childless, all my property will be subject to the king's authority."
Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other specific deities;
that is to say, he supplicated the deities of groves, the deities of forests, the deities of crossroads, the deities of junctions, and the deities who receive offerings.
He also supplicated those deities who are innate, those associated with his dharma, and those who are constantly attached to him.
There is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of prayers;
but that is not so.
If it were otherwise, every single person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Moreover, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three conditions?
The mother and father must be in love and united.
When the mother is healthy and in her season,
and a gandharva is present—
through the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.
Even though he worshipped the deities, he had neither a son nor a daughter.
The thought occurred to him:
"I shall take a second wife;
perhaps she might be possessed of a virtuous nature."
He brought a second wife from a family of equal status. He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her;
and as he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, in the course of time she became pregnant.
Filled with joy, satisfaction, and delight, she announced to her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, you prosper!
I have become pregnant."
"And since he stays resting against my right side,
it will certainly be a boy. With a joyful heart, he raised his upper body, extended his right arm, and uttered this inspired utterance:
"Perhaps I might behold the face of my son, whom I have long desired."
"May one who is born to me not be base-born; may he perform my duties; being supported by me, may he support me in return."

He would obtain an inheritance such that my family lineage might endure for a long time; and when we have passed away, he will give gifts, whether small or great, and perform meritorious deeds, dedicating the merit in our names with these words: "May this be for our sake."
"May this [child] follow them wherever they may go, whatever their future rebirth," he thought.

And knowing she was pregnant, he kept her in the upper chambers of the palace, attending to her without restraint; in the cold he provided her with cold requisites, and in the heat with warm requisites, and he fed her with foods prescribed by physicians that were neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty.
She was nourished with foods that were neither too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent, being entirely free from bitter, sour, salty, sweet, pungent, and astringent flavors.
Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove; she moved from couch to couch and seat to seat without ever descending to the ground below.
And for as long as it took for the fetus to reach maturity, she never heard any unpleasant sound whatsoever.
Then, seeing that she had been cherished with great affection by her former husband, the first wife of the Prajāpati, jealousy arose within her,
and she thought:
"If she gives birth to a son, he will certainly cause me trouble; therefore,
by all means, a strategic plan must be devised."
"For one who indulges in sensual pleasures, there is indeed no evil deed that should not be committed."

By her, who was deluded by the prospect of falling into an undesirable rebirth, confidence was instilled and such a substance for inducing miscarriage was given that, as soon as it was drunk, the fetus of that poor woman miscarried.
Then, having assembled all the kinsmen, that second wife interrogated the first wife:
"Having instilled confidence in me, you gave me a substance for inducing miscarriage."
"By whom has my fetus been destroyed?
Thereupon, that first wife began to take an oath in the midst of her kinsmen:
"If I have provided any substance for the destruction of the fetus..."
"Having become a preta, may I devour my sons as each one is born."
"What do you think, Nālada? That wife of the merchant—she is this very female ghost (preta).
Because she, being of an envious nature, administered an abortifacient, she has been reborn among the pretas."
Because she made an oath with false speech,
as the ripening of that karma, she gives birth to five sons day and night and devours them.
Therefore, Nālada, you must strive for the abandonment of verbal misconduct, so that such faults as those of hers may not exist after death.
In this way, Nālada, you should train yourself.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Jāmbāla, the others, and the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth, were uplifted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Jāmbāla (edited by Speyer, Vol. I).
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.

Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples in dependence on Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake.
Now at that time, five hundred hungry ghosts resided in a certain city moat in Vaiśālī.

They eat what has been vomited and consume what has been discarded; they subsist on saliva and urine, feeding on pus, blood, and excrement—terrible beings who are miserable by their very nature. And it is said:
"Those who eat what is vomited and those who consume what is discarded, who live upon saliva and urine..."
"Those who desire pus, blood, and excrement are terrible and inherently miserable. Thus [it is said].
Now in that Vaiśālī, there was a certain brahmin who brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant;
moreover, a foul odor arose from her body.
Thereupon, that brahmin summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them.
They said,
"This is the power of that boy who stays within her womb.
Eventually, after the passing of nine months, she gave birth.

A boy was born who was ill-favored, unsightly, hunchbacked, with limbs smeared with filth, and foul-smelling. Nevertheless, though he was most loathsome, he was reared by his mother and father, who were bound to him by the snares of affection.
He took delight only in places of impurity, such as heaps of refuse and mud.
He plucked out his hair and threw filth into his mouth;
thus, he became known by the name Bāla-jāmbāla.
As he was wandering here and there, he was seen by Pūraṇa Kāśyapa,
who thought to himself:
"In what kind of places this man delights."
"Surely this is a perfected man (siddhapuruṣa). What if I were to ordain him? Thinking thus, he ordained him; the man wandered about naked and engaged in acts of disrespect.
Then, as he was wandering about, he saw five hundred hungry ghosts in the moat of Vaiśālī.

Due to the connection with the ripening of his past karma, he descended into that city moat, joined and came together with them, and took pleasure in their company, entering into friendship with them.
Then, at another time, the boy Jāmbāla, being preoccupied with some business, entered Vaiśālī;
and the Blessed One arrived at the moat of that city.
Those hungry ghosts saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
With his body resplendent with the eighty minor marks, adorned with a fathom-wide aura of light, and possessing a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns—
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides—
they fell at the feet of the Blessed One the very moment they saw him.
The Blessed One asked them, "What is troubling you?
They replied, "We are thirsty, Blessed One."
Then the Blessed One released five streams of water endowed with the eight qualities from his five fingers,
by which those five hundred pretas were fully satisfied. Thereupon, having developed a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One, they passed away.
They were reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) for a son or daughter of the gods who has recently been reborn that three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?
They see that they have passed away from among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
They were reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven because they had conceived a mind of deep faith toward the Blessed One.
Then, it occurred to those sons of the gods who had previously been hungry ghosts:
"It would not be fitting for us to approach the Blessed One for a visit while our period of probation remains unfulfilled."
"What if we were to approach the Blessed One for a visit even before our period of probation has expired?

Then those sons of the gods who had previously been hungry ghosts— wearing swaying, stainless earrings, their bodies adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, their heads crowned with various jewels and gems, their limbs smeared with saffron, tamāla leaves, and spṛkkā, and carrying divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and mandārava flowers— that very night...

Having filled the lap of his garment with flowers and illuminated the entire hall of the gabled pavilion with a sublime radiance, he scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One [discerned] the disposition and underlying tendencies of those sons of the gods who had previously been hungry ghosts.
Having understood their elements (*dhātu*) and dispositions (*prakṛti*), he delivered a teaching of the Dharma that leads to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths;

upon hearing it, five hundred sons of gods shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with its twenty peaks, and attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Having seen the Truth, he was like merchants who have obtained their profit,
like farmers whose crops have ripened,
and like heroes who have won the battle.
As if cured of all their diseases, they returned to their own abodes after circumambulating the Blessed One three times with the same splendor with which they had approached him.
Then Jāmbāla, having come to the city moat, did not see those hungry ghosts (preta).
Thereupon, he began to search for them;
and while searching for them, he became exhausted, yet he could not find them.
In this interval, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

It is indeed the nature of things that for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are greatly compassionate, who act for the benefit of the world, who are guardians of the one [Dharma], who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, and who have crossed over the four floods with their feet firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power— [nothing remains hidden].

Those who have long practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), who are free from the five factors [of the lower realms], who have transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), who are teachers of the eightfold path,

who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), who possess the power of the ten strengths (*daśabala*), whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand [worlds] ruled by the Lord of Vaśavartin.
Three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, his knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into hardship, calamity, and distress? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms?"
Who is leaning toward the states of woe?
Whom might I rescue from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation? To whom, sunk in the mire of sensual desires, might I extend a helping hand?
Whom, being destitute of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereign mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?
Whose eyes, veiled by the cataract of the darkness of ignorance, shall I purify with the ointment-stick of wisdom?
For whom, whose roots of virtue have not yet been planted, shall I plant them?
Whose [roots of merit] have been planted that I might bring them to maturity?
Whose [roots of merit] are matured that I might liberate them? And it is said:
Even the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might exceed its tide; but the Buddha would never abandon those who have approached him for refuge.
But the Buddha would not let the time pass by for those who are like calves to be tamed.

Then the Blessed One, for the sake of favoring the young man Jāmbāla, dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, entered Vaiśālī for alms.
Proceeding in due order as he wandered for alms, he eventually descended into the street.
And Jāmbāla, wandering here and there, stood before the Blessed One;

then he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a walking mountain of light.
Like a mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides;
and upon merely seeing him, his mind was purified in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having become filled with faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and, with palms joined, said:

“If, Blessed One, there is ordination in this Dharma and Vinaya for beings such as myself, may I receive ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Then the Blessed One, his heart encompassed by great compassion and knowing the dispositions and latent tendencies of beings, perceiving that he was a worthy vessel, extended his gold-colored arm— which resembled the trunk of a royal elephant— and said this:

"Come, monk; practice the holy life. As soon as the Blessed One had spoken these words, he stood there with hair as if shaved seven days prior, possessing the deportment of a monk ordained for twelve years, his hands occupied with a bowl and a water-strainer. He said: Vaidya, p. 126: "Come, monk; practice the holy life.
