When addressed by the Tathāgata with the words "Come," his head was shaven and his body was clothed in the saṃghāṭī robe;
with his senses immediately calmed, he stood thus, established in the Buddha's own intention.
Then the Blessed One gave him instructions for mental attention (*manasikāra*).

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states (*saṃskāra*) by means of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and perish, [he attained realization].

Through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward an axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings,
and turned away from existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became one worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indra;
yet, even though he had attained arhatship, he took delight in what was coarse.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, this is the foremost among my monks, my disciples who are devoted to austerity,
namely, the monk Jāmbāla."
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was committed by the Elder Jāmbāla, such that he experiences such suffering?
The Blessed One said:

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Jāmbāla himself in previous births; their conditions have been met, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a surging flood, and being inevitable, these actions were performed and accumulated by Jāmbāla himself.
Who else shall experience them?
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, both wholesome and unwholesome actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases:
"Actions do not perish, even after hundreds of eons."
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, in this very same Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was forty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Truly Enlightened One named Krakucchanda— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital Śobhāvatī.

In that capital, a certain householder had constructed a monastery where monks dwelling in various regions and countries thought it proper to come, to go, and to reside. And in that monastery, there was a resident monk who was an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
And he was exceedingly and intensely envious;
seeing incoming monks, he became resentful, grew angry, became malicious, was dejected, remained fixed in ill-will, and gave rise to anger.
Whenever monks departed from that monastery, seeing them, he would go out to meet them with an abundance of joy and gladness and address them;
then, at another time, an Arhat monk arrived from the countryside.
And that owner of the monastery was a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Because of his deportment, he was recognized as an arhat.
Thereupon, having conceived faith, he invited him together with the community of monks for a meal on the following day and for a bath in a steam-heated bathhouse (*jentāka*).
That resident monk was not there.
Then, on the second day, when the bathhouse bath had been prepared and the meal set out, the resident monk arrived;
he too entered the bathhouse.
He saw the owner of the monastery, dressed in a single garment, performing services for an incoming monk;
thereupon, stinginess arose within him,
and with a corrupted mind, he [spoke] harshly.
This verbal action has been uttered:
"It would indeed be better for you, O monk, if your body were smeared with impurity."
"But I have not accepted attendance from such a donor.
Then that Arhat consented by remaining silent, thinking:
"Lest this poor man should become a partaker of even more grievous karma."
When the assembly, place, and time had come together, a resident monk heard:
"You have conceived a malicious thought toward an Arhat.
Upon hearing this, remorse arose within him.
Then, prostrating at the feet of the Arhat monk, he said:
"Noble one, forgive me for the harsh words I uttered toward you.
Thereupon, the Arhat, in order to increase his faith, ascended into the expanse of the sky and began to display various miraculous feats.
Thereupon, a profound sense of remorse arose within him.
In the presence of that [monk], he confessed, revealed, and laid bare that deed as a transgression;
yet, he was unable to produce the ultimate knowledge.
At the time of his death, he began to make this aspiration:
"Since I harbored a corrupt mind toward an Arhat and uttered harsh words, [may the fruit of that karma be exhausted]."
"May I not experience the ripening of this [present] action;
rather, through the ripening of whatever I have studied, recited, given as gifts, and offered service to the Saṅgha,
may I please the future Perfectly Enlightened Ones and never displease them."
"What do you think, monks? That monk who was the resident of the monastery at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Jāmbāla.
Because he uttered harsh words toward an Arhat,"
Through the ripening of this karma, he experienced endless suffering in *saṃsāra*.
And by the very remainder of that same karma, even now in his final existence, he has become so foul-smelling, supremely malodorous, and intent upon dwelling in places of impurity and refuse-heaps.

Furthermore, because of what he there recited, studied, and mastered—the skill regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), the skill regarding the elements (*dhātu*), the skill regarding the sense-bases (*āyatana*), the skill regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the skill regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*)—[he has attained this].
Having gone forth in my teaching, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in this way: you must strive for the abandonment of stinginess.
For what reason?
These faults that belonged to Jāmbāla when he was an ordinary person will no longer exist;
rather, this very collection of virtues will come to be.
"This is for him who has attained arhatship;
thus, monks, you should train yourselves."
The Blessed One said this;
and those monks, as well as the other gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth, with uplifted minds, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The sixth chapter. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
The black cobra, the moon, the *sāla* tree, and Śrīmati;
clothing, the parrot, the messenger, the buffalo, and indeed Poṣadha;
[and] the swan—this is the last.
AVŚ_51 The Black Snake.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, possessed of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with the community of his disciples.
He was dwelling in dependence on Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

At a city gate in Rājagṛha there was a certain householder who was wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, with extensive and vast holdings; he had accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
Yet he was miserly, stingy, and grasping regarding his belongings; he did not even resolve to offer an oblation to the crows.
Upon seeing ascetics, brahmins, and mendicants, he conceived a corrupt state of mind.
A great heap of silver and gold had been deposited in his own garden;
being greedy for and attached to it, he passed away.
Having died, he was reborn right there as a great venomous black snake with poison in its gaze.
Then, whenever groups of people entered that park,
he deprived them of their lives by a mere glance.
And this report spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha on all sides: "Whoever enters that particular garden,
they all meet their death."
And the multitude of people informed King Bimbisāra.
Then this thought occurred to King Bimbisāra:
"Who is capable of training him, other than the Buddha, the Blessed One?
Then King Bimbisāra, surrounded by a great multitude of people, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As King Bimbisāra sat there to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then King Bimbisāra, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Lord, here in this city of Rājagṛha, in such-and-such a park, there dwells a great venomous black serpent whose very glance is poisonous."
"He is causing great harm to the people;
it would be well if the Blessed One, out of compassion, were to discipline him.
The Blessed One consented to King Bimbisāra by remaining silent.
Then King Bimbisāra, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, rose from his seat, and departed.

Then, at the end of that very night, the Blessed One dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and approached that park. Having arrived, the Blessed One emitted golden rays of light, surpassing the brilliance of a thousand suns.
By these, that entire grove was illuminated;
and rays of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), cultivated over a thousand eons, were emitted, by which his body was gladdened the very moment it was touched.
Then that venomous snake began to look here and there, wondering, "By whose power has my body been so refreshed?
Then he saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
His body was resplendent with the eighty secondary marks, adorned with a fathom-wide halo, and possessed a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns;
like a moving mountain of jewels, he was auspicious on all sides.
Upon merely seeing him, the mind of this man was purified through faith in the presence of the Blessed One.
And to him whose mind was serene, the Blessed One taught the Dharma by means of his own mode of existence and his own birth:
"O gentle-faced one, this very wealth was acquired by you yourself,
by which you were caused to be reborn in the state of a venomous serpent."
"It is well that you have inspired faith in me; now, turn your mind away from this treasure.
Lest, having passed away from here, you should be reborn in the hells."
When his birth was made known to him by the Blessed One,
he began to weep.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Now that you have entered the womb of an animal and have fallen into a state of no opportunity, what shall I do for you? Why do you weep so fruitlessly?"
"It is well; let your mind be pacified toward the Conqueror of great compassion.
Having become detached from this animal rebirth here, you shall then go to heaven. Thus [he spoke].
When the Blessed One had placed it in his alms-bowl and led it to the Bamboo Grove,
in the meantime, King Māgadha and the multitude of people heard that the venomous serpent had been tamed by the Blessed One.
Then that venomous serpent, loathing its own body, undertook a fast;
having conceived a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One, he passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) for a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods who has recently been reborn that three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?
He sees: "I have passed away from among the venomous serpents."
They were reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven because they had developed a serene mind toward the Blessed One.

Then this thought occurred to the son of the gods who had formerly been a venomous serpent: "It would not be fitting for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit while my period of probation remains unfulfilled."
"What if I were to approach the Blessed One for a visit even before my period of probation has expired?

Then, that son of the gods who had formerly been a venomous serpent— wearing shimmering, stainless earrings, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, his crest variegated with precious jewels, and his limbs anointed with saffron,
tamāla leaves, spṛkkā, and other fragrant substances— during that very night [took up] divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and mandārava flowers.
Having filled his lap with flowers, illuminating the entire Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka-nivāsa, with a sublime radiance,
he scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the devaputra who had formerly been a venomous serpent, delivered a discourse on the Dharma such that it led to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard it, the Devaputra formerly known as Āśīviṣa shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times:

"Venerable Sir, what has been done for us by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by our deceased ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins—this [which you have done]..."
The Blessed One has done this for us:
the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up,
and the mountains of bones have been crossed.
The doors to the lower realms have been closed, the doors to heaven and liberation have been opened, and we have been established among gods and humans. And it is said:
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many defects, has indeed been closed.
The most meritorious path to heaven has been opened,
and the way to Nirvana has been found by me.
Through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure and faultless [vision], O one with the perfectly purified eye;
and I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones.
And I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods,
you whose appearance is difficult to encounter even in a thousand lifetimes, and who are free from birth, old age, death, and disease.
"O Sage, today your sight has borne fruit!
Having spoken thus, Pralambahāra, filled with joy, bowed down and paid homage at both the sage's feet.
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies on the right,
he departed for heaven, facing the world of the gods.

Then the son of the gods, formerly a venomous serpent, with the same splendor with which he had approached the Blessed One— like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease— [departed].
On that very night, having approached King Bimbisāra and illuminated the entire royal palace with a sublime radiance, he awakened the king and said this:
"Great King, arise! Arise!"
"Why are you sleeping?
Then the king, having awakened, beheld that sublime radiance and that son of the gods.
Seeing him, with a joyful mind, he asked: "Who are you?"
He said:
"I am that very serpent-venom of wrong views who was disciplined by the Blessed One in that park; having passed away, I have been reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods in the sublime celestial realm."
Having attended upon the Blessed One, I have realized the vision of the Truths.
Now I shall inform you:
go to that grove, and from such-and-such a place, unearth a great treasure and, in my name, feed the Blessed One together with the community of his disciples.
"And cause the instruction of the sacrificial fee to be performed.
King Bimbisāra consented to the son of the gods by remaining silent.
Then, the son of the gods who had previously been a venomous serpent, perceiving the king's consent through his silence, vanished right then and there.
Then King Bimbisāra, having informed the citizens and countryfolk of Magadha during that very night,
went to that park, unearthed the treasure, and after feeding the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for three months, he questioned the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what actions were performed by the son of the gods who was formerly a venomous serpent,
by which he was reborn among the venomous serpents;
and what actions were performed by which he was reborn among the gods?"
"And has the vision of truth been attained?
The Blessed One said:
"Because an excessive degree of greed was produced by him."
Because his mind was corrupted toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and beggars,
he was reborn among venomous serpents; yet, because his mind was filled with faith toward me, [he has attained this state].
Because of that, he was reborn among the gods;
and having become a lay follower under the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, he undertook the taking of refuge and the precepts of training, and by that means, he attained the vision of the Truths.
Therefore, Great King, you should exert yourself for the abandonment of stinginess;
these faults that belong to a venomous serpent will no longer exist,
and this very multitude of virtues will arise.
"O Great King, you should train yourself in this way: 'As it was for that very son of the gods...
Then King Bimbisāra, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
and the monks, with joyful minds, as well as the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
AVŚ_52 Candra. The Buddha,
the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—honored by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus revered by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
In Śrāvastī there was a certain brahmin farmer who had brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing, bringing delight to the minds and eyes of all people.
Upon his birth, a birth festival was held, and his name was determined:
"What shall be the name of this boy?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since at his birth he brought delight to the eyes of all the world, therefore let this boy's name be Candra."
And he was obtained with great difficulty by that brahmin;
moreover, he had no other son or daughter.
He was raised, nurtured, and became a great man.
Because he brought joy to the entire world, he was paraded through the whole city by brahmins and householders.
That brahmin, becoming even more deeply attached to him, remained constantly intent on guarding him during his walking, standing, and reclining.
That brahmin’s house was near Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then, through association with Anāthapiṇḍada, that young brahmin went to the Jeta Grove and heard the word of the Buddha;
he thereby gained faith in the teaching of the Blessed One.
Having had a short life and passed away, he was reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, who dwell in the sublime realms.
It is indeed the natural law that as soon as a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods has been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? And by what karma?"
He saw that, having passed away from among humans, he had been reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven because he had conceived a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One.
Then, this thought occurred to the son of the gods who had previously been a brahmin:
"It would not be fitting for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit once my probation has expired;
rather, I shall approach the Blessed One for a visit before my probation has expired."
Then, preceded by a brahmin, a son of the gods— wearing swaying, stainless earrings, his body resplendent with necklaces and half-necklaces,

his crest adorned with various jewels and gems, and his limbs anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā, and other fragrant substances— filled his lap with divine flowers of blue lotuses, white water-lilies, white lotuses, and mandārava blossoms during that very night, and [arrived] at the entire Jeta Grove.
Having illuminated [the area] with a sublime radiance and scattered flowers over the Blessed One, he sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the son of the gods who was formerly a brahmin, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.

Having heard it, the son of the gods who was formerly a brahmin shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truths, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times: "Venerable Sir, what has been done for us by the Blessed One is not something that could have been done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by our ancestors, nor by ascetics and brahmins."
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed; and the gates to the lower realms have been closed.
The gates to heaven and liberation have been opened; we have been established among gods and humans. And it is said:
[Vaidya, p. 132]
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many faults, has been closed;
the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened.
And the path to nirvāṇa has been found by me. // AVŚ_52.1 //
And through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure, stainless eye of supreme clarity;
I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones.
And I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods,
you for whom birth, old age, death, and disease have ceased— your vision is extremely difficult to obtain throughout thousands of lifetimes.
"O Sage, today your sight has borne fruit!
Having spoken thus, Pralambahāra, filled with joy, bowed down and pressed both feet in salutation.
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies on the right,
he departed for heaven, facing toward the world of the gods.

Then the son of the gods, preceded by the brahmin, departed for his own abode with the same splendor with which he had come into the presence of the Blessed One— like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease.
The monks dwelt devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
They saw a sublime radiance in the presence of the Blessed One;
having seen it, they were filled with doubt and questioned the Blessed One:
"Lord, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the Lord of Devas, and the four World Protectors approach the Blessed One during this night to see him?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the Lord of Devas, nor the four World Protectors have approached me to see me."
Furthermore, that only son of this brahmin, who was short-lived and has passed away,
having conceived a serene faith in my presence, has been reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the sublime deities;
he approached me during this very night.
I taught him the Dharma,
and having seen the truth, he returned to his own abode.

In the meantime, that brahmin, having carried his only son—who was beloved, charming, dear, pleasing, patient, and compliant—to the cremation ground, placed him on his lap and lamented most piteously, crying out, "Alas, my little son! Alas, my only son!
Although his kinsmen offered many attempts to dispel his grief, they were unable to make him rise.
Surrounded by crows, ospreys, dogs, jackals, and vultures, followed by women with disheveled hair and watched by a great multitude of people, he stood there.

Then his son, who had become a god, seeing his father lamenting, was moved by compassion and his heart trembled; in order to dispel his father’s grief, he manifested himself in the guise of a seer and remained near the cremation ground practicing the "five-fire" austerity.
Then that brahmin asked the seer: "O Great Seer, what do you seek by means of this asceticism? The seer replied: "I seek a kingdom."
May my chariot be made of gold, variegated with various jewels;
may the sun and moon be its two wheels,
and may the four world-protectors bow down before it.
"Therefore, having mounted that chariot, I shall travel across this great earth.
The brahmin said:
"Even if you were to heat it continuously for a full hundred years,"
"For you shall not obtain that state, even through supreme austerity. Thus [he spoke].
The seer said:
"And what do you seek with this corpse—this impure, most foul-smelling, dead body that has become like a piece of wood?
The brahmin replied:
"My only beloved son has passed away;
request him [to return]," he said. The seer replied:
"Even if you were to weep incessantly for a full hundred years, you would not regain that son; for what is the use of your weeping? Thus [he spoke].
Then, that brahmin, having understood the words of the seer to be true, felt faith arise within him; and having become faithful, he asked:
"Who are you?"
Then the seer, having made that disguise disappear and standing in his own form, said to his father:
"I am that only son of yours who, having developed faith in the Blessed One, passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven."
"I have come here for the sake of dispelling your sorrow. Come, dear son, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One;
in this way, you too may bring about your transcendence of saṃsāra."
Then that brahmin, having abandoned the dead body, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
For him, the Blessed One gave a teaching on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.
Having heard this, that brahmin shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having achieved his rise and obtained his gain, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed.
Then the monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Blessed One, how this son of the gods, having dispelled the grief of his father, has established him in the vision of the Truth."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, what is the wonder here that he, having now seen the Truths, has saved his father?
Rather, it is this: in the past, while still an ordinary person, he saved his father even as he was being deprived of life up to three times."
Listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain adulterer.
His son was virtuous, of noble intention, and exceedingly well-regarded by the world. Eventually, his father committed a theft.
Then the king commanded, "Let him be executed!
Thereupon, the son petitioned the king as many as three times and spared his life by means of a favor.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the adulterer, is this very brahmin."
This very brahmin boy is the son of an adulterer.
The monks asked: "What karma was performed by which father and son attained the vision of the Truth?
The Blessed One said:
When Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, was still alive, they had become lay followers and had undertaken the training precepts of taking refuge;
therefore, they have now realized the vision of the truths.
For this reason, monks, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
"All phenomena are without self;
Nirvana is peace. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves with diligence toward Nirvana.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
the monks, with joyful minds, as well as the others—the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
AVŚ 53: Sāla.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Now at that time, a festival called Sālabhañjikā had arrived in Śrāvastī;
there, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered, taking sāla flowers, playing, enjoying themselves, and diverting their pleasure.
Just then, a certain merchant’s daughter, having taken *sāla* flowers, was entering Śrāvastī;
and the Blessed One, surrounded by a multitude of monks, was departing from Śrāvastī after wandering for alms.
That girl beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Having seen him— his body radiant with the eighty minor marks, adorned with a fathom-wide halo, possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect— and having seen him, she was filled with serene faith and scattered *sāla* flowers over the Blessed One.
Then, having circumambulated him and turned back,
she thought, "I shall bring yet other things for the sake of the house," and while she was climbing a *sāla* tree, she fell.

Having performed services for the Blessed One, she passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; eventually, adorned with a celestial palace of *sāla* flowers, she approached the assembly of gods.
At that time, Śakra, the lord of the gods, was in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, in the midst of the host of deities, speaking in praise of the Buddha,
and speaking in praise of the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, beheld that celestial maiden, adorned with a celestial vehicle made of *sāla* flowers, whose roots of merit were fully ripened.
Having seen him, he replied with a verse:

"By whom was your body polished until it resembles refined gold? Your body possesses the luster of a lotus and a blue water-lily; this incomparable splendor of your body—whence has this radiance issued forth from your person?"
"O goddess, tell me by what [action] your face has become like a blossomed lotus and possesses the luster of gold; tell me this fruit which is experienced as born of karma."
The deity said:
"That Sun among Men, together with his disciples, is adorned with excellent marks;
having performed that wholesome deed, he shines even more brilliantly than I."
His face, lovely to behold, possesses a radiance as pure as the moon rising from the water.
Śakra said:
"Aho! This field consists of virtues and is free from all defects;
it is here that the seed you have sown for the sake of rebirth in heaven has been placed."
Who would not worship the Buddha, who is as fair as a magnificent heap of gold, whose eyes are like the broad petals of a pure lotus?
There, the faces of the excellent women, with eyes as broad as lotuses, shone forth, produced by their [respective] offices.
It is indeed the natural law that as soon as a son or daughter of the gods has been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?"
She saw that she had passed away from among humans and been reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven because she had conceived a serene faith in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, this thought occurred to that divine maiden:
"It would not be fitting for me that I should approach the Blessed One for a visit after my period of probation has expired;
rather, let me approach the Blessed One for a visit while my period of probation is still unexpired.
Then that celestial maiden, wearing shimmering and stainless earrings, her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and her crest decorated with various jewels and gems—

Her body was anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā, and other fragrant substances; surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of deities, she approached the presence of the Blessed One together with that very palanquin of *sāla* flowers.
Having scattered flowers over the Blessed One, she sat before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood that goddess’s disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, delivered a discourse on the Dharma conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Upon hearing it, that celestial maiden shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, she uttered this inspired exclamation three times:

"Venerable Sir, this which has been done for us by the Blessed One was not done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the deities, nor by the king, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by our ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins;
it is that the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up."
The mountains of bones have been leaped over;
the gates to the states of woe have been closed; the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened.
"We have been established among gods and humans. And he said:
"By your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many defects, has been closed."
The most meritorious path to heaven has been opened,
and the way to Nirvana has been found by me.
And through taking refuge in you, O one with the perfectly pure eye, I have today attained the pure [vision] that is free from all defects.
I have attained the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones,
and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods,
you whose appearance is extremely difficult to encounter throughout thousands of existences, and who are free from birth, old age, death, and disease.
"O Sage, today your sight has borne fruit! Having spoken thus, she— her necklace hanging low—
bowed down and, filled with joy, paid homage at both his feet.
And having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies on the right,
she departed for heaven, facing the world of the gods.
Then that celestial maiden, like a merchant who has gained profit,
like a farmer rich in grain, like a hero who has won a battle,
or like a sick man freed from all disease, returned to her own abode with the very same splendor with which she had come into the presence of the Blessed One.
The monks dwelt devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night.
By them was seen a magnificent radiance in the presence of the Blessed One.
Seeing this, they became doubtful and asked the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a visit this night?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor even the four world-protectors who approached me for a vision;
rather, did you not see that girl by whom I was strewn with *sāla* flowers along the way?"
"So it is, Venerable Sir. Having developed a mind of serene faith toward me, she passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
She has approached my presence this very night."
The Dharma was taught to her by me, and having seen the Truths, she departed for her own abode.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall honor, revere, respect, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. [Avadānaśataka 54] Śrīmatī (edited by Speyer, Vol. I)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt near Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, together with the community of disciples.
In the city of Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra reigned; it was prosperous, flourishing, secure, and well-supplied with food.

And he ruled a kingdom that was crowded with many people, free from strife, quarrels, riots, and tumults, devoid of thieves and disease, abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffaloes, entirely without thorns, and protected as if it were his only son.
This was when King Bimbisāra had seen the Truths in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, during the night, he approached the Blessed One together with his harem.

Later, at another time, when the spring season had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, King Bimbisāra, surrounded by his queen and his harem, went to a forest grove resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvakas.
He went out to the park grounds,
and there the women of the harem addressed the king: "Your Majesty, we are unable to approach the Blessed One day after day."

"Therefore, it would be well if the Lord would have a stūpa for the hair and nails of the Tathāgata established here in this inner apartment, wherein we might repeatedly perform worship with flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, parasols, banners,
and flags. Thereupon,
King Bimbisāra made a request to the Blessed One.
"Let our hair and nails be given to us, so that we may install a stūpa of the Tathāgata within the inner apartments.
When the Blessed One had granted his hair and nails,
King Bimbisāra, together with the women of the harem, installed a stūpa for the hair and nails of the Tathāgata within the inner apartments with great honor.
And there in the inner apartments, the women of the harem performed worship with lamps, incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.

Furthermore, when King Ajātaśatru, instigated by Devadatta, deprived his father— the righteous Dharmarāja— of life and himself took over the kingdom, all the offerings for the sake of the Blessed One’s teaching were completely cut off.
And a formal agreement was made that no one should perform services at the stūpa of the Tathāgata;
however, when the *pravāraṇā* ceremony took place on the fifteenth day, [the agreement was disregarded].
At that time, no one was performing any cleaning, nor offering lamps, incense, or flowers at the Hair-and-Nail Stūpa.
Then, the women of the inner apartments, recollecting the Hair-and-Nail Stūpa and King Bimbisāra in such a state, began to weep most piteously, saying:
"Alas, what misery! Through separation from the Dharma-King, we have been deprived of our merit."
And there was a woman of the inner apartments named Śrīmatī;
disregarding her own life and recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, she cleaned the stūpa of hair and nails and offered a garland of lamps.
When Ajātaśatru, having gone to the upper terrace of the palace, saw that sublime radiance, he asked, "What is this?"
When another person reported,
"Śrīmatī has made a garland of lamps at the stūpa of hair and nails," he then summoned Śrīmatī and said to her:
"Why do you transgress the king's command?
She replied,
"Even though I have indeed transgressed your command,"
"However, I have not transgressed the command of King Bimbisāra, the King of Dharma.
Thereupon, he, being enraged, hurled a discus and deprived her of life.
Having died with a mind full of faith toward the Blessed One, she was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
At that time, an assembly of gods had gathered.
Then the divine maiden Śrīmatī, illuminating a full yojana with a circle of divine radiance, approached the assembly of gods.
Thereupon, Śakra, the lord of the gods, seeing that sublime illumination and divine splendor extending for a full yojana, asked:
By what means has your body become like polished gold and radiant as a lotus and a blue water-lily?
This incomparable splendor of your limbs—whence has this radiance issued forth from your body? And by what means has your face become like a blossomed lotus and the color of refined gold?
Tell me, O deity, what is this fruit born of karma that is being experienced? AVŚ_54.1 //
The deity said: Having beheld the Buddha, the Lord of the three worlds, the lamp of the universe, endowed with the excellent marks,
she lit a lamp for that best of speakers, who dispels darkness and removes the gloom of the afflictions.
Seeing the radiance, which was the color of moonbeams, he conceived a state of serene faith toward the Sage;
and beholding that light with joy, he paid homage to the Teacher, the best among speakers.
By that deed, my body shines exceedingly with splendor;
my face, pure as the moon and a lotus, is lovely to behold.
Śakra said:
"Aho! This field consists of virtues and is free from all defects;
it is here that you have sown the seed for the sake of rebirth in heaven."
Who would not worship the Buddha, who is as radiant as a magnificent heap of gold, whose eyes are like the broad petals of a pure lotus?
There, the faces of the excellent women, with eyes as broad as lotuses, shone forth, produced by their [sexual] passion.
It is indeed the natural law that as soon as a son or daughter of the gods has been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?"
She saw that she had passed away from among humans and been reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven because she had developed a serene mind toward the Blessed One.
Then, this thought occurred to the divine maiden Śrīmatī:
"It would not be fitting for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit while my period of probation is still unfulfilled;
rather, I shall approach the Blessed One for a visit before my probation has expired.
Then the divine maiden Śrīmatī, enveloped by the radiance of her celestial power, [took] celestial blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and *mandārava* flowers...
Having filled her lap and illuminated the entire Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, with a sublime radiance,
she scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat before him to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the glorious divine maiden, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that leads to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Upon hearing this, the illustrious celestial maiden shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose with twenty peaks, with the vajra of knowledge, and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, she uttered this inspired exclamation three times:

"Venerable Sir, this which has been done for us was not done by mother, nor by father, nor by king, nor by deities, nor by beloved kinsmen and relatives, nor by deceased ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins."
The Blessed One has done this for us:
the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up,
and the mountains of bones have been crossed.
The gates to the lower realms have been closed, the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened, and we have been established among gods and humans. And it is said:
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many defects, has been closed;
the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened.
And the path to nirvāṇa has been found by me.
And through reliance upon you, O one with the perfectly pure eye, I have today attained the pure [vision] that is free from all defects.
I have attained the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones,
and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods,
you for whom birth, old age, death, and disease have vanished— your appearance is extremely difficult to encounter even in a thousand lifetimes.
O Sage, today your sight has become fruitful for me.
Then, bowing down with her long necklace hanging low, she worshipped his two feet with joy;
having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies, keeping him to her right—
Facing the world of the gods, she went to heaven.
Then the illustrious celestial maiden, like a merchant who has gained profit,
like a farmer rich with a bountiful harvest, like a hero who has won a battle,
and like a sick man freed from all disease, returned to her own abode with the very same splendor with which she had come into the presence of the Blessed One.
The monks, devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, dwelt there;
by them was seen a magnificent radiance in the presence of the Blessed One.
Seeing this, they became doubtful and asked the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a visit this night?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of gods, nor even the four world-protectors who approached me for a vision.

Rather, it was a woman of King Bimbisāra’s harem named Śrīmatī who, disregarding her own life and recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, offered a garland of lamps at the stūpa of the Tathāgata’s hair and nails;
she was subsequently deprived of her life by the enraged King Ajātaśatru."
Having developed a mind of serene faith toward me, she passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
She approached my presence during this very night,
and the Dharma was taught to her by me.
Having seen the truths, she returned to her own abode.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher."
"Having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of the Cloth] (Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— he was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwells at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with the community of disciples. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered the Jeta Grove to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
And gradually, he gave a hundred koṭis for the teaching of the Blessed One;
at that time, the thought occurred to him:
"What is so wonderful in this, that I am giving gifts?"
"Or rather, let me perform meritorious deeds;
suppose I were to solicit alms from the body of people residing in Śrāvastī for the sake of favoring the poor, and thereby attend upon the Blessed One together with his community of disciples?
In this way, a great benefit will have been rendered by me to the multitude of people."
"And much merit will be generated by him.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada reported this matter to the king,
and the king caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout all of Śrāvastī:
"Listen, citizens residing in Śrāvastī!
Today, on the seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, mounted upon the back of an elephant, intends to solicit voluntary offerings for the sake of the Tathāgata and his community of disciples.
Whatever amount each of you is able to relinquish, that should be given."

On the seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, mounted upon the back of an elephant, began to solicit alms for the sake of the Tathāgata and his community of disciples. There, those who possessed wealth to a certain extent proceeded to give that much; some gave a single garment.
Some [offered] bracelets, some armlets,
and some garlands of gold.
Some [offered] finger-rings, some pearl necklaces.
Some [gave] silver, some gold, and some even as much as a kārṣāpaṇa coin.
The householder also accepts [the gift] for the sake of benefiting others.
Now, there was a certain woman who was extremely poor;
after three months of great hardship, she had earned a single piece of cloth.
Having put on that cloth, she went out into the street.
And as Anāthapiṇḍada was approaching from afar,
he was seen by her while conch shells and drums were being sounded;
she then asked a certain lay follower:
"If this householder is so wealthy, possessing great riches and vast property, and can even see treasures hidden beneath the ground, why does he wander for alms among other families?
She was thus addressed by the lay follower:
For the sake of benefiting others:
he bestows favor upon those who are unable to feed the Blessed One together with the community of disciples.
"How can so many gathered together present [this] to the Blessed One?
Then, this thought occurred to that girl:
"I, for one, have not performed meritorious deeds."
"I do not have the power to provide a meal for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples by myself;
what if I were to give him something from here?"
Looking at her own possessions, she saw nothing except for a cloth;
she began to think:
"If I give this cloth while remaining right here,"
"I shall become naked;
what if I were to climb onto the roof of the shelter and throw down my cloth?
Thereupon, she climbed onto the roof of the shelter, removed the cloth from her body, and threw it over Anāthapiṇḍada.
The householder observed her and thought:
"Surely this is the very wealth she possesses, that she has thrown [this] while staying in the shelter.
He then gave an order to his own servants.
"Go, sirs,
and investigate by whom this cloth was thrown down.
They investigated until they saw her sitting there in a squatting posture.
Then she was questioned by them, and she said:
"Whatever wealth I possessed, having promised it for the purpose of proclaiming the virtues of the Blessed One, I became terrified by the fear of poverty."
"Out of fear of poverty,
she gave [it] to the community of monks headed by the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, they informed Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then, filled with supreme wonder, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada clothed that girl in various garments and ornaments;
however, being short-lived, she passed away and was reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, who possess exquisite splendor. As soon as she was reborn, such garments appeared for her.
It belongs to no other son of the gods or daughter of the gods.
It is indeed the natural law that as soon as a son or daughter of the gods has been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?"
She saw that she had passed away from among humans and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven because of her gift of a cloth to the Blessed One.
Then the goddess who had given the garment appeared, wearing shimmering, stainless earrings, her body radiant with necklaces and half-necklaces, and her crest adorned with various jewels and gems.

Her body anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā, and other fragrant substances, she filled her lap that very night with divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and mandārava flowers— and having illuminated the entire Jeta Grove with a magnificent radiance,
she scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the divine maiden who had offered the cloth, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.

Upon hearing it, the divine maiden who had offered the cloth shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, she uttered this inspired exclamation three times:

"Venerable sir, this which has been done for us was not done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by those who have passed away before, nor by recluses and brahmins; that which has been done— [by you]—
the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up."
The mountains of bones have been leaped over;
the gates to the states of woe have been closed; the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened.
"We have been established among gods and humans. And he said:
"By your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many faults, has been closed."
The most meritorious path to heaven has been opened,
and the way to Nirvana has been found by me.
And through taking refuge in you, O one with the perfectly pure eye, I have today attained the pure [vision] that is free from all defects.
I have attained the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones,
and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods,
you whose appearance is difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes, and who are free from birth, old age, death, and disease.
O Sage, today your sight has been fruitful for me.
Then,
bowing down with her long necklace hanging low, she joyfully saluted his two feet and circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies, keeping him to her right.
Facing the world of the gods, she went to heaven.
Then the celestial maiden who had presented the cloth, like a merchant who has gained profit,
like a farmer rich with crops, like a hero who has won a battle,
and like a sick man freed from all disease, returned to her own abode with the very same splendor with which she had approached the presence of the Blessed One.
The monks were dwelling devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night.
They saw a magnificent radiance in the presence of the Blessed One;
having seen it, they were filled with doubt and questioned the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a vision during this night?
The Blessed One said:
“Monks, neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor the four world-protectors have approached me for a vision.”
The poor girl who, while the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was soliciting alms for cloth, gave him a garment and passed away,
has been reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods of exquisite splendor;
she approached me this very night.
I taught her the Dharma;
having conceived faith, she departed, and having seen the Truths, she went to her own abode.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall perform services for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and not unkind acts.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 56: The Parrot (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed great merit.

The Blessed One, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a community of disciples.
In the city of Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra reigned; it was prosperous, flourishing, secure, and well-supplied with food.

And he ruled his kingdom— which was crowded with many people, free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and disturbances, devoid of thieves and disease, abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo, and entirely without thorns— as if it were an only son.
And that king was faithful, auspicious, and of noble intent;
he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, and affectionate toward his subjects like a father toward his children.
While he remained there, longing to see the Blessed One, resting his cheek upon his hand and lost in thought,
the minister asked him:
"Your Majesty, for what reason do you grieve?"
The king said: "It has been a long time since I last saw the Sugata;
therefore, I long for a vision of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, having retired for his midday rest, heard with his pure, superhuman divine ear that King Bimbisāra was longing [to see him].
In this interval, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

It is indeed the nature of things that for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are great in compassion, who act for the benefit of the world, who are guardians of the one [Dharma], who dwell in tranquility and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, who have crossed over the four floods, and whose feet are firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power— [there is nothing hidden].
Those who have long practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), who are free from the five factors, who have transcended the five destinies,

who are endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), who are teachers of the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), who possess the power of the ten strengths (*daśabala*), whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods.
Three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, his knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms? Who is heading toward the lower realms?"
Whom shall I rescue from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation? To whom, sunk in the mire of desire, shall I extend a helping hand?
Whom, bereft of the wealth of the noble ones, shall I establish in the sovereignty and mastery of the wealth of the noble ones?
Whose eyes, shrouded by the film of the darkness of ignorance, shall I cleanse with the salve-stick of wisdom?
Whose unplanted roots of merit shall I cause to be planted? Whose already-planted roots shall I bring to maturity?
