"What do you think, monks? That buffalo was this very Tripita."
Those who were his disciples are these buffalo-herders;
by that karma, they were reborn among buffaloes for five hundred births.
And these five hundred keepers of the queen have become so;
because they purified their minds toward me, they were reborn among the gods and have realized the vision of the Truths.
Therefore, monks, you must strive for the abandonment of verbal misconduct so that these faults which befell the buffalo and the buffalo-herders shall not occur;
instead, this very collection of virtues that belonged to him when he was a son of the gods shall come to pass.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 59:
Upoṣadha (ed. Speyer, vol. I)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras,
garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus worshiped by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; the Buddha, the Blessed One, was renowned and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a community of disciples. Now at that time, a son of the gods among the Trāyastriṃśa deities named Upoṣadha approached the Blessed One again and again to listen to the Dharma.
Then, at another time, a son of the gods named Upoṣadha, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the son of the gods Upoṣadha, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that it leads to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard this, the divine son Upoṣadha shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times:

"Venerable Sir, this which has been done for us was not done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by our ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins."
The Blessed One has done this for us:
the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up,
and the mountains of bones have been crossed.
The doors to the lower realms have been closed;
the doors to heaven and liberation have been opened; we have been established among gods and humans. And it is said:
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils, has been closed;
the auspicious path to heaven has been opened wide.
And the path to nirvāṇa has been found by me.
Through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure, stainless eye of perfect clarity, free from all defects.
I have attained the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones; I am one who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering. (Speyer: *suviśuddha-cakṣuḥ*) AVŚ_59.2 //
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods,
you whose appearance is difficult to encounter even in thousands of lifetimes, and who are free from birth, old age, death, and disease.
O Sage, today your sight has been fruitful for me.
Then, bowing down and having saluted both feet with his long pendants hanging down, he was filled with joy;
and having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies, keeping him to his right—
Facing the world of the gods, he went to heaven.
Then, monks, as they dwelt devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night,
they saw a sublime radiance in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having seen it, they were moved with awe and questioned the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, have Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approached the Blessed One for a vision this night?
The Blessed One said:
“Monks, neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor even the four world-protectors have approached me for a vision.”

"Furthermore, among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, a son of the gods named Upoṣadha, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, approached me for a vision. I taught him the Dharma, and having seen the Truths, he departed for his own abode."
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, from what did the birth and the manifestation of the name of the divine son Upoṣadha arise?
The Blessed One said:
"Do you monks wish to hear?— Yes, Venerable Sir. Therefore, monks, listen."
Listen well and attend closely; I shall speak.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, in this very Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Truly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He was dwelling in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
Then, at another time, King Kṛkī approached the Blessed One for the purpose of seeing him and paying him honor. At that same time, two brahmins also went to Ṛṣipatana on some business.
The king was seen by them with great royal splendor and great royal majesty; a desire for sovereignty arose in them,
and they questioned a certain lay follower:
"O Buddhist lay follower,
what karma must one perform so that whatever he thinks of or prays for, all of it succeeds?
The lay follower replied:
"Whoever observes the pure fast endowed with the eight factors,
whatever they contemplate or whatever they pray for, all that shall be fulfilled for them.
Thereupon, those two brahmins, having received from the householder Āṣāḍha the fast endowed with the eight factors, observed it.
Then, one [of them] was purified and protected;
having passed away, he entered into the state of being the son of King Kṛkī,
and the name Sujāta was established for him.
Upon his father's passing, he was established in the kingdom.
By the second [act], his fast was broken;
having died, he was reborn among the nāgas.
Above him, day after day, hot sand falls seven times, by which he is reduced to nothing but bones.
This thought occurred to him:
"Of what action is this the fruit? Of what action is this the ripening of the fruit, by which I experience such suffering?
He saw: "Having undertaken the eightfold fast (*upavāsa*), I was negligent regarding the training; it is because of that that I now experience such great suffering."
But by him who, having undertaken it, protected it, the kingdom was regained.
This thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now also..."
"For that long, I shall observe the fast endowed with its eight limbs,
so that perhaps there might be liberation from this birth as a nāga."
Then, having made his serpent-form disappear and having manifested himself in the form of a brahmin, he approached the king.
Having approached and greeted him with wishes for victory and long life, he said:
"Great King, I have need of the fast endowed with its eight limbs."
Therefore, Your Majesty ought to observe the fast endowed with its eight limbs;
otherwise, if you do not observe it,
I shall certainly split your head into seven pieces.
Having said this, he vanished right there.

Then the king, terrified, trembling, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, tied a basket of gold to the tip of his banner and caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout his entire realm:
"Whoever shall teach me the fast endowed with the eight limbs..."
"I shall give him this golden casket and honor him with great hospitality.
Now, there was a certain elderly woman who was the daughter of a mason.
She showed the king the pillar, saying:
"My father repeatedly performed worship with perfumes, incense, and flowers at this pillar;
pull it up and examine it."
Then the king gave an order to his attendants:
"Let this pillar be uprooted.
Thereupon, the king's men uprooted the pillar.
Beneath it, the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) inscribed upon a golden leaf was obtained,
along with the five precepts of a lay follower (upāsaka-śikṣāpada) and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣya-dharma).
Then, the king, having written down the eightfold fast for that nāga, gave it to him.
And by twelve thousand ṛṣis dwelling at Ṛṣipatana, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening were realized.
That nāga, having observed the fast endowed with the eight limbs, emerged onto dry land and remained there with his body cast aside;
having undertaken abstinence from food, he passed away and was reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, who are sublime, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred.
Therefore, monks, this is the origin and the manifestation of what is called the Uposatha.
The Blessed One spoke thus.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [Avadānaśataka 60:
The Geese] (ed. Speyer, vol. I)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas; thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwells at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a community of disciples.
In Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit of Kosala rules; the kingdom is prosperous, flourishing, and secure.
The kingdom was abundant in food, crowded with many people, free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest; it was devoid of thieves and disease,
rich in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo, entirely without thorns,
and he protected it as if it were his only son.
Then, at another time, King Prasenajit of Kośala went out to the Jetavana to approach and attend upon the Blessed One.
King Pañcāla had sent five hundred swans as a gift to King Prasenajit of Kośala;
when the king went out to the Jetavana, those five hundred swans were presented to him.
Then King Prasenajit, having granted them the gift of fearlessness, released them right there in the Jeta Grove. When the Blessed One, surrounded by great disciples, sat down near the Ajina tree,
Then those swans approached the presence of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One, as well as the great śrāvakas, also gave them morsels of food.
Having eaten and being satisfied, they remain with their senses composed.
Whenever the Blessed One rises from his seclusion and teaches the Dharma to the fourfold assembly, those swans go into the presence of the Blessed One and listen to the Dharma.
Having passed away with short lifespans, they were reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
It is indeed the natural law that as soon as a son or daughter of the gods has been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?"
They saw that those who had fallen from among the swans had been reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven because they had conceived a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One.

Then those sons of the gods, who had previously been swans, wearing shimmering, stainless earrings, their bodies adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and their crests variegated with jewels and gems—

With their bodies anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā, and other unguents, they filled their laps with divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-lotuses, white lotuses, and mandārava blossoms— and having illuminated the entire Jeta Grove with a sublime radiance that very night,
they scattered flowers over the Blessed One and sat before him to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and natures of those sons of the gods who had previously been swans, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.

Upon hearing it, those sons of the gods who had previously been swans shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, they were like merchants who had gained a profit.
Like farmers with abundant crops, like heroes who have won a battle,
or like the sick freed from all disease, they returned to their own abodes with the very same splendor with which they had come into the presence of the Blessed One.
The monks were dwelling devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night. They saw a magnificent radiance in the presence of the Blessed One,
and having seen it, they became doubtful and questioned the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, have Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approached the Blessed One for a vision this night?
The Blessed One said, “Monks, neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor the four world-protectors have approached me for a vision.”
"Furthermore, monks, did you see those five hundred swans released here by King Prasenajit of Kośala?
Yes, Venerable Sir. Having conceived a mind of serene faith toward me, they have passed away."
They were reborn among the sublime gods;
they have approached my presence this very night,
and the Dharma has been taught to them by me.
And those who had seen the truths returned to their own abodes.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by these sons of gods who were formerly swans, as a result of which they were reborn among the swans;
and what deeds were performed by them as a result of which they were reborn among the gods and attained the vision of the Truth?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by them in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and being inevitable, these actions were performed and accumulated by them."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element,
but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— reach their maturation.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Long ago, monks, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One,
was dwelling in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
There, these who had gone forth into homelessness became lax in their training.
"Because they had developed a mind of faith toward me, they were reborn among the haṃsas; because they had developed a mind of faith toward me, they were reborn among the gods;
and because of the remaining precepts they observed, they have realized the vision of the Truth."

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having set aside actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The seventh chapter. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Suvarṇābha, Sugandhi, Vapuṣmat, Balavat, Priya, Padmākṣa, Dundubhi, Sūrya, and Mallapatākā were his sons. Suvarṇābha.

(Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. I)

Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, was dwelling at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove.

In Kapilavastu, there was a certain Śākya who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging possessions; he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born who was handsome, beautiful, and pleasing, surpassing human appearance yet not having fully attained divine color, resembling refined gold from the Jambū river.
And by this golden-colored radiance, the entire city of Kapilavastu was illuminated.
Upon seeing it, his parents and other beings who had gathered out of curiosity were struck with great wonder and thought:
"Whence has such a distinguished being come?
Having performed a birth festival for him at his birth, they established his name, asking:
"What shall be the name of this child?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since, by the mere birth of this child, the entire city of Kapilavastu has been illuminated with a golden radiance, therefore let the boy's name be Suvarṇābha."
The boy Suvarṇābha was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean him, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nourished by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent provisions of the finest quality.
He grows quickly like a lotus in a pond;
he is learned, discerning, wise, faithful, auspicious, of noble intention, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma.

Then, at another time, while he was sporting outside the monastery, intoxicated by the pride of his physical form, many Śākyas went to the Nyagrodha Grove. Thereupon, Suvarṇābha saw them and questioned them:
"Where are you going, sirs?
They replied, "We are going to the Nyagrodha Grove to see the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Upon hearing the name "Buddha Suvarṇābha," which he had never heard before, all his pores bristled with joy.
And a supreme curiosity arose in him;
he thought to himself:
"What if I were also to approach the Buddha, the Blessed One, in order to see him?"
He also went to the Nyagrodha Grove;
there he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides;
and upon merely seeing him—
That pride of his regarding physical form vanished;
having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One then taught the Dharma to him.
Having heard that Dharma, he became desirous of going forth.
Having obtained permission from his mother and father, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
may I practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, extending his gold-colored arm which resembled the trunk of an elephant, said this to the boy Suvarṇābha: "Come, young man!"
"Practice the holy life," said the Tathāgata; and being thus addressed with the words "Come," he stood there with shaven head and body wrapped in the saṃghāṭī robe,
his senses immediately calmed, established thus by the Buddha’s mental resolve.
For seven days he kept his hair and beard shorn, maintaining for twelve years the deportment of one fully ordained; with bowl and outer robe held in his hands, he stood before the Blessed One.
The Blessed One bestowed upon him mental attention (*manasikāra*).
By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he [pierced] this very five-faceted wheel of saṃsāra.

Having understood that all conditioned states are unstable and having struck them down by realizing their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights.
Averse to existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshiped, revered, and saluted by the gods including Indra and Upendra.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Suvarṇābha such that he is so handsome and pleasing to behold, and having gone forth, he has realized arhatship before long?
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Suvarṇābha in previous births; their conditions have been met, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
These actions were performed and accumulated by Suvarṇābha—who else shall experience them?"
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— do not ripen in the element of wind, but rather ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
for actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one eons ago, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Vipaśyin appeared in the world—

endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī.

When the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, having fulfilled the work of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder— like a fire extinguished for lack of fuel— King Bandhumat performed the funeral rites for the Blessed One’s body and erected a stupa made of the four jewels, one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height.
A festival for the stūpa had been prepared.
While that stūpa festival was underway, a certain householder went out;
there he saw a golden-colored mirror fallen from that stūpa.
Having had a crest-jewel fashioned by him, it was placed upon that stūpa;
and having performed worship with perfumes, incense, and flowers, he prostrated at the feet [of the Buddha] and made this aspiration:
"May I too become a possessor of such qualities as these."
"May I please a Teacher exactly such as this."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was the householder at that time and on that occasion was this very Suvarṇābha."
Because he performed acts of service at the stūpa of the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin, he has come to possess such an excellence of form;
and because he made that aspiration, he has realized arhatship in this very life.

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having set aside entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white deeds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. *Sugandhi* (Avadānaśataka 62).
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples in Kapilavastu at the Nyagrodha Monastery.

In Kapilavastu there lived a certain son of good family, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and dallied with her.
While he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and dallying, a son was born to him—handsome, beautiful, and pleasing, surpassing human appearance yet not having fully attained divine appearance.
From his mouth the fragrance of a blue lotus wafts forth, and from his entire body the fragrance of sandalwood. Having performed the birth festival for him at his birth, his name was established:
"What shall be the name of this boy?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since from his mouth the fragrance of a blue lotus wafts forth, and from his body the fragrance of sandalwood."
"Therefore, let the boy's name be Sugandhi.
The boy Sugandhi was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
He was reared and nourished by eight nurses with milk, curds, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various excellent provisions most refined.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
By the power of his past causes, he became faithful, noble, of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma.
Whenever the boy Sugandha, adorned with armlets, necklaces, and bracelets, descended into the street,
he filled the entire city with the fragrance of sandalwood;
and the multitude of people, smelling that divine scent, were struck with supreme wonder.
And he spoke thus: "Oh, how great is the power of merits! Then, at another time, the boy Sugandha went to the Nyagrodha Grove.
Then he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body resplendent with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide aura, possessing a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, his mind was filled with serene faith;
having developed such faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Knowing his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, the Blessed One gave him a teaching on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.

Upon hearing it, the youth Sugandhika shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he requested permission from his parents and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he [pierced] this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra.

Having understood all conditioned states to be unstable and having struck them down by realizing their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings.
Turning his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Sugandhin such that the fragrance of a blue lotus wafts from his mouth and the fragrance of sandalwood from his entire body?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, Sugandhin indeed performed and accumulated these actions in previous births; their provisions were gathered, their conditions have ripened, they have arrived like a flood, and being inevitable, these actions were performed and accumulated by Sugandhin."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element,
but rather it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

"What shall be the name of this boy?

he gathers together ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and beggars through various distributions of gifts.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a community of disciples. In Śrāvastī there was a certain brahmin who was wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, with extensive and vast holdings, and endowed with wealth equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa.

Rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, he had mastered the three Vedas along with the Nighaṇṭus and Kaiṭabhas, including the analysis of phonemes and the Itihāsas as the fifth; he was capable of explaining them word by word.
He taught the Vedic mantras to five hundred young Brahmin students. By him—
For the sake of a son, he brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a girl was born, beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
When she was born, after the birth festival had been performed, her name was being determined:
"What shall be the name of this girl?
The kinsmen said:
Generally, names beginning with "Soma" are given to our sons and grandsons.

Thus, the girl Soma was reared and nourished on milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other most excellent and refined nourishments.
He grows quickly, like a lotus situated in a lake.
When she had gradually grown up,
she became wise, articulate, intelligent, quick-witted, mindful, and possessed of a retentive memory;
meanwhile, her father was teaching the young brahmin students the sacred mantras.
Upon merely hearing it, she grasped it; and having heard it, she provided an exposition of those treatises from beginning to end. Consequently, Śrāvastī became completely filled with her fame.
The non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthya) came to her for an audience day after day and reached a definitive conclusion with her.
When the Blessed One had awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he then arrived at Śrāvastī.
Generally, those who are wise and reckoned as wise approach to see the Blessed One;
not seeing them, she addressed her household people:
"What is the reason, sirs, that those learned in the treatises do not approach here at this time?
They replied:
"The Blessed One, the omniscient Śākyamuni by name, has arrived here."
"All have become inclined toward him.
Then, upon hearing this sound "Buddha," which she had never heard before, all the pores of her skin bristled with joy.
There, the maiden Somā, having heard the word "Buddha," approached the presence of the Blessed One.
Then she beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides,

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the girl Somā, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that it leads to the penetration of the four noble truths.
Having heard it, Somā shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, she went forth into homelessness in the presence of Mahāprajāpatī.
By applying herself, striving, and exerting effort, she [perceived] this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra.

Having understood that all conditioned states are unstable and having struck down their course by means of their nature of falling, decaying, scattering, and destruction, she realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

She became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights.
Averse to existence, gain, greed, and honor,
she became worthy of worship, veneration, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
When the Blessed One gave the command to the monks, saying, "O monks, you yourselves shall recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month," then Mahāprajāpatī [said]:

Now at that time, that bhikṣuṇī was seated and present in that very assembly.

The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what actions were performed and accumulated by the nun Somayā, by which she was born into a wealthy family, became beautiful, handsome, pleasing, and a retainer of what she had heard?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it was by Soma herself that in former births actions were performed and accumulated; the necessary conditions having been gathered and their causal factors having matured, those actions—like a surging flood—have arrived and are now inevitable.

Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
rather, actions performed— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, during this very Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

Then, at the time of her death, the nun Somā made this aspiration:

"Just as my preceptor was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who uphold the teachings, so may I also, in a future time, [be the foremost] of that young brahmin named Uttara who was prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa."
"Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni;

"What do you think, monks? That brahmin girl who was there was this very bhikṣuṇī Somā.
Because she made that aspiration..."
For this reason, she was designated as the foremost among those who possess the power of retaining what they have heard;
for whatever was taught, recited, and studied by her,
she has now realized arhatship through that.

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having set aside entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white deeds.

Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

Through that same sense of spiritual urgency, those actors also realized arhatship by abandoning all afflictions.

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into hardship, calamity, and distress? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms? Who is heading toward the lower realms?"
Whom shall I rescue from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation?
For whom shall I plant roots of merit that have not yet been planted? And for whom shall I bring to maturity those roots of merit already planted?
"Whose ripened [faculties] shall I liberate? And he said:
"Even though the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might overstep its shore, the Buddha would never overstep the time for those who are to be trained, like his own young calves. (Avś 80.1)
Then the Blessed One, while staying in the Jeta Grove, emitted a golden-colored radiance by which that house was illuminated as if by a thousand suns.
Approaching through supernatural power, he released the noose from her neck and comforted the girl.
The appearance in the world of these six conditions is marvelous and wonderful:

the appearance of a Tathāgata; the appearance of the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata; birth as a human being; birth in a noble realm; the possession of unimpaired faculties; and the desire for wholesome qualities—the appearance in the world of these is marvelous and wonderful.
Then the Blessed One gave that girl such a teaching of the Dharma that,

upon hearing it, she shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity— which rises up with its twenty peaks— and realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having attained serene faith, she served the Blessed One with a meal and covered him with a cloth.
Then misfortune departed from the girl and fortune appeared;
she remained illuminating the inner chamber like a celestial maiden.
The Blessed One also departed.
Then an idea occurred to the members of the assembly:
"Surely his wife has become most beautiful;
it is because he is jealous by nature that he is willing to inflict punishment."
And he did not wish to show her.

"What if we were to make him drink strong, disagreeable liquors, take him by force to his house, and look for his wife? Then they made him intoxicated with a heavy draught of strong, disagreeable liquor.
Having made a noise and departed, they went home, opened the door, and saw the girl;
having seen her, they were struck with great astonishment and thought: "It is only right that she did not show herself to us."
Then, having returned once more, they woke him up while he was asleep under the influence of liquor and said: "O Gaṅgā, you have gained great profit; it is well-earned by you."
"Since such a beautiful girl belongs to you," Gaṅgā then became even more sorrowful and dejected, thinking,
"I myself have given this punishment."
Thinking, "I have become disgraced," he returned home dejected.
Having opened the door, he saw his wife shining intensely like a forest goddess in the midst of flowering blossoms.
Then he asked:
"Noble lady, what is this? By what means has this excellence of form been produced?"
Then she related everything exactly as it had happened to her husband;
having heard it, he too acquired faith in the Blessed One.
Eventually, that young woman, having gradually obtained her husband’s permission, went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying herself, striving, and exerting effort, she understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and shifting; she struck down all conditioned states by realizing their nature of decay, falling, scattering, and destruction.

Through the abandonment of all afflictions, she realized arhatship; she became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher cognitions, and the analytical insights,
and turning her back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
She became one to be worshipped, honored, and saluted by the gods, including Śakra and Upendra.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Gaṅgarasthā, by which she was born into a wealthy family?"
"What karma was performed by which she became deformed, yet having gone forth, realized arhatship?
The Blessed One said:

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Gaṅgarā in previous births; their conditions were fulfilled, their causes had ripened, they stood before her like a surging flood, and being inevitable,
these actions performed and accumulated by Gaṅgarā—
who else shall experience them?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the wind element;
rather, actions—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that have been performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain merchant’s wife who was fierce, impetuous, and harsh.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world—those who have compassion for the lowly and the miserable, who delight in remote lodgings and seats, and who are the sole objects of offerings for the world.
Now, a certain Pratyekabuddha, who was unsightly, entered that house.
Having been severely rebuked by her, he was cast out from the house with the words:
"By whom was this deformed man brought into my home?
Thereupon, for the sake of showing favor to her, the Pratyekabuddha rose into the expanse of the sky like a king of swans with outspread wings and began to display various miraculous feats.
Then, overcome with remorse, the merchant’s wife said, "Forgive me.
When he had thus been forgiven, she provided him with alms-food and made this aspiration:
"May I not experience the ripening of this karma for having reviled a Pratyekabuddha,
and may I become a recipient of such qualities as these."
And may I please a Teacher who is even more distinguished.
"What do you think, monks? That wife of the merchant was this very Gaṅgarasthā."
Because she provided alms-food to a Pratyekabuddha, through the ripening of that karma, she has been reborn into a wealthy royal family;
because he addressed her with insults regarding her ugliness and expelled her from his home, [she has now suffered this].
Because of that, she became ugly.
Furthermore, she had previously gone forth as a nun under the Blessed One Kāśyapa;
there, she studied and recited, and she mastered skill in the aggregates, skill in the sense bases, skill in dependent origination, and skill in what is possible and impossible.
And the life of celibacy was fully maintained;
by that, he has now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black.
For those that are exclusively white, [the result] is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, [the result] is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, [one should cultivate those that are exclusively white].
"One should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely pure;
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The ninth section. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Samudra and Sumanas, Hiraṇyapāṇi and Tripuṣṭa, Yaśomitra and Upapāda, Śobhita and likewise Kapphiṇa,
Bhadrika and Rāṣṭrapāla— this is the group that has been proclaimed.
AVŚ_81 Samudra. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
In Śrāvastī, there was a certain caravan leader.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal standing.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was thus sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, the thought occurred to him:
"As long as I am young, I shall accumulate wealth."
"Later, in my old age, I shall attain liberation in happiness.
Then the caravan leader, accompanied by his wife and a retinue of five hundred merchants, took a ship and set out upon the great ocean.
When Prajāvatī became pregnant,
she gave birth right there in the middle of the ocean;
a boy was born who was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
When he was born, a birth festival was held and his name was established:
"Since he was born in the midst of the ocean, therefore his name shall be Samudra.
Eventually, that caravan leader returned from the great ocean with his ship successfully and safely completed.
When the boy Samudra had grown up, his father established him in the office of a caravan leader and sent him forth upon the great ocean accompanied by a retinue of five hundred merchants.
Wandering by stages and observing villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, royal capitals, and ports, he eventually reached the shore of the ocean.

Having hired a ship for five hundred *purāṇas*, taken five crew members, and provided food, a sailor, a fisherman, and a helmsman, he made a proclamation by ringing a bell three times and set out upon the great ocean.
Then, while they were in the midst of the sea, that ship was tossed hither and thither by a tempestuous wind.

And the caravan leader Samudra was devoted to the non-Buddhist heretics; terrified by the fear of untimely death, he began to supplicate the six teachers. Nevertheless, that ship continued to be driven about by the wind.
Meanwhile, other merchants began to invoke thousands of deities, saying:
"Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāyu, Agni, Mahendra, and Tuṣitamaheśvara on earth; Viśvadeva and the great ṛṣis!"
Afflicted by death here, we have sought refuge in you; may you quickly desire to protect this caravan that has fallen into this calamity.
Then, even as they were lamenting in this manner, there was no one to protect them;
meanwhile, a certain lay devotee (upāsaka) had mounted [the vehicle] there.
He said: "What will your six teachers and other deities do for you?
Go with devotion for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the manifest deity;
he will be your protector."
Then five hundred merchants, headed by Samudra, took refuge in the Blessed One with one voice.

In this interval, there is nothing whatsoever unknown, unseen, unperceived, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Indeed, it is the natural law (dharmatā) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are possessed of great compassion, who are engaged in favoring the world, who are guardians of the one [Dharma],

who dwell in tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), who are skilled in the three bases of self-mastery, who have crossed over the four floods, and whose feet are firmly established on the soles of the four bases of psychic power.
[To those] who are free from the five hindrances, who have transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with the six limbs, who have fulfilled the six perfections,
who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, who are teachers of the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments,
who possess the power of the ten strengths, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods— for three nights...
Three times a day, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, his knowledge and vision proceed thus:

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone toward the lower realms? Who is heading toward the lower realms?"
Whom shall I rescue from the states of woe and establish in heaven and liberation?
