Then, while the Blessed One was staying at Jetavana, he emitted golden rays with a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
by which those merchants were illuminated on all sides;
and he emitted rays cultivated over a thousand eons.
By these [means] they were refreshed,
and the dark wind returned.
When the merchant Samudra returned safely with his ship successfully completed its voyage, he— driven by that very same sense of spiritual urgency regarding death—

gave gifts and offerings, comforted his kinsmen, and gratified the ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars; then, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred merchants, he went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction,
he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the masteries,
turned away from existence, gain, greed, and honor, and became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods including Indra and Upendra.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"It is wonderful, O Venerable One, that by the Blessed One these five hundred merchants headed by Samudra were shielded with their dear lives and rescued from calamity."
"And they have been established in the ultimate goal, which is Nirvana.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, what is the wonder here, that now by me—who am free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion—"
Being liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, these five hundred merchants, headed by Samudra, were saved by their beloved lives.
They have been rescued from calamity and established in the ultimate goal of nirvāṇa.

Yet, in the past, while I was still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, and not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, these merchants were rescued by me.
Listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak.

Long ago, monks, in the past, there lived on a certain seashore a seer endowed with the five superknowledges; he subsisted on roots, fruits, and water through great austerity, wore garments of antelope skin and bark, and maintained the sacred fire.
That compassionate, high-souled one, who desired the Dharma and was affectionate toward his subjects, was a protector of those fallen into calamity.
Now, five hundred merchants in Vārāṇasī, desiring to set out upon the ocean,
were traveling by stages and eventually reached the shore of the sea.
Upon seeing that seer, they were filled with faith; prostrating at his feet, they began to entreat him:
"O Blessed One, if any misfortune should befall us while we are in the midst of the ocean, you must protect these [beings]."
He consented,
saying, "So be it.
Then those merchants, taking their jewels, set out toward Jambudvīpa.
When they began to be terrified by the Kālikā rākṣasī,
they were rescued by that ṛṣi. Then, having returned with their ship successfully completed, they approached the ṛṣi and said:
"O Great Seer, what do you seek through this difficult undertaking and out of your compassionate nature?
He replied: "May I become a Buddha in a world that is blind and without a leader; may I be the deliverer of beings who have not crossed over, and the liberator of those who are not yet liberated."
"You are the one who provides consolation to those who have not yet found consolation, and you are the one who brings final nirvana to those who have not yet attained it.
They said: "When you become a Buddha, please take us into your care as well."
The seer said: "So be it."
"What do you think, monks? He who was the seer at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Those who were the merchants are these very men, headed by Samudra; even then, they were rescued by me."
Furthermore, they went forth as monastics under the Blessed One Kāśyapa;
there, they brought their faculties to maturity,
and by that means, they have now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black there is an entirely black ripening; for those that are entirely white, an entirely white ripening; and for those that are mixed, a mixed ripening.
Therefore, monks, having set aside entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white deeds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 82:
Sumanāḥ (ed. Speyer, vol. II)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed great merit.

The one who obtains robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of disciples, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

In Śrāvastī there was a certain householder, wealthy, of great means and great possessions, with extensive and vast holdings, possessing wealth equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he sported with her.
He took his pleasure and enjoyed himself.
As he was sporting, taking pleasure, and enjoying himself, sons were born to him and also died.
And in that house lived the elder Aniruddha, who had entered the family as a guest.
Then this thought occurred to the householder:
"This Elder Aniruddha is one who possesses great power over the ripening of karma;
I shall first make a request of him."
"If a son is born to me,
I shall give him as a junior attendant (paścācchramaṇa) to you.
Thereupon, the householder invited the Elder Aniruddha to a meal within his home.
Then, having been provided with alms-food, he was requested:
"If my son, once born, survives,
I shall give him as a junior attendant (paścācchramaṇa) to the Elder."
The Elder Aniruddha said: "So be it; however, you must remember your promise."
Then, at another time, while he was sporting, enjoying himself, and dallying with his wife,
his wife became pregnant.
From her body a fragrant scent wafted forth.
When nine months had passed, she gave birth;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing, clothed in a divine garment of *sumana* flowers.
Upon his birth, they held a birth festival and established the name "Sumanas" for him.
Then, having invited the Elder Aniruddha to the house for a meal, that boy was presented to him.
Thereupon, the Elder Aniruddha gave him the saffron robes and uttered a blessing:
"May he be long-lived."
When he had reached the age of seven, he was given to the Elder by his mother and father.
Thereupon, the Elder Aniruddha ordained him and gave him instructions for mental cultivation (*manasikāra*).
By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he [perceived] this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra.

Having understood that all conditioned states are unstable and having struck them down by means of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and perish, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings.
Averse to existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods including Indra and Upendra;
moreover, his faculties were sharp.
When he repairs his rag-robe, at each individual needle-puncture, he enters into and emerges from the eight liberations.
Then, at another time, the Elder Aniruddha said to him:
"Go, my son,
and fetch water from the Ajiravatī River."
Then the novice Sumanas, taking a water jar, descended into the Ājiravatī River;
having bathed there and filled the jar with water, he set out through the air.
The jar went ahead of him.
Then Sumanas was a novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśa*).
At that time, the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion, was teaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
There, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Behold this novice monk, Śāriputra, as he approaches, having filled his water-jar, mindful and with his faculties well-composed.
Having abandoned passion, hatred, and covetousness, and becoming dispassionate,
this water-carrier shines as he sustains this body."
When the Blessed One praised and extolled the novice Sumanas in the presence of the community of monks,
a doubt arose among the monks.
"Venerable sir, what actions were performed and accumulated by Sumanas,
by which he was born handsome, beautiful, pleasing, clothed in a divine mantle of *sumana* flowers,
and possessed of sharp faculties?"
"And he attained Arhatship.

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Sumanas in previous births; their conditions had been fulfilled, their causes had ripened, they stood before him like a surging flood, and their result was inevitable.
Those actions were performed and accumulated by Sumanas.
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element,
but rather within the very appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one eons ago, a Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin appeared in the world—

endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Now, there was a certain caravan leader;
while he was in the prime of youth, the thought of going forth arose in him,
but he was unable to go forth.
When he had grown old, remorse arose within him:
"It was not well done by me that I did not go forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
Thereupon, he offered *sumana* flowers at the hair-and-nail stupa.
The Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin, together with his community of disciples, was provided with almsfood by him.
Then, prostrating at his feet, he made this aspiration:
"By this root of merit, this generation of the thought of awakening, and this renunciation of the gift, may I please the future Perfectly Enlightened Ones."
"And in whose teaching I might go forth, there, in my youth, I would realize the noble dharmas.
Once again, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
There, he maintained the practice of celibacy for ten thousand years;
by that means, he has now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black karmas is entirely black.
For those that are exclusively white, the result is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, [you should cultivate those that are exclusively white].
"One should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely pure;
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [Avadānaśataka 83] Hiraṇyapāṇi.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. II)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

In Śrāvastī, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he had accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself.
He had neither son nor daughter;
placing his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth."
"I have no son and no daughter;
after my passing, since all this wealth and property will be considered ownerless, it will fall under the control of the king.
He was then addressed by the ascetics, brahmins, friends, relatives, and kinsmen:
"Perform the propitiation of the deities.
Now, there is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of making petitions;
however, that is not so.
If it were so,
each person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
However, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
Which three?
The mother and father are full of passion and have come together;
the mother is healthy and in her fertile season.
And a gandharva becomes present.
Through the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.
And he remains thus intent on his prayers.
And a certain being, having passed away from one or another of the divine hosts, descended into the womb of that Prajāpatī.
Five unique qualities belong to certain women who are of a wise nature.
What are these five?
He knows a man who is impassioned; he knows a man who is dispassionate.
He knows the time; he knows the season.
She knows that the embryo has entered;
she knows from whom the embryo has descended;
and she knows whether it is a boy.
He knows whether it is a girl:
if it is a boy, he remains resting against the right side of the womb;
if it is a girl, she remains resting against the left side of the womb.
With a joyful heart, she informed her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, you are prospering;
I have become pregnant."
And as he remained resting against my right side, it was certain that it would be a boy;
he too, being delighted, raised his upper body.
Stretching out his right arm, he uttered this inspired utterance:
"May I indeed behold the face of a son long desired;
may one be born to me who is not base-born."
He should perform my duties; being supported, he should support me in return;
and he should receive his inheritance.
"May my family lineage endure for a long time;
and when we have passed away, may someone, having given small or great gifts and performed meritorious deeds, dedicate the merit in our names, saying:
'May this follow those two wherever they go, whatever their rebirth.'"
Knowing that she had conceived, he kept her in the upper chambers of the palace, free from restraint;

he attended to her with cooling provisions in the cold season and warming provisions in the heat, and provided her with food prescribed by physicians— food that was neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty,
nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent, but rather free from those qualities of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.

Her limbs were adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces; she was like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, moving from couch to couch and from seat to seat without descending to the ground below.
And for her, there was not even the slightest hearing of an unpleasant sound until the full maturation of the fetus.
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born who was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
On both his palms there were two dīnāras, struck with the marks [of a seal], born as the ripening of karma.
When that [previous state] has been removed, then another arises;
having performed the birth-festival for its birth, a name is established, [discussing]:
"What shall be the name of this child?"
The kinsmen said: "Since, as soon as he was born, two dināras— marked with signs and produced by the ripening of karma— appeared in his two hands, therefore let the boy's name be Hiraṇyapāṇi."
The boy Hiraṇyapāṇi was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to clean him, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nourished by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent and most refined provisions.
He grows quickly like a lotus in a pond—
he who is faithful, auspicious, of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, and compassionate.
The Great-souled One, who desires righteousness and is affectionate toward his subjects,
whenever he has descended onto a street, sees ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars, and extends both his hands.
Then a heap of gold and bullion, struck with the [royal] mark, appeared,
by which he satisfied them;
all of Śrāvastī was filled with his fame.
At another time, when the boy Hiraṇyapāṇi had gone out to the Jeta Grove,
he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.

Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides, his mind was filled with serene faith upon merely seeing the Blessed One. Having developed such faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One taught him the Dharma. He said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Teacher, I wish to provide a meal for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples."
The Elder Ānanda said,
"My son, what need have you for kārṣāpaṇas?
Thereupon Hiraṇyapāṇi, standing before the community of monks headed by the Buddha, extended both hands and set down a great heap of gold and bullion.
Upon seeing this, the elder of the Saṅgha and the other monks, as well as the elder Ānanda, were filled with supreme wonder.
Then, after the boy Hiraṇyapāṇi had fed the community of monks headed by the Buddha, he sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Knowing his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, the Blessed One delivered a teaching on the Dharma that leads to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard this, the daughter Hiraṇyapāṇidārikā shattered with the vajra of wisdom the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the Truths, she distributed her inheritance among her kinsmen, satisfied the ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars, and having obtained permission from her parents, she went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying herself, striving, and exerting effort, she [pierced] this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra.

Having understood that all conditioned states are unstable and having struck them down by means of their nature of decay, falling, scattering, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings.
Turning his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Hiraṇyapāṇi, as a result of which two dīnāras marked with auspicious signs appeared upon his two hands?"
"Having gone forth, he realized arhatship.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Hiraṇyapāṇi in previous births; their conditions have been fulfilled, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable."
By Hiraṇyapāṇi, actions were performed and accumulated;
who else shall experience them?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element.
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—reach their maturation:
"Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (AVŚ 83.1)
Monks, in the past, in a former time, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years,
there appeared in the world a Samyaksaṃbuddha named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed one.
The charioteer of those to be tamed by man, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One,

was dwelling in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. Then the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, having completed the entire work of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.

After King Kṛkī had performed the funeral rites for his body, he erected a stūpa made of the four jewels, one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height. While the festival for that stūpa was underway, a gambler placed two dīnāras upon the staff of that stūpa;
then, prostrating at its feet, he made this aspiration:
"Wherever I may be born, there may I have gold already in my hand."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the gambler, is this very Hiraṇyapāṇi."
Because he offered two dīnāras to this stūpa,
such a distinction as this came about for him;
and because he made that aspiration, he has now realized arhatship.

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having set aside entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white deeds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The 84th Avadāna of the Tripiṭaka]

(Buddha the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. II)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Now at that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala was ruling in Śrāvastī;

it was prosperous, flourishing, secure, and well-supplied with food; it was crowded with many people and inhabitants, free from strife, quarrels, riots, and disturbances, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo.
He protected the kingdom as if it were his only beloved son.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with the queen,
his wife became pregnant as he continued to sport, enjoy himself, and divert himself.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born wearing saffron-colored robes, bearing the appearance of a śramaṇa, and endowed with the memory of his past lives.
As soon as he was born, he asked:
"Is the Blessed One right here in Śrāvastī, as are the great disciples such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and the rest?
Then his mother, filled with wonder and joy, said:
"My dear son, the Blessed One is indeed right here in Śrāvastī, as are the great disciples."
When this matter was reported to King Prasenajit: "A son has been born to you;
he was born wearing saffron robes, bearing the appearance of a śramaṇa, and possessing the memory of his former births."
He was searching for news regarding the Blessed One and the great disciples.
Then, King Prasenajit, in order to show him favor, invited the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for a meal.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, surrounded by a host of monks and preceded by the community of monks, proceeded to where King Prasenajit’s meal was being prepared.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, taking his son onto his lap, presented him to the Blessed One, saying:
"Blessed One, this is my son; as soon as he was born..."
He recollects the Blessed One and the great śrāvakas as well.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth:
"Are you in good health, Tripiṭaka?
He replied:
"I pay homage to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit was filled with supreme wonder.

When he had reached the age of seven, he went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One, clothed in those very saffron robes. By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, having understood this five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable, and having struck down all conditioned states as being subject to decay, falling away, scattering, and destruction, [he realized the truth].

Through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward an axe or sandalwood paste, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights,
and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indras.

The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Tripiṭa such that he was born clothed in saffron robes, wearing the garb of a śramaṇa, and possessed of the recollection of his former births?"
"Having gone forth, he realized arhatship.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Tripiṭa himself in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable."

Actions performed and accumulated by Tripiṭa—who else will experience them? Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element; nor do they ripen in the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. Rather, these actions performed and accumulated ripen in the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases that belong to one's own continuity. When the [necessary] conditions are present and the time is right, they ripen. Indeed, no actions performed and accumulated ever come to fruition in vain. [The Buddha said: "Monks, in the past, in a certain city, there lived a householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast property. He had a son named Tripiṭa, who was intelligent, wise, and skilled in the arts. At that time, in that city, there was a courtesan named Sundarī, who was beautiful, attractive, and possessed of supreme charm. She was sought after by many people and received much wealth from them. Now, this householder’s son, Tripiṭa, went to her house and, having seen her, became infatuated with her. He gave her much gold and silver, and she accepted it all. From that time on, he would go to her house every day, and she would accept his gifts. One day, while Tripiṭa was staying at her house, he saw a monk entering the city for alms. Seeing him, he felt a surge of faith and thought: 'It is wonderful, it is marvelous! This person has renounced such pleasures and gone forth into homelessness. Having developed this thought, he approached the monk, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side. Seated there, he said to the monk: 'Venerable sir, please accept my invitation to take your meal tomorrow at my house. The monk consented by remaining silent. Then, having understood his acceptance, Tripiṭa rose from his seat, circumambulated the monk three times, and departed. The next day, he prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink in his house and invited the monk. When the monk arrived, he personally served him with his own hands, until the monk had finished eating and withdrawn his hand from the bowl. After the meal, he took a low seat, sat to one side, and said to the monk: 'Venerable sir, may you accept me as a lay follower; from this day forth, until life ends, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. May you remember me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth until life ends. The monk replied: 'Householder, you have indeed become a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth until life ends. [The Buddha said: "What do you think, monks? The householder’s son who was named Tripiṭa at that time is none other than me. Because I offered a single meal to that monk, I experienced happiness for eighty-four thousand years in the heavens of the Thirty-three Gods. Furthermore, because I developed the thought of faith upon seeing that monk, I have now attained supreme, perfect enlightenment. Monks, you should know that even a small wholesome deed, when cultivated repeatedly, leads to great fruit. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall cultivate even small wholesome deeds repeatedly. It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves. not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that the actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen:
"Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (AVŚ 84.1)

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Kāśyapa— one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He was dwelling in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. Eventually, the son of King Kṛkin went to Ṛṣipatana,
and there he saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
His body was resplendent with the eighty minor marks, adorned with a fathom-wide aura of light, and possessed a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns;
like a moving mountain of jewels, he was auspicious in every respect. Upon merely seeing him, faith arose within him.
Filled with serene faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before him to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that inspires detachment from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Upon hearing it, perceiving the faults of cyclic existence and seeing the virtues of Nirvana, he made a request to the king:
"Father, grant me permission;
I shall go forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
The king said: "I cannot do this."
"Because your consecration as crown prince will take place before long," [the king said]. The prince replied:
"Enough for me with kingship, which is filled with dharmas corrupted by many faults."
"I shall certainly go forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
Not being permitted by his father,
he skipped one meal.
When two, three, or up to six fasts had been performed,
his companions informed the king:
"Your Majesty, please grant permission for the prince to go forth into the religious life."
"Lest he should pass away," [he thought].
Then the king made a vow regarding his son.
He was told: "You must not grant us an audience until you have studied the Three Piṭakas.
Thereupon, having obtained his father's permission, he went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he mastered the three Piṭakas before long;
he became a preacher of the Dharma possessed of ready eloquence in what is fitting and well-spoken.
Then this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now to fulfill my former vow?
Thinking thus, he went into the presence of his father,
and was asked:
"Son, have you studied anything?
He replied, "The three Piṭakas.
Thereupon, he gave his father such a teaching of the Dharma.
Upon hearing this, the king became joyful;
then, filled with faith, he said:
"My son, what is your need?"
He said: "I wish to invite the Blessed One together with the community of disciples and provide them with the six requisites.
The king replied:
"Do as you please."
"The royal palace is vast.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, together with a retinue of twenty thousand, was regaled with exquisite food by Tripiṭa;
and each individual monk was provided with the six requisites.
Then, prostrating at his feet, he made this aspiration:
"Since I have now obtained the going forth with such difficulty,
and have performed services for the Tathāgata and the community of disciples,"

"By this root of merit, by this generation of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of gifts, wherever I may be born, may I be clothed in saffron robes, bear the appearance of a śramaṇa, and possess the recollection of my past lives."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the son of Kṛkin, is this Tripiṭa."

By that very same cause, a son was born into a wealthy royal family—one who was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and possessed the recollection of his former births. Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed,
one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Avadānaśataka, 85: Yaśomitra]

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. II)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.

In Śrāvastī, there was a certain caravan leader who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging possessions; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself. He took a wife from a family of equal status, and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
At that time, there was indeed a famine, a hardship,
and food was as difficult to obtain as in a wilderness.
Alms were sought by a beggar,
and it was indicated by those skilled in omens that the god would not send rain.
Eventually, the caravan leader’s wife became pregnant;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with all physical limbs.
On the very day the boy was born, that very day the drought was broken.
All of Śrāvastī was filled with his fame. Having performed the birth festival upon his birth, they established his name:
"What shall be the name of this boy?
The kinsmen said:
"Because his fame has spread in every direction..."
"Therefore, let the boy's name be Yaśomitra.
The boy Yaśomitra was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide breast milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nurtured by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various excellent provisions;
he grew rapidly, like a lotus in a pond.
When Yaśomitra had grown up, he went out to the Jeta Grove on some business.
There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, he was auspicious on all sides;
upon merely seeing him, faith arose within him.
Having given rise to faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One gave him such a teaching on the Dharma concerning detachment from cyclic existence that, upon hearing it, he came to perceive the defects of cyclic existence and perceive the qualities of nirvāṇa; having obtained permission from his parents, he went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he [pierced] this very five-faceted wheel of cyclic existence.
Having understood that all conditioned states are unstable and, having struck them down by means of their nature of decay, fall, scattering, and destruction,
he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings.
Turning his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods including Indra and Upendra;
from his two tusks, water endowed with the eight qualities flows forth.
Because of this, thirst does not afflict him.
Monks, when during the summer heat those afflicted by thirst enter the Saṅgha for the sake of a drink,
even then he does not enter.
Then the most excellent monks asked him:
"For what reason does thirst not afflict you? He replied:
"From these two fangs of mine flows water endowed with the eight qualities,
by which my thirst is not afflicted."

The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what actions were performed by Yaśomitra, by which he became handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing?"
"From between his fangs, water endowed with the eight qualities flows forth,
and having gone forth, he has realized arhatship. The Blessed One said:

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Yaśomitra himself in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and being inevitable,
these actions performed and accumulated by Yaśomitra—
what other than he shall experience them?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Neither in the element of wind,
but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do actions performed— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Long ago, monks, in the past, during this very Fortunate Eon when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

He was dwelling in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. At that time, a certain son of a guild-president went forth as a monk under a certain elderly bhikṣu; however, he was lazy and did not wish to practice the conduct of the monastic rules.
Thereupon, he was appointed as an attendant to an elder by the student-brahmins.
Considering himself an attendant, he accepted service from even more senior monks;
his roots of unwholesomeness were boundless.
Then, at another time, he fell ill.
The Elder, following the physician’s advice, gave him ghee to drink. At night, he was overcome by thirst. (Speyer)
Terrified by thirst, he took hold of his own water-pot, thinking, "I shall drink water," but he saw that it was without water. It is the same for teachers and preceptors.
When he entered the monastery’s water pavilion,
he saw that it too was without water;
then he entered the river path.

That river, too, became devoid of water. Distressed, he went out onto the road along the river, surrounded by trees, for the purpose of causing alarm among his fellow celibates and to demonstrate the gravity of what has been given in faith.
[He was] on another tree; having tied his garment there, he climbed up,
and perceiving "my own actions [are mine]," he remained relying upon his karma.
Abiding in reliance upon karma,
when the night had turned into dawn on the second day, he reported this account to his fellow religious practitioners (*sabrahmacārin*).
Then, having heard of his death, those fellow practitioners were deeply distressed.
They began to look here and there;
then his preceptor offered him water,
but he did not even see that.
Deeply moved by this, he informed the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
The Blessed One Kāśyapa said to him:
"Let the gaṇḍī be struck."
Then the attendant struck the gong,
and the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, assembled.
This news spread throughout the city of Vārāṇasī,
and consequently, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered together.
Then, the preceptor, having seated him at the head of the elders, gave him a water-pot filled with water.
"Child, distribute this water among the Saṅgha.

Seeing the immediate fruit [of his action], he was moved by that very same spiritual urgency; having conceived faith in the Blessed Buddha and in the Śrāvakas, he distributed that water among the Saṅgha with intense resolve.

Then, for the sake of favoring him, the Blessed One extended his arm, which resembled the trunk of an elephant, and—acting as a source of consolation for those who were afraid—the water was received by him and by the great Śrāvakas.
And it is not exhausted;
even when it has been distributed among the entire Saṃgha,
it is still not exhausted.
Having witnessed that most wonderful miracle, which captivated both gods and humans, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained the vision of the Truth (*satyadarśana*).
Furthermore, the roots of unwholesomeness (*akuśalamūla*) were eradicated within his own mental continuum. When he had recovered from that illness, [he was restored].
Then, by him, the community of monks headed by the Buddha was provided with water without much effort;
for twelve thousand years he distributed water to the Saṅgha.
At the time of his death, he made this aspiration:

By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this relinquishment of things to be given, may I please— and not displease— that very Blessed One named Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, whom the Blessed Kāśyapa prophesied for the young brahmin named Uttara, saying: "Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."
And from between my fangs, water endowed with the eight qualities shall flow forth.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was the monk at that time, on that occasion, is this very person."
Because he distributed drinking water to the Saṃgha for twelve thousand years and made a formal vow,
as a result of that, in this present birth, water endowed with the eight qualities issues from between his teeth.
By that very cause, he realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed,
one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Story of the Spontaneously Born One] (AVŚ 86)

(Buddha the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. II)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— entered the rains retreat among the Trāyastriṃśa gods on the Pāṇḍukambala stone, not far from the Pārijāta and Kovidāra trees.
He teaches the Dharma to his mother, his progenitor,
and to other gods. At that time, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had entered the rains retreat at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then the four assemblies approached the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
having bowed their heads at the feet of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, they sat down to one side.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the four assemblies with a discourse on the Dharma.

Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, he remained silent. Then the four assemblies rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and extending their joined palms toward the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, they said this to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, have you heard where the Blessed One has entered the rains retreat at present?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied:
"Gentlemen, I have heard that the Blessed One has entered the rains retreat among the Trāyastriṃśa gods."
On the Pāṇḍukambala stone, not far from the Pārijāta and Kovidāra trees,
he teaches the Dharma to his mother, his progenitor, and to the other gods of the Trāyastriṃśa realm.
Then the four assemblies, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, bowed their heads at his feet, rose from their seats, and departed.
Then, after the three months of the rainy season had passed, the four assemblies approached the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and sat down to one side.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana instructed, inspired, and gladdened the four assemblies with a discourse on the Dharma.
He demonstrates it,
encourages it, inspires it, and rouses it.
He gladdens them.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, he remained silent.

Then the four assemblies rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and extending their joined palms toward the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, [they addressed] the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
He said this:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should indeed know that..."
—Maudgalyāyana, you should know: it has been a long time since we last saw the Blessed One;
we are parched with thirst for a sight of the Blessed One.
"We wish to see the Blessed One.
If it is not troublesome for the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
it would be well if the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to approach the place where the Blessed One is."

Having approached, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Blessed One in our name, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness of body, vigor, well-being, strength, blamelessness, and his dwelling in comfort.
And speak thus:
"Venerable sir, the four assemblies in Jambudvīpa desire to see the Blessed One.
And they say: 'Venerable sir, indeed the humans of Jambudvīpa do not possess such supernatural power or majesty by which the humans of Jambudvīpa [might go] to the Trāyastriṃśa gods.'"
They would ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa [heaven] in order to approach, see, and attend upon the Blessed One.
Indeed, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa possess such supernatural power and majesty.
"By what means might the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven descend to Jambūdvīpa to approach, visit, and attend upon the Blessed One?
It would be well if the Blessed One, out of compassion, were to descend from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to Jambūdvīpa.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to the four assemblies by remaining silent.
Then the four assemblies, perceiving through the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s silence that he had consented, bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, rose from their seats,
and departed.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, perceiving that the four assemblies had departed not long ago, entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, [he vanished from his seat and appeared before the Blessed One].
In this very way, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana vanished from Śrāvastī and reappeared among the Trāyastriṃśa gods on the Pāṇḍukambala stone, not far from the Pārijāta and Kovidāra trees.
At that time, the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma to an assembly of many hundreds of gods.
And Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw the Blessed One seated before an assembly of many hundreds of gods, teaching the Dharma.
And having seen this, he again manifested a smile, thinking:
"Even here the Blessed One dwells surrounded, just as in Jambūdvīpa he dwells surrounded by the four assemblies.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the thought in the mind of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
Indeed, Maudgalyāyana, it is not that they act according to their own will;
rather, when it occurs to me, "Let them come," [then they come].
Then they come;
when it occurs to me:
"Let them go," [they go].
Then they go;
thus, having understood my thought with their own minds, they both come and go.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Maudgalyāyana, having surveyed the entire assembly of gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Truly wonderful is this assembly of deities gathered and assembled here!
In this assembly of deities, there are deities who, having attained unwavering confidence in the Buddha, have been reborn here upon the dissolution of their bodies;
there are [deities] in the Dharma..."
There are those in the Saṅgha who, being endowed with the virtues beloved by the Noble Ones, have been reborn here upon the dissolution of the body.
Then the Blessed One, commending what the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had said, addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana as follows:
"It is so, Maudgalyāyana."
It is even so; it is even so.
Truly wonderful is this assembly of deities gathered and assembled here!
Among them are deities who are endowed with verified clarity of faith in the Buddha.
Upon the dissolution of the body, they have been reborn here;
they have faith in the Dharma and they have faith in the Saṅgha.
There are those endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, who, upon the dissolution of the body, have been reborn here.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, praising the words of the Blessed One and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"So it is, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana; so it is!
Truly, this assembly of gods gathered and assembled here is most diverse."
In this assembly of gods, there are deities who,
being endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha,
have been reborn here upon the dissolution of their bodies.
There are [those] in the Dharma,
there are [those] in the Saṅgha,
and there are those endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones.
Upon the dissolution of the body, they have been reborn here.
Then a certain son of the gods, praising what had been spoken by the Blessed One, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and Śakra, the lord of the devas, said this to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"So it is, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana; so it is."
"How wonderful indeed is this assembly of deities, gathered and assembled!
Among this assembly of deities, there are gods who,
being endowed with verified clarity toward the Buddha, have been reborn here upon the dissolution of their bodies."
There are those who, having been endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones within the Dharma and the Saṅgha, have been reborn here upon the dissolution of the body.

There, many hundreds of deities, many thousands of deities, and many hundreds of thousands of deities, having each individually realized the fruit of stream-entry in the presence of the Blessed One, vanished right then and there.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, perceiving that the assembly of gods had retired to their private quarters, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in salutation toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the four assemblies in Jambudvīpa bow their heads at the feet of the Blessed One; they inquire after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, ease of movement, well-being, strength, blamelessness, and state of comfort."
The Blessed One said:
"May the four assemblies in Jambūdvīpa and you yourself be happy, Maudgalyāyana.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"Venerable Sir, the four assemblies in Jambudvīpa desire to see the Blessed One.

They say this: 'Venerable Sir, the humans of Jambudvīpa do not possess such supernatural power or majesty by which the humans of Jambudvīpa might ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa gods in order to approach the Blessed One for a vision and to attend upon him.'"

"Venerable Sir, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven possess such supernatural power and majesty that by means of it the Trāyastriṃśa gods could descend to Jambūdvīpa to approach the Blessed One for the purpose of seeing him and attending upon him.
It would be well if the Blessed One, out of compassion, were to descend to the Trāyastriṃśa gods."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, go to Jambūdvīpa, Maudgalyāyana;
having gone there, announce this to the fourfold assembly:"
"Sirs, on the seventh day from now, the Blessed One will descend from the Trāyastriṃśa gods to Jambūdvīpa, at the Udumbara tree in the Āpajjura grove in the city of Sāṃkāśya."
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having assented to the Blessed One and bowed his head at his feet, entered into such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed,
it was as if a strong man were to stretch out his contracted arm.
Or as one might extend an arm and then contract it,
even so the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana disappeared from among the Trāyastriṃśa gods and reappeared in Jambūdvīpa.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having returned to Jambūdvīpa, announced to the fourfold assembly: "Sirs, on the seventh day from now, the Blessed One will descend from the Trāyastriṃśa gods to Jambūdvīpa, at the Udumbara tree in the Āpajjura grove in the city of Sāṃkāśya."
The Blessed One then descended from the Trāyastriṃśa gods on the seventh day at the city of Sāṃkāśya, in the Āpajjura grove, at the foot of an udumbara tree.
When the Blessed One had descended to the city of Sāṃkāśya, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered to behold him.
There, a monk of miraculous birth appeared.
He invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, as well as those gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, to a meal.
When the time for the striking of the gong arrived, simultaneously with the arising of his thought, divine seats covered with magnificent cloths appeared.
And there were divine foods, both solid and soft;
then the Blessed One was satiated by that spontaneously born being with divine nourishment,
and those gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas attended upon him perfectly.

Then, the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, element, and nature, gave such a teaching of the Dharma that, upon hearing it, the spontaneously born monk perceived this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra as moving and unstable; he struck down all conditioned states by realizing their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction, and through the abandonment of all afflictions—

He realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, for whom an axe and sandalwood were the same, who had split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, who had attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the special knowledges,
and who turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indras.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by this being so that he has become one who is born spontaneously?"
And from the very moment that thought arises in him, whatever he thinks of, whatever he aspires for, all that is fulfilled.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it was by one born spontaneously that in previous births actions were performed and accumulated; those actions, having gathered their requisite conditions and matured their causal factors, have arrived like a flood and are inevitable—actions performed and accumulated by one born spontaneously."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element,
but rather it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one eons ago, there appeared in the world a Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt residing near the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Meanwhile, in a certain village hermitage, five monks had entered the rains retreat; there, one monk [spoke] to four [others]...
[Vaidya, p. 217]
He performed services for the monks.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, they realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
The fifth one, having prostrated at his feet, made this aspiration:
"Just as they have realized arhatship by relying on me,
may I, through this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of gifts, never lack for the specific requisites of one who has gone forth."
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, performed the service—he is this very one, Upapāduka.
The monks said:
"What karma was performed by which he became one born spontaneously?
The Blessed One said:
"In the past, monks, in a former age, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan was twenty thousand years—" (Speyer: [continues])
When the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years,

there appeared in the world a Perfectly Enlightened One named Kāśyapa— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

He was dwelling in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. There, a certain merchant had a wife who, at the time of childbirth, was overcome by painful sensations and cried out with a voice of distress.
Hearing that sound, he was overcome with great agitation;
entering his chamber of grief, he rested his cheek upon his hand and remained lost in thought.
Then, this thought arose in him:
"What if I were to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and make a vow, by means of which I would never again experience the bed of a womb?
With that very sense of spiritual urgency, he went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed Kāśyapa.
He made this aspiration:
"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this relinquishing of gifts, wherever I may be born, may I there be of spontaneous birth."
"May I never again experience the bed of the womb."
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the caravan leader, he is this spontaneously born being (upapāduka). This is the vow that was made."
Thereupon, he became one of spontaneous birth (*upapāduka*).
Because his faculties had been ripened there, he has now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, it is entirely white;
and for those that are mixed, it is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having set aside actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are exclusively white.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. AVŚ 87: Śobhita (edited by Speyer, vol. II)

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, the wealthy, citizens, guild-masters, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed great merit.
Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples in Kapilavastu at the Nyagrodha Grove.

In Kapilavastu there was a certain Śākya, wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, with extensive and vast holdings, possessing wealth equal to Vaiśravaṇa and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status. He played, took pleasure, and dallied with her;
while he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and dallying, his wife became pregnant. She...
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing, surpassing human appearance yet not having fully attained divine appearance.
At his birth, many wonders appeared,
by which the city of Kapilavastu was adorned on all sides. Having performed the birth festival for him, his name was established:
"What shall be the name of the boy?
The kinsmen said,
"Since at his birth the city of Kapilavastu was adorned on all sides,"
"Therefore, let his name be Śobhita. Thus, the boy Śobhita was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to clean him, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nurtured by eight nurses with milk, curd, butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent provisions most refined;
he grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
When he had grown up, he went to the Nyagrodha Grove to see the Blessed One.

There he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns— like a mountain of jewels walking.
It was auspicious on all sides.
Upon merely seeing him, his mind became serene in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having developed this serenity, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One, having understood his intention, latent tendencies, disposition, and nature, delivered a discourse on the Dharma conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, the youth Śobhita shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he requested permission from his parents and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and perish, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the higher faculties;
he turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor, and became one to be worshipped,
revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.

The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Śobhita, because of which he is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing, surpassing the human complexion yet not having fully attained the divine complexion?"
"At his birth, many wonders appeared by which the city of Kapilavastu was adorned on all sides.
The Blessed One said:

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Śobhita himself in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Since these actions were performed and accumulated by Śobhita himself, who else shall experience their results?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, both auspicious and inauspicious actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
In the past, monks, in a time long gone, during this very Fortunate Eon (*bhadrakalpa*), when the lifespan of beings was forty thousand years,
there appeared in the world a Perfectly Enlightened One named Krakucchanda, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata.
The Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One,
was dwelling in dependence upon the royal capital of Śobhāvatī.
King Śobha had established a stūpa for the hair and nails [of the Buddha].
When a certain festival had arrived, a group of lay associates went near the stūpa.
Upon seeing the stūpa, they were moved by faith and began to offer flowers.
Then, one of the lay associates said:
"I will not do it;
I have no wealth.
Thus, he was expelled from the midst of those companions.
Remorse arose within him;
having gathered various flowers, he offered them as an adornment upon that very stūpa.
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the member of the assembly who, having become remorseful, made an offering of flowers at the hair-and-nail stupa of Krakucchanda—"
This is that very Śobhita.
For indeed, monks, other deeds were also performed and accumulated by Śobhita.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain merchant chief.
There he saw a sick Pratyekabuddha;
then, having conceived a sense of faith, he prostrated at his feet, provided him with alms-food, and covered him with a cloth.
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the merchant, is this Śobhita.
Furthermore, during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he was a poor wood-gatherer."
For the sake of firewood, he entered a mountain cave;
there he saw a stūpa,
and upon the courtyard of that stūpa, grass had grown.
Then, having conceived a sense of faith, he pulled up some grass, took up a broom, and swept the courtyard of the stūpa.
Thereupon, prostrating at [the Buddha's] feet, he began to make a formal vow:
"By this root of merit, by this generation of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of gifts, may I be handsome, beautiful to behold, and inspiring."
And may I please the Buddhas of the future, and not displease them.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the wood-gatherer, is none other than this Śobhita."
Because he swept the courtyard of the stūpa,
wherever he was born, he became handsome, beautiful to behold,
and pleasing; by that very cause, he has now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black there is an entirely black ripening; for those that are entirely white, an entirely white ripening; and for those that are mixed, a mixed ripening.
Therefore, monks, having set aside entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves solely to entirely white deeds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. AVŚ 88:
Kapphiṇa (ed. Speyer, vol. II)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.
Receiving robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, [the Buddha],
together with the community of disciples, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

He protected his kingdom as if it were his own beloved only son.
At a later time, he played, took pleasure, and enjoyed himself together with his queen.

On that very same day, sons were born to eighteen thousand ministers,

Then, at another time, King Mahākapphiṇa, surrounded by eighteen thousand ministers, went out for the purpose of hunting.

Then the ministers, who spoke pleasantly, said:

Now, merchants from the Middle Country had gone to the Deccan.

"Who is the king there?

Then King Mahākapphiṇa dispatched messengers to the six great cities, beginning with Śrāvastī, with the command:

"Otherwise, I shall punish you with the highest penalty.

Having heard these words, the kings residing in the six great cities became afraid, terrified, agitated, and their hair stood on end; they gathered together as one body, arrived at Śrāvastī, and then went into the presence of the Blessed One.

The horses are like Bālāhaka;

One must not sit down;
one must return quickly.
"Or else, if you do not come,

Then the messenger went and reported everything that had been instructed— the letter and the oral message— to King Mahākapphiṇa.

Then, the Blessed One, perceiving his arrival, miraculously created the Jetavana as consisting of the four jewels, like the city of Sudarśana belonging to the gods,
wherein the four Great Kings were stationed as gatekeepers.
The elephants were like Airāvata,
the horses like Bālāhaka,
and the chariots like Nandīghoṣa.
The men were like fierce yakṣas;
the Blessed One himself manifested the appearance of a universal monarch (cakravartin),
and he likewise manifested everything else, including a lion throne rising seven palm trees high.
Then King Mahākapphiṇa entered Jetavana; upon seeing him, whatever pride he had in his physical form vanished,
