yet even now, the pride of power still obstructs him.
Thereupon, the Blessed One generated a mundane thought:
"Oh, would that Śakra, the lord of the gods, were to come taking Indra’s bow!
As soon as this thought arose in the Blessed One, Śakra, the lord of the gods, appearing in the guise of a charioteer, presented Indra’s bow to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One then handed it over to Mahākapphiṇa.
And King Mahākapphiṇa was not even able to lift it, much less raise it;
then the Blessed One manifested seven iron drums.
He himself then fixed that bow with a crescent-shaped arrow and released it,
by which those seven iron drums were pierced;
then a sound emerged:
Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket. AVŚ_88.1 //
"For whoever shall practice with heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Thus that sound reached as far as the Akaniṣṭha gods.
Then, King Kapphiṇa’s pride in his own strength vanished,
and this thought arose in him:
"What is this?
Then the Blessed One, perceiving the state of King Mahākapphiṇa’s mind, made his royal attire disappear and began this discourse:

"Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with the ten powers and confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, claims for himself the noble, preeminent position of a bull."
He promotes the holy life and utters the perfect lion's roar before the assembly:
namely, "When this exists, that comes to be."
From the arising of this, that arises; namely:
conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces;
conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness.
Conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form;
conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases;
conditioned by the six sense bases is contact.
Conditioned by contact is feeling;
conditioned by feeling is craving;
conditioned by craving is grasping.
With clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering;
that is to say: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; from the cessation of this, that ceases.
That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
From the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling;
from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging.
From the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
from the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Monks, the Dharma has been well-expounded by me; it is clear, revealed, with its cross-threads cut, and perfectly elucidated for gods and humans alike."

Thus, in this well-expounded Dharma of mine— which is clear, revealed, with its bonds severed, and perfectly illuminated for gods and humans— monks, it is indeed sufficient for a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith; it is sufficient for application, sufficient for heedfulness, and sufficient to apply oneself to the teaching of the Teacher.
Granted, let only the skin, sinews, and bones remain;
let the flesh and blood of the body wither away.

Nevertheless, that which is to be attained by one who has initiated vigor—one who is steadfast, heroic, energetic, firm in prowess, and who does not cast off the burden regarding wholesome qualities—must still be achieved.
Having reached that vehicle, there will be no slackening of his vigor.
Why is that?
For one who is indolent dwells in suffering, being defiled.

Through evil, unwholesome states— those which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by fever, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to birth, aging, and death in the future— there occurs a great loss of one's welfare; however, one who has initiated vigor dwells in happiness, untainted by evil, unwholesome states— those which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by fever, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to birth, aging, and death in the future— and there occurs the fulfillment of a great welfare.
"I shall adorn this teaching, namely: the Teacher is present in person;
and the Dharma is being taught—leading to tranquility, leading to final Nirvana, leading to full awakening, proclaimed by the Sugata.
Therefore, O monks, those who regard their own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both, [should practice accordingly]."
This should be trained in:
"May our going forth not be in vain; may it be fruitful, giving rise to happiness and resulting in happiness."
And for those from whom we shall enjoy robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
may the services rendered to them indeed become exceedingly fruitful,
of great benefit, great splendor, and great expansion.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, King Mahākapphiṇa, accompanied by a retinue of eighteen thousand ministers,

shattered with the thunderbolt of wisdom the mountain of the view of a self-identity that rose up in twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the Truths, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and perish, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the masteries;

The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Kapphiṇa,

"Having gone forth, he realized arhatship.

Kapphiṇa performed and accumulated these karmas;

Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,

Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, both auspicious and inauspicious actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases:
"Actions do not perish even after hundreds of millions of eons."
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

Monks, in the past, ninety-one aeons ago, a Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin arose in the world, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī, in the forest grove of Bandhumatī.
When a certain caravan leader had brought back abundant jewels from the great ocean,
he invited the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, together with the community of disciples, for a meal for three months;
having also constructed a monastery, he dedicated it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters.
"What do you think, monks? That caravan leader at that time and on that occasion was none other than King Kapphiṇa.
Because he invited the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin, together with his community of disciples, to take his meal within his own home for three months,"

Having caused a monastery to be built, he dedicated it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters; because of that, he has now become handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing. Furthermore, monks, other deeds were performed and accumulated by Kapphiṇa.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta.
He ruled the kingdom, which was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people and inhabitants,
free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle,
and buffalo. He was righteous, a king of Dharma, and he governed the kingdom according to the Dharma.
Then, at a later time when the spring season had arrived,

while the trees were in full bloom and the forest groves resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvaka birds, he went out to the park surrounded by a retinue of eighteen thousand ministers.

There, in that park, he saw a sick pratyekabuddha. He attended to him for three months with wholesome food. After the pratyekabuddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, he had a reliquary stūpa constructed and, together with his circle of ministers, offered an anointing of oil.
By means of that empowerment of the Mahānagna strength, he became possessed of a retinue;
furthermore, when the Blessed One Kāśyapa had gone forth,
he himself went forth and there brought his faculties to maturity.
Thus, he has now realized arhatship.
For it is thus, monks: the ripening of entirely black karmas is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white [karmas] is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed,
one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
He was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

When the Blessed One, having attained enlightenment six years prior and twelve years after his departure, arrived at Kapilavastu, then many thousands of Śākyans, headed by Droṇodana and Amṛtodana, realized the vision of the Truth, with the exception of King Śuddhodana.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana, seeing that splendor of his son, was struck with supreme wonder.
The thought occurred to him:
"If my son had not gone forth into homelessness, he would have become this very universal monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror of the four quarters, righteous and a king of dharma."
"He does not look well now with this retinue of matted-hair ascetics;
what if I were to ordain one person from each of the Śākya clans?
Then King Śuddhodana had a proclamation made by the ringing of a bell throughout the city:
"All the Śākyas must assemble.
Then, when all the Śākyas had assembled, King Śuddhodana said: "Listen, venerable Śākyas!"
"If Prince Sarvārthasiddha had not gone forth,
you yourselves would have performed his service;
therefore, now that he has gone forth, each individual Śākya man must go forth as an attendant to him."
Then five hundred princes, headed by Bhadrika, Aniruddha, Revata, and Devadatta, went forth into homelessness.
Among them was a barber named Upāli who served as their attendant; seeing that they had gone forth, he began to weep.
Thereupon, the Śākyas asked him:
"For what reason, Upāli, do you weep?
He replied with words that were piteous, distressed, and drawn out:
"You have gone forth into homelessness."
"Who will now provide for my protection with food and clothing?
Then the Śākyas said: "In that case, Upāli..."
"Spread out a cloth! he said. He spread out the cloth, and then the Śākyas made a great heap of necklaces, half-necklaces, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, armlets, and rings that had clung to the body.
Then, having seen those [princes] and beholding that wonderful ornament, a thorough mental reflection (*yonisomanasikāra*) arose in Upāli the barber:

"These Śākyans, though possessed of noble lineage, beauty, and youth, have gone forth into homelessness, casting away their harems and this ornament as if it were phlegm. How much more so should I, who possess little wealth—should I take this ornament home? Enough of this!"
"What if I were to go forth following them?
Then Upāli the barber approached the Blessed One;
having approached and prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, there is the going forth for those such as myself, may I obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya;
may I practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."
Then he was ordained by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula.
Then five hundred Śākyas, headed by Bhadrika, wearing the attire of monks (*bhikṣu*), proceeded to pay homage to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
Knowing Upāli to be endowed with noble lineage, beauty, and wealth, they did not wish to pay him homage.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Bhadrika:
"Bhadrika, you must pay homage to him,
for this teaching of mine does not depend upon lineage, physical form, youth, power, or the purity of the four castes."
Then, like trees cut at their roots, the five hundred Śākyas headed by Bhadrika, relying upon the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), prostrated themselves at his feet.

At the very moment they paid homage at his feet, this great earth shook in six ways. Thereupon, the Venerable Bhadrika, through application, exertion, and striving, [attained] this very five-fold aggregate...

Having understood the wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and mobile, and having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature of falling, decaying, scattering, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, for whom an axe and sandalwood were the same, who had split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and who had attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific understandings.
Averse to existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became worthy of worship, veneration, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra;
and that Great Being was compassionate toward the lowly and the miserable.
At a later time, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, he set out for Śrāvastī for alms.
Eventually, he entered a certain Caṇḍāla settlement for alms.
At that very time, King Prasenajit of Kośala, having mounted the noble elephant Ekapuṇḍarīka with Cārāyaṇa as his charioteer, was setting out to see the Blessed One.

King Prasenajit of Kośala saw Bhadrika, whose senses were stilled and whose mind was at peace, endowed with the highest tranquility and self-control; he was dressed in a robe of rags from a dust heap and was coming out from that cemetery of the Caṇḍālas, carrying coarse alms-food.
Having seen him, he addressed his charioteer, Dīrgha Cārāyaṇa:
"Could this, Cārāyaṇa, be the monk Bhadrika?
"It is exactly as you say.
Upon hearing this, King Prasenajit of Kośala fell into a state of confusion.
He fell upon the earth in a swoon;
then, his breath and consciousness restored by the sprinkling of water, he regained his senses and was raised up by the charioteer Ārāyaṇa.
Then the king, having approached the Blessed One and paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet, said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I have seen something wonderful!

There is that Bhadrika, the Śākya king, clad in rag-robes and carrying coarse alms-food; with an exceedingly peaceful deportment that wins over both gods and men, he is taking his alms-food from the dwellings of the Caṇḍālas.”
Having gone out, this thought occurred to me:
"How wonderful! To what an extent the teaching of the Blessed One is well-disciplined!"
"How is it that such youths, though raised in comfort, have become so well-disciplined in their conduct?
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Great King, hear of another marvel concerning Bhadrika."
"Great King, this Bhadrika, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, utters three times:
‘Oh, what happiness!

When I was not yet a renunciant, while staying in the midst of the royal court, well-protected by ministers, merchants, and country folk, hidden behind walls, moats, gates, and watchtowers, my heart was full of apprehension and agitation.’"
Being suspicious on all sides, I could not find sleep; but now, being indifferent toward both body and life, I dwell happily wherever I may be.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what actions did Bhadrika perform in previous births,
by which he became handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, and was reborn into a wealthy royal family?"
"Having gone forth, he realized arhatship.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Bhadrika himself in previous births; their conditions have been met, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a surging flood, and their fruition is inevitable."
Bhadrika performed and accumulated these actions;
who else shall experience their results?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.

rather, both wholesome and unwholesome actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even after hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain beggar whose body was completely overcome by hunger; he wandered here and there until he encountered a certain girl who was going along carrying some cakes. Then that beggar overpowered the girl for the sake of those cakes.
Then, having forcibly seized a single small cake, he began to flee here and there.
And that girl followed closely behind him.
Then that beggar suddenly crossed the river-path.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, devoted to remote lodgings and seats, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
Then a certain Pratyekabuddha stood before that Koṭṭamallaka.
Thereupon, seeing that Pratyekabuddha’s peaceful deportment, a great faith arose in the Koṭṭamallaka;
disregarding his own misfortune, he offered a cake to the Pratyekabuddha.
In order to produce great joy in him, he rose into the expanse of the sky like a king of swans with outspread wings and began to display various miraculous feats.
Then Koṭṭamallaka, having seen that most wonderful miracle which captivated both gods and men, fell at his feet like a tree cut at its root and began to make this vow:
"Since I have offered a cake to one who has fulfilled his vows and is worthy of offerings..."
By this root of merit, by this generation of the thought of awakening, and by this relinquishing of gifts, wherever I may be born,
may I there be of high birth and may I be a recipient of such qualities as these.
And may I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and never displease him.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was Koṭṭamallaka, is this very Bhadrika."
Because he offered a cake to a pratyekabuddha, through the ripening of that karma, he was reborn among the wealthy Śākyas;
furthermore, he went forth as a monk under the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
There, he maintained the practice of celibacy for ten thousand years;
by that, he has now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black.
For those that are exclusively white, the result is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, [one should cultivate those that are exclusively white].
"One should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely pure;
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

Observing that the time for his conversion had come, the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sthūlakoṣṭhaka for alms, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks.

Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

Then Rāṣṭrapāla approached his parents;

Having renounced a vast universal sovereignty and sixty thousand women of the inner apartments, I have gone forth;
shaven-headed and clad in the saṃghāṭī robe, I wander for alms right here in Sthūlakoṣṭhaka. Therefore, it is fitting that you two grant me your permission.
When he thought, "I shall go forth following that Blessed One who has gone forth," his parents did not grant him permission; thereupon,
he skipped one meal.

Then the parents of Rāṣṭrapāla approached the place where Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, was staying.
Having approached him, they said this to Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder:
