For you are delicate and a seeker of pleasure;
you do not know suffering.
The holy life is difficult to practice.
Solitude is difficult to practice; dwelling alone is hard to enjoy;
forest retreats and wilderness dwellings are difficult to master.
"Go to dwell in remote lodgings.
But you, dear Rāṣṭrapāla, sit right here, enjoy sensual pleasures,
and give gifts."
"And perform meritorious deeds.
When this was said, Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, remained silent.
Then the mother and father of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla urged his kinsmen, saying:
"Come now, kinsmen, raise up our dear Rāṣṭrapāla!"
Then the kinsmen of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla approached where the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla was;
having approached, they spoke thus to the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla:
"Indeed, dear Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know this:"
For you are delicate and a seeker of pleasure;
you do not know suffering.
The holy life is difficult to practice.
Solitude is difficult to practice; dwelling alone is hard to enjoy;
forest retreats and wilderness dwellings are difficult to comprehend.
"Son Rāṣṭrapāla, dwell here; remain right here, enjoy sensual pleasures, and give gifts, rather than going to occupy remote lodgings."
"And perform meritorious deeds.
When this was said, Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, remained silent.
Then the parents of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla urged the companions of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
"Come now, young men, raise up our dear Rāṣṭrapāla."
Then the friends of Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, approached where Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, was;
having approached, they said this to Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son:
"Indeed, dear Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know this:"
For you are delicate and a seeker of pleasure;
you do not know suffering.
The holy life is difficult to practice.
Solitude is difficult to practice; dwelling alone is hard to enjoy;
forest retreats and wilderness dwellings are difficult to comprehend.
"Live in remote lodgings;
rather, gentle Rāṣṭrapāla, sit right here, enjoy sensual pleasures,
and give gifts."
"And perform meritorious deeds.
When this was said, Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, remained silent.
Then the companions of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla approached the parents of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla.

Having approached them, they said this to the parents of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla: "Mother, father, please grant permission for the gentle Rāṣṭrapāla to go forth from the home into the homeless state with perfect faith."
"What will you do with him dead? If our father takes delight in the life of renunciation,
you shall see him alive."
"If he does not take delight [in this], what other recourse is there for a son except his very parents?
Thus, young men, we two shall give our permission for our father Rāṣṭrapāla."
If he should present himself as one who has gone forth into homelessness.
Then Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, having gradually regained the physical stamina and strength of his body, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, said this to the Blessed One:
"I have been granted permission by my parents, Blessed One.
May I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
May I practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."
Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, obtained the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.

Having thus gone forth, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and perish, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, and indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood;
he had split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the masteries, and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became one to be honored, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Śakra and Indra.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my monks, my disciples who dwell in the forest—namely, the monk Rāṣṭrapāla."
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Rāṣṭrapāla, by which he was reborn into a wealthy royal family?"
"He was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing;
having gone forth, he realized arhatship.
The Blessed One said:

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Rāṣṭrapāla himself in previous births; their conditions have been met, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a flood, and being inevitable, these actions performed and accumulated by Rāṣṭrapāla must be experienced by him.
Who else shall experience them?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, both auspicious and inauspicious actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Long ago, monks, in the past, the King of Videha, together with his retinue, reached a forest wilderness while terrified by a hostile army.
At midday, scorched by the intense rays of the sun, he and his host wandered here and there,
unable to find the path.

And when Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world—those who have compassion for the lowly and the wretched, who delight in remote lodgings and seats, and who are the sole objects of veneration in the world.
At that time, a certain Pratyekabuddha was dwelling on that desolate path.
Having conceived compassion, he pointed out the way to that King of Videha.

And a lake of water was shown, by which the king was preserved through his desired life. Then, having conceived faith, the king brought him to his own city and attended to him for three months with all necessary provisions.
And after he had passed into parinirvāṇa, he caused a reliquary stūpa for his body to be constructed and made this aspiration:
"May I too become a possessor of such qualities as these."
And may I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and never displease him.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time, on that occasion, is this very Rāṣṭrapāla."
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, other deeds were performed and accumulated by him.

In this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a perfectly awakened Buddha named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, the teacher of gods and humans,
was dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, King Kṛkī reigned over a kingdom that was prosperous and flourishing.

It was secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, free from strife, quarrels, riots, and disturbances, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo; there,
a righteous king who ruled by Dharma governed the kingdom according to the Dharma.
His younger son went to Ṛṣipatana.
There he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides;
from the mere sight of him—
And his mind became filled with serene faith toward the Blessed One. Having developed such faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then, the Blessed One Kāśyapa taught the Dharma to him.
Having conceived faith, he attended upon the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his retinue;
he took the refuges and the precepts,
and after [the Buddha] had attained parinirvāṇa, he offered a parasol at his stūpa.
"What do you think, monks? That prince was none other than Rāṣṭrapāla at that time and on that occasion.
Furthermore, other deeds were also performed and accumulated by Rāṣṭrapāla."
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain Brahmin who was a root-gatherer.
For the sake of roots, he climbed a certain mountain.
While wandering there, at the edge of a forest, he saw a sick Pratyekabuddha.
Then, having conceived faith, he attended upon him;
when [the monk] had recovered from his illness, he provided him with almsfood and made this aspiration:
"May I too become a possessor of such qualities as these;
may I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and never displease him."
"What do you think, monks? That brahmin who was a root-gatherer at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Rāṣṭrapāla.
As the ripening of that karma, he never experienced suffering anywhere in saṃsāra."
Even now, he has been reborn into a wealthy royal family, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing;
by that very same cause, he has realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black.
For those that are exclusively white, the result is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, [one should cultivate those that are exclusively white].
"One should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely pure;
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
The Blessed One spoke thus;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Tenth Chapter. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
The Elder Subhūti, as well as Hastaka Āḷavaka,
Saṃsāra, Guptika, Virūpa, Gaṅgika, Dīrghanakha, and Saṃgīti— this constitutes the chapter that has been fully set forth.
AVŚ_91 Subhūti: The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens,
guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
When the Blessed One, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, appointed his disciples to those various regions for the sake of favoring those people to be trained,
at that time those who were practitioners remained intent on meditation upon the terraces of Mount Sumeru.
Meanwhile, the king of birds, Suparṇin, drew a young nāga from the great ocean.
Having placed him upon the terraces of Mount Sumeru, he began to devour him.
Then the young nāga, while being deprived of his life, passed away with a mind full of serene faith toward the great śrāvakas.
Having passed away, he was reborn in Śrāvastī in the womb of the chief queen of a brahmin named Bhūti;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold. Upon his birth, a birth festival was celebrated, and his name was established as follows:
"What shall be the name of this boy?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since his father is Bhūti, let the boy's name be Subhūti."
The boy Subhūti was raised and grew up until he became a man.

Due to the influence of his past causes, he was exceedingly prone to anger and frequently overwhelmed by outbursts of rage; having been turned away from the Atharvanic spells by his parents, he was ordained among the rishis.
There, devoted to meditation and self-restrained, he dwelt relying upon a certain forest grove.
In that forest grove there dwelt a deity who had realized the truths. Compassion arose in her, [thinking]:
"This son of good family, being overwhelmed by a great abundance of anger, does not attain spiritual distinction."
"What if I were to urge him toward a vision of the Blessed One?
Then, in the presence of Subhūti, that deity spoke the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Thereupon, a longing for a vision of the Blessed One arose within Subhūti.
Then, by the power of the deity's supernatural might, he was brought into the presence of the Blessed One.
Then he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
And at the mere sight of him, whatever animosity he had toward sentient beings vanished.
Then, filled with serene faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before him to hear the Dharma.
Knowing his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, the Blessed One delivered a discourse on the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths;

having heard it, the noble son Subhūti shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, with the thunderbolt of wisdom, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he tamed his mind through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and, by abandoning all afflictions (*kleśa*), realized arhatship.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the sciences (*vidyā*).
Turning his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshiped, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti began to reflect:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?"
He saw: "For five hundred births, having passed away from among the nāgas, I was reborn only among the nāgas.
Then this thought occurred to him:
"I have accumulated such an excessive store of conditions for hatred."
"By that very cause through which I was reborn among the nāgas for five hundred lifetimes, I have now experienced this great calamity.
Now, however, I shall act in such a way that no accumulation of hatred will arise toward others."
Endowed with which [faults], one is reborn after the breakup of the body in a state of deprivation, a miserable destination, a downfall, in the hells;
yet he undertakes and dwells in the practice of forest-dwelling.
When he wishes to wander for the sake of alms in a monastic community, a village, a region, or a country, [he does so].
Then he first surveys his surroundings, thinking:
"May no one, even down to an ant or an insect, see me for some reason and become malicious in mind."
He delights them with his graceful deportment,
and by that means, those beings develop clarity of mind;
such is the sense of shame he experiences, even though he has attained arhatship.
Then, the thought occurred to the Venerable Subhūti:
"What if I were now to act for the benefit of the great multitude?
Thereupon, by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he manifested five hundred *suparṇis*.

Seeing these, the nāgas became afraid, terrified, agitated, and bewildered as they fled hither and thither; then, by the power of his supernatural faculties, Subhūti rescued them once more. Thereupon, he taught loving-kindness to their minds, which had become serene.
Again, having manifested a massive form as a nāga, five hundred garuḍas rushed toward him;
to them, too, who were terrified, he taught loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
In this way, he disciplined five hundred families of both nāgas and garuḍas.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"This, monks, is the foremost among my monks, my disciples who dwell in the state free from strife—namely, the noble son Subhūti."
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Subhūti, as a result of which he was designated as the foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*)?
The Blessed One said:

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Subhūti himself in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, they have reached maturity, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and being inevitable, these actions performed and accumulated by Subhūti must be experienced by him—
by whom else could they be experienced?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, the deeds performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Deeds do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, during this very Fortunate Eon when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana;
there he became a renunciant,
and there he gave gifts of charity.
For ten thousand years, he maintained his life of celibacy and made this vow:
"By this root of merit, by this generation of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of gifts, may I become that young man named Uttara who was prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa."

"Young man, you will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years; having gone forth in his teaching, may I be the foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-affliction."
What actions were performed by which he was reborn among the nāgas?

Because his afflictions were not abandoned, because his faculties were deranged, and because he had not brought the paths of action to an end, he became corrupt in mind toward monks who were both trainees and those beyond training, and he behaved toward them with the speech of a venomous serpent;
therefore, he was reborn among the nāgas.
Because he gave gifts and practiced the giving of charity, and because he maintained the life of celibacy, he has now realized arhatship.
And he was declared to be the foremost among those who dwell in the state of passionlessness (*araṇā*).
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having set aside entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, one should apply oneself only to entirely white deeds.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [The Elder] (AVŚ 92, ed. Speyer, vol. II)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.

The Blessed One, having obtained robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, dwelt with the community of disciples near Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
There was a certain merchant who was wealthy, of great fortune and vast possessions, with extensive and wide-ranging holdings; he was as rich as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her;
while he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, his wife became pregnant.
She did not give birth;
rather, she continued to play, sport, and enjoy herself with him for some time longer.
While he was thus playing, sporting, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him.
That first embryo remains exactly as it was in the mother’s womb until,
for her, the ten [months] gradually [pass].
Sons were born;
that first-born son was still within his mother's womb when the householder’s wife fell ill.
She was attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
yet that illness did not subside.
And when her terminal agony had manifested, such that she would soon pass away—
Then she said to her husband:
"Noble son, you should know that my first pregnancy is established here;
when I have died,"
"Then, having struck the right side with a weapon, you should extract the first-born boy. Having said this:
"All accumulations end in exhaustion; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation; for life ends in death. (AvŚ 92.1)
Having spoken thus, she was joined with the law of time.
When she had passed away, they adorned her bier with blue, yellow, red, and white cloths, carried it to the Śītavana cemetery, and summoned Jīvaka,
the king of physicians.
And this report spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha in all directions:
"In such a manner, a fetus has remained in the womb of such-and-such a woman for so many years,
and ten other sons have been born to her."
"And that fetus which had been situated there first has not yet emerged;
today Jīvaka, the king of physicians, having opened the womb of the deceased woman with a surgical instrument, will extract that child who was situated first.
Hearing those words, out of curiosity, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered at the Śītavana cemetery.
And there were six teachers, beginning with Pūraṇa, who each claimed the status of a teacher.
In that regard, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda."
Tell the monks:
"The Blessed One wishes to go on a journey to the cremation grounds; whoever wishes to see wonders [should come]."

"Let him come. Thereupon the Blessed One, surrounded by the great śrāvakas such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Bāṣpa, Mahānāman, Aniruddha, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Revata, and others, went to the Śītavana cemetery.
When the multitude of people saw the Blessed One, they made way for him.
Thereupon, Jīvaka incised the woman’s right flank,
and from it emerged a man whose body was covered with wrinkles and grey hair, his limbs completely decayed and aged.
With his senses failing, emaciated, and lacking strength,
as soon as he had emerged and beheld that mass of people, he uttered these words: "Sirs,
do not utter harsh speech toward your elders, those who stand in the place of elders, your parents, teachers, and preceptors."
"May you not experience such a state as this,
wherein I have dwelt for sixty years between the stomach and the intestines.
Having said this, he remained silent.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Be satisfied, monks, with all rebirths in existence;
be satisfied with all the requisites for rebirth in existence."
Since such is the condition even of a being in his final existence,
the Blessed One addressed that boy:
"Boy, are you an elder?"
"I am an elder, Blessed One. "Are you an elder, child?
"I am an elder, Sugata."
The name "Sthaviraka" arose for him.
Then the Blessed One performed a discourse on the Dharma based upon that [occasion],
hearing which many hundreds of sentient beings, filled with spiritual urgency, attained a great distinction.
Having lived as a householder for ten years, he became seventy years old when he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.
He entered the rains retreat on Vulture Peak Mountain together with twenty-five monks.
There, he was made to enter into a formal agreement by the senior of the Saṅgha:
"No ordinary person (pṛthagjana) should offer the invitation.
After the passing of three months, twenty-four monks attained arhatship;
only one elder remained who was still an ordinary person.
Then, while the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) was underway, the elder of the community (*saṃghasthavira*) rebuked him severely and expelled him from the midst of the assembly.
Taking up a weapon, he entered his hut and, weeping, lamented in many ways, saying:
[Vaidya, p. 235]
The entire forest is ablaze and even the mountains are set on fire;
yet this evil mind is still not released. (AVŚ 92.2)
The sounds of the mountain rivers have become stilled, their waters reduced;
yet even now, this evil mind is not liberated.
For these egg-born birds have become silent and their cries have ceased;
yet even now, this evil mind is not released. AVŚ_92.4 //
For this forest has leaves as pale as a sickle, and the lord of the forest has withered leaves;
yet even now, this evil mind is not released.
"I shall take up the blade; what indeed is the use of my life?
How could one who is but an ordinary person approach the Teacher?
In this interval, there is nothing whatsoever that the Blessed Buddhas do not know, do not see, do not understand, or do not perceive.

It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are possessed of great compassion, who act for the benefit of the world, who are the sole protectors, who dwell in tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), who are skilled in the three bases of taming, who have crossed over the four floods, who are firmly established on the soles of their feet through the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), who are free from the five hindrances, who have transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with the six limbs, and who have fulfilled the six perfections (*pāramitā*).
To those who are enriched with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, who teach the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling,

who possess the power of the ten strengths, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods— three times during the night and three times during the day, having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, their vision of knowledge proceeds:
Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into hardship, distress, and calamity all at once?
Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who is prone to the lower realms? Who is leaning toward the lower realms? Whom shall I lift out from the lower realms and establish in heaven and liberation?
"Whose unplanted roots of merit shall I plant? Whose planted ones shall I bring to maturity?
And whose matured ones shall I liberate? And it is said:
"The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might even exceed its tide-line,"
But the Buddha would not let the time pass by for those who are like calves to be tamed.

Then the Blessed One, having taken him into his care and approached him, gave such a Dharma teaching that, upon hearing it, the Elder Sthaviraka understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; he struck down all conditioned states by realizing their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction, and through the abandonment of all defilements, he realized arhatship.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to the axe or sandalwood paste, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the higher faculties;
he turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor, and became one to be worshipped,
revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Then the Elder, having attained arhatship, began to reflect:
"Is there anyone who is to be converted by me as well?"
He saw about five hundred merchants terrified by a black storm, facing ruin and calamity, thinking: "I must protect them from that danger;
thus they will become my disciples."
Then the Elder, having gone there by means of his supernatural power, rescued them from that danger.
Thereupon, filled with faith, they all went forth into the religious life and applied their minds to this very practice of mental attention.
While all of them were thus applying themselves, striving, and exerting themselves, they realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements;
yet, no one among them was perceived by anyone else for their virtuous qualities.
Consequently, the group of six monks began to criticize them:
Having become an elder, he established five hundred co-residents.
"These too shall likewise become disciplined."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, who was affectionate toward his fellow celibates and devoted to the welfare of others, desiring to bring forth the Venerable Elder named Sthaviraka, approached the place where the Venerable Elder named Sthaviraka was staying.
Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Venerable Elder named Sthaviraka, and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Elder named Sthaviraka:
"Venerable Ānanda, we would ask the venerable elder named Sthaviraka about a certain matter, if you would grant us the opportunity to have our question answered."
"Having heard it, I shall inform you.
Venerable Elder, what dharmas should be frequently brought to mind by a monk who has gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling?
He replied: "Venerable Ānanda, two dharmas should be frequently brought to mind by a monk who has gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling:"
There are both calm abiding and insight.
What purpose does calm abiding fulfill when it has been practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed by a venerable elder?
"What benefit does insight (vipaśyanā), when practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced, bring about?
"Venerable Ānanda, when serenity (śamatha) is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced, one is liberated by means of insight;
when insight is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced, one is liberated by means of serenity."
"Venerable Ānanda, the mind of the learned noble disciple, when cultivated through calm abiding and insight, is liberated element by element.
In this regard, Elder, what are those elements? Venerable Ānanda, it is the element of abandonment."
That which is the element of dispassion and that which is the element of cessation—
by the abandoning of what, Elder, is it called the "element of abandoning"?
Through the fading away of what is the element of fading away (virāgadhātu) so called?
Through the cessation of what is the element of cessation (nirodhadhātu) so called?
It is, venerable Ānanda, through the abandoning of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that the element of abandoning (prahāṇadhātu) is so called.
"Because of detachment from all conditioned phenomena, it is called the realm of detachment (*virāga-dhātu*);
because of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena, it is called the realm of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*).
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having rejoiced and approved of what the elder monk named Sthaviraka had spoken, approached the five hundred monks.
Having approached, he said this to the five hundred monks:
"Venerable ones, what dharmas should be frequently brought to mind by a monk who has gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling?
"Venerable Ānanda, two dharmas should be frequently brought to mind by a monk who has gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling:"
There are both calm abiding and insight.
Venerable ones, what benefit does calm abiding bring when practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced? What benefit does insight bring when practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced?

"Venerable Ānanda, when serenity (śamatha) is practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed, one is liberated by means of insight (vipaśyanā). When insight is practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed, one is liberated by means of serenity.
Venerable Ānanda, for the learned one, [the mind] is thoroughly permeated by both serenity and insight."
The mind of the noble disciple is liberated element by element. In this regard, venerable ones, what are those elements?
And as for that element of abandonment, venerable Ānanda,
and that element of dispassion, and that element of cessation—
Venerable ones, through the abandoning of what is the element of abandoning (prahāṇadhātu) so called? Through the fading away of what is the element of fading away (virāgadhātu) so called?
Through the cessation of what is the element of cessation (nirodhadhātu) so called?
Venerable Ānanda, through the abandoning of all conditioned phenomena, it is called the element of abandoning;
through the fading away of passion for all conditioned phenomena, it is called the element of fading away;
through the cessation of all conditioned phenomena, it is called the element of cessation.
The venerable Ānanda, having rejoiced and approved of what those five hundred monks had said, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"Venerable sir, what dharmas should be frequently brought to mind by a monk who has gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling?
Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling should frequently bring two dharmas to mind: serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā)."
"Venerable sir, what benefit does one experience when *śamatha* is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced?
What benefit does one experience when *vipaśyanā* is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced?
"Ānanda, when *śamatha* is practiced, cultivated, and frequently practiced, one is liberated by relying upon *vipaśyanā*."
Insight, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed, brings liberation by relying upon tranquility.
O Ānanda, the mind of the learned noble disciple, thoroughly permeated by both tranquility and insight, is liberated element by element.
In this regard, Venerable Sir, what are those elements?
And whatever, Ānanda, is the element of abandonment, the element of dispassion, and the element of cessation.
"Venerable sir, through the abandoning of what is the element of abandoning (prahāṇadhātu) so called?
Through the fading away of what is the element of fading away (virāgadhātu) so called?
Through the cessation of what is the element of cessation (nirodhadhātu) so called?"
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, because of the abandoning of all conditioned phenomena, it is called the element of abandonment;
because of the fading away of passion for all conditioned phenomena, it is called the element of dispassion."
Because of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena, it is called the "element of cessation.
It is marvelous, O Venerable One,
how the meaning of the Teacher and the meaning of his disciples correspond so perfectly.
Word follows word, and syllable accords with syllable, converging and meeting precisely with the foremost words.
For what reason is that?
"Venerable sir, I approached the elder monk named Sthaviraka;
having approached him, I asked the elder monk named Sthaviraka this very same matter with these words and these syllables as a question.
When questioned with these words and these syllables regarding this very matter, he gave me this very same answer."
Just as it was done by the Blessed One here and now, I too, having rejoiced and approved of what was spoken by the venerable elder named Sthavira, approached those five hundred monks;
having approached them, I asked those five hundred monks this very same matter using these very words and these very syllables.

By them also, this very same meaning was explained through these words and these syllables when the question was asked, just as it has been by the Blessed One now. This, Venerable Sir, is a marvel, in that the meaning of the Teacher and the meaning of his disciples coincide.
Word follows word and syllable accords with syllable, converging and meeting in accordance with the primary words.
"Ānanda, whom do you consider to be the Elder Bhikṣu?

Venerable Sir, the Elder Bhikṣu is an Arhat whose taints are exhausted, who has accomplished his task, completed what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose mind is well-liberated through right knowledge.

And all those hundreds of bhikṣus are likewise Arhats whose taints are exhausted, who have accomplished their task, completed what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds are well-liberated through right knowledge."
When the Blessed One had thus brought forth and revealed the Elder Ānanda and those monks,
the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Elder, what actions were performed and accumulated by you, such that you dwelt in your mother’s womb for sixty years?
What actions were performed such that you became slow, even extremely slow?"
"And having gone forth, he realized arhatship?
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Elder in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable."
The Elder Keṇa performed and accumulated these karmas;
who else would experience them?
Monks, performed and accumulated karmas do not ripen in the external earth element.
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen:
"Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (AVŚ 92.8)

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, during this very Fortunate Eon when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

He dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. There, a certain son of a merchant chief went forth into homelessness in the presence of an elder; and that elder was an arhat.
He was free from passion.
Then, when a festival had arrived in that region,
the young bhikṣu raised the elder:
"Arise, let us go to the village for alms.
The Elder said,
"Child, it is still too early."
"Go now and attend to the side of wholesome qualities.
A second and even a third time, the young bhikṣu rouses the elder, saying: "Arise! We shall go to the village for alms."
A second and even a third time the Elder said: "Child, it is still early; go now and attend to your side of wholesome practice."
Then, that young monk, greedy for food, uttered harsh words.
"Do not sleep in the house for sixty thousand years"—
by the ripening of that karma, he dwelt within his mother's womb for sixty thousand years;
because there was stinginess regarding the Dharma, he became one of poor wisdom.
With great difficulty his faculties were brought to maturity;
because he had there recited, studied, and cultivated skill in the aggregates, skill in dependent origination, and skill in what is possible and impossible,
he has now gone forth in my teaching and, through the abandonment of all defilements, realized arhatship.
Therefore, monks, you should strive for the abandonment of verbal misconduct;
thus these faults will not exist, such as those which befell the Elder Sthaviraka when he was still an ordinary person.
"These very same qualities shall belong to him once he has attained Arhatship.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
AVŚ_93 Hastaka.
(ed. Speyer, vol. II) The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—worshipped by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

In Śrāvastī there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he had accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, endowed with all major and minor limbs, and naturally possessed of the memory of his former births.
Taking hold of his own hand, he embraced it, kissed it, and clasped it, speaking these words:
"Oh, at last my hands have been obtained! Oh, at last my hands have been obtained!
Having performed the birth rites for him, his name was established:
"What shall be the name of the boy?
The kinsmen said:
"Since he clutches and kisses his hands as soon as he was born," [they named him Hastaka].
"Therefore, let the boy's name be Hastaka.
The boy Hastaka was entrusted to eight nurses: two shoulder-nurses, two milk-nurses, two dirt-nurses, and two play-nurses.
He was reared and nourished by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various highly refined articles of sustenance.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
Whenever there was some cause for fear in that region, [he would be brought forth].
Then that crowd of people, terrified and wandering here and there, guarded their goods;
he, however, guarded his hands and spoke thus to the crowd:
"O sirs, do not harbor malice toward those worthy of offerings;
do not speak harsh words.
Alas! My two hands have been obtained after a very long time!"
"Alas! My two hands have been recovered after a very long time."
Then, at another time, Hastaka went to Jetavana.
There he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides,
his mind was filled with serene faith upon merely seeing the Blessed One.
Having developed that faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, element, and nature, delivered a discourse on the Dharma conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, Hastaka shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up in twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he obtained permission from his parents and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and moving; having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and perish, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to the axe or sandalwood, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the masteries,
and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indra.
Even after attaining arhatship, he taught the Dharma to the monks in this very way:
"Sirs, do not harbor malice toward those who are worthy of offerings."
"Do not utter harsh words!
Oh, how my hands have finally been obtained after so long! Oh, how my hands have finally been obtained after so long!"
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what actions were performed and accumulated by Hastaka, such that even though he has attained arhatship, he speaks thus:
'Alas! It is only after a very long time that my two hands have been obtained'?"
"Alas! After such a long time, my two hands have finally been regained!
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, this person is one who perceives the fruits of karma directly before his eyes."
"Do you wish to understand?
It is so, venerable sir.

Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Hastaka himself in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable."
"Handaka, the actions performed and accumulated by you—
who else shall experience them?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element."
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that the deeds performed—whether auspicious or inauspicious—reach their maturation:
"Deeds do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (AVŚ 93.1)
In the past, monks, in a time long gone, during this very Fortunate Eon when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years,

a Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. There, two monks were of pure conduct; among them, one was a learned Arhat.
The second is one of little learning who is still a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).

Among them, that arhat who is of great learning is renowned, possesses great merit, and is a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; he also receives many invitations.
He would take that Saṃśīlika bhikṣu along as his attendant wherever he was invited;
this continued until one day an Arhat was invited.
One who wished to go to an invitation ceremony followed after a companion-monk,
but did not find him; consequently, because he could no longer see that monk, he took another monk with him.
Then, while some young monks there, with a mischievous intent, said: "Venerable sirs, look! Today this junior attendant was not taken by him;
instead, another was taken," he, overcome by anger, conceived a malicious thought toward the Arhat and uttered harsh words.
Because of that, he was born without hands for five hundred lifetimes;
however, when— out of a sense of remorse arising from his underlying intention— he confessed his transgression as a transgression, revealed it, and made it plain, he regained his two hands.
Furthermore, whatever he has recited and studied— his skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*), skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*),
skill in the sense-bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*), and his cultivation of skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*)— *Vaidya, p. 241*— all that [is included therein].
Having gone forth in my teaching, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed,
one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [Avadānaśataka 94: Lekuñcika]

(Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer, ed., vol. II)

Thus the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

In Śrāvastī, there was a certain brahmin who was wealthy, of great means and great enjoyment, possessing extensive and vast estates; he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the riches of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal status, and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born who was ill-colored, unsightly, and deformed.
As soon as he was born, milk disappeared from his mother's breasts;
even when another nurse was brought by that brahmin,
her milk also disappeared.
Due to the ripening of that girl's karma,
when the production of milk for him was not possible by any means whatsoever, he was then raised on a gruel of parched grain.
He was first drawn out [from the water], and the name Lekuñcika was given to him. He was one of little power and little merit.
When he had grown up, he could not even obtain enough to fill his belly.
He saw monks well-robed and well-clad, entering Śrāvastī for alms with bowls as dark as bees,
and departing with their hands full and their bowls full.
Upon seeing this, a desire for ordination in the teaching of the Blessed One arose within him.
Having obtained permission from his mother and father, he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One; yet, even though he had gone forth, he did not obtain enough food to fill his belly.
Driven by that very same sense of spiritual urgency, through application, exertion, and striving, he [realized] this very five-factored [cycle of existence].

Having understood the wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and unsteady, and having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature of falling, decaying, scattering, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and having attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the specific knowledges.
Turning his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he became one to be worshiped, revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Then, at another time, when he had set out to sweep the Blessed One’s perfumed chamber,
he swept it and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Then he obtained abundant and excellent alms-food, by which his sense-faculties and great elements were fully satisfied.
Having thus had his faculties satisfied, he spent the entire night in meditative absorptions, liberations, and attainments.
Then the thought occurred to him:
"This is an excellent means; what if I were to inform the community of monks?
He then informed the entire community of monks:
"Venerable Sir, I am one of little merit; whenever I enter for alms after having swept the fragrant chamber, I obtain satisfaction.
May the Saṅgha show compassion toward me."
"The fragrant chamber of the Blessed One must not be swept by anyone else.
Thereupon, the Saṅgha made a formal agreement:
"The fragrant chamber of the Blessed One must not be swept by anyone at all."
Having confidently swept the Gandhakuṭī, he afterwards enters Śrāvastī for alms.
At that time, the Venerable Śāradvatīputra, having spent the rains retreat in the countryside with a retinue of five hundred, arrived at Śrāvastī.
Out of reverence for the Teacher, he began to sweep the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī).
He was noticed by the Venerable Lekuñcika.
Therefore it was said: "Elder, you have struck me in my belly because you swept the fragrant chamber.
The elder asked: "How so?"
Lekuñcika said: "Elder, whenever I have not swept the fragrant chamber, I do not obtain almsfood.
Then the Elder Śāriputra said:
"If that is so, I have been invited elsewhere;
you need not worry.
I shall give you almsfood there."

Then the Elder Śāriputra set out for the invitation with a retinue of five hundred, and Lekuñcika also set out together with him. When they arrived near the householder’s home, due to the ripening of Lekuñcika’s karma, a great quarrel broke out in that house.
Then it occurred to the venerable Lekuñcika:
"Because of my own lack of merit, a quarrel has broken out there.
Thereupon, he turned back, went to the monastery, and undertook a fast by refusing food.
Then, on the second day, the Elder Śāriputra asked:
"For what reason did you not go? He replied: "The Elder did not understand."
"Because of my meager merit, such a quarrel broke out there.
Thereupon, on another day, the Elder Śāriputra escorted him into that house,
and as he sat in the midst of the Saṅgha, food was served to him in a clockwise direction.
In that regard, the server forgot; because of that, a second interruption of the meal was caused within the Saṃgha.
When this news was heard by the Elder Ānanda, he said to Lekuñcika:
"In that case, you should remain right here in the Jeta Grove."
"I shall bring you almsfood"—
such was the mindfulness of the Elder Ānanda,
even though he had mastered eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.

Due to the karmic obstruction of Lekuñcika, the Elder Ānanda forgot [to visit him]. Consequently, Lekuñcika underwent a third fast there. On the fourth day, the Elder Ānanda, having resolved to go, gave him almsfood.
He too was seized by dogs as he was going out;
there, he underwent his fourth fast from food.
On the fifth day, having heard of this, the Elder Maudgalyāyana took almsfood for the sake of Lekuñcika and set out by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Due to the ripening of Lekuñcika’s karma, he was struck by the wings of Suparṇin, the king of birds, and cast down into the great ocean.
There, he performed the fifth severance of his flesh.
On the sixth day, Śāriputra heard of this,
and it occurred to him:
"What if I were to stand at the door of Lekuñcika’s hut while he is receiving almsfood?"
Then, due to the ripening of Lekuñcika’s karma, that gate was likewise blocked by rocks.
Thereupon, Śāriputra, thinking "I shall release it through my supernatural power," placed his alms-bowl upon the ground;
yet even that was [blocked] by the ripening of Lekuñcika’s karma.
Then, eighty thousand yojanas away, it was situated upon a golden earth.

Even from there, the Elder Śāriputra drew it up by means of his supernatural power; yet when that alms-food was brought close to the opening of his mouth, because of the obstruction of his karma, his mouth became completely closed.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra, realizing Lekuñcika’s lack of capacity for spiritual attainment, was filled with a sense of urgency.
And by that venerable one, six fasts were observed.
Then, on the seventh day, the Venerable Lekuñcika, for the purpose of causing living beings to tremble with awe, to demonstrate that actions do not perish,

and to manifest the power of karma, filled his bowl with ashes, sat before the community of monks headed by the Buddha, stirred it with water, drank it, and passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder.

Beholding him, the monks were moved with spiritual urgency; having performed the funeral rites for his body, they, being filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Venerable Sir, what deeds were committed by Lekuñcika, such that even though he had attained Arhatship, he underwent six fasts and on the seventh day passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, by Lekuñcika himself, in former births, actions were performed and accumulated; their conditions have been met, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and being inevitable, these actions were performed and accumulated by Lekuñcika."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element,
but rather it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain householder’s wife who was faithful, auspicious, and of noble intention. She constantly gave gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, and supplicants. At a later time, her husband passed away.
Eventually, her son became the master of his own household;
however, he was miserly, stingy, and grasping regarding his possessions, such that he did not even resolve to offer a portion of food to a crow.
Upon seeing ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars, he would become filled with malice.
His mother, following that same previous practice, continued to bestow gifts upon ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and beggars.
Her son, overcome by stinginess, said: "Mother, this does not please me."
"Do not give the gift," he said.
She replied,
"My son, in this family, such is our family custom."
Then she was established by him on a separate portion of food;
nevertheless, she continued to bestow half of her own gift.
He enjoys half for himself;
then, overcome by stinginess and with his intellect clouded by anger, he continues to prevent [the other] from doing so.
When he is unable to prevent it under any circumstances, [he gives].
Then he said to his mother: "Mother, there is something that must be done;
please enter the inner chamber."
Because of her straightforward nature, she entered the inner chamber;
then, having closed the door, he made her go without food for one day.
She said:
"Son, I am hungry. Then he uttered these harsh words:
"Eat ashes!"
When she had fallen into such hardship, distress, and confinement, he made her cry out most piteously until she was deprived of food for six meals;
yet even so, he did not release her, and she passed away.
Then, as he was enveloped by stinginess, remorse arose in him due to his separation from his mother.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the householder’s son, is this very Lekuñcika."
Because he committed an offense against his mother, through the ripening of that karma, he was reborn for an eon in the great Avīci hell.
By that very same cause, even now, having attained arhatship, he passed into final nirvāṇa without food after enduring six missed meals while covered in ashes.
Furthermore, monks, other karmas were also performed and accumulated by Lekuñcika.
Bhikṣus, in the past, in a time long gone, there was in the city of Vārāṇasī a certain brahmin who worshipped the deities.
He was honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and beloved by all the brahmins and householders of Vārāṇasī, as well as by all people.

Now, it is the natural law that when Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the destitute, they delight in remote lodgings and seats, and they are the sole objects of offerings for the world.
Meanwhile, a certain pratyekabuddha entered Vārāṇasī for alms;
he emerged from there with his hands and bowl full,
and he was seen by that brahmin.
Avarice arose within him, and he said:
"Bring it here so that I may see the bowl.
For the knowledge and vision of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas does not function without focused attention.
The venerable one offered it to him;
then, having cast it upon the ground, he trampled it with his foot.
Consequently, that pratyekabuddha was deprived of his meal.
And no regret arose in that brahmin.
"What do you think, monks? That brahmin was none other than this Lekuñcika.

Therein, he fully maintained the holy life;
by that means, he has now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black.
The result of exclusively white actions is exclusively white;
that of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, having abandoned exclusively black actions as well as mixed ones, [you should cultivate exclusively white actions].
"One should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely pure;
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
The Blessed One spoke thus;
with joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas—thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; he was renowned and possessed of great merit.
Receiving robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, [the Blessed One],
together with the community of disciples, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

In Śrāvastī, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he had accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself. He took a wife from a family of equal status, and he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
As soon as he was born, upon looking around the house, he uttered these words:
"Suffering, O sirs, is saṃsāra;
saṃsāra is supreme suffering."
Having said this, he remained silent.
When his birth had been celebrated with a birth-festival, the naming ceremony was established, and it was asked:
"What shall be the name of the boy?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since he proclaims 'saṃsāra' as soon as he was born, let the boy's name be Saṃsāra."
The boy Saṃsāra was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nourished by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various excellent and highly refined provisions.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
When the boy Saṃsāra had gradually become a great man, because he was naturally endowed with the recollection of his former births, he taught the Dharma to the body of people:
"Sirs, do not utter harsh words toward your teachers, those who stand in the place of teachers, your parents, or your preceptors and instructors;
[do not say] 'Samsara is suffering.
Later, at another time, while wandering here and there, he emerged from the Jeta Grove.
Then he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.

Upon seeing the Blessed One, his mind became serene in the presence of the Blessed One. Having developed this serenity, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
For him, the Blessed One gave a teaching on the Dharma intended to produce detachment from cyclic existence.
Having heard this, the boy Saṃsāra, perceiving the defects of cyclic existence, requested permission from his parents and went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he understood this very five-fold wheel of cyclic existence to be unstable and unsteady; having struck down all conditioned states with the realization that they are subject to decay, falling away, dispersal, and destruction, [he attained liberation].

Through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher cognitions, and the analytical insights,
and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indra.
Even though he had attained arhatship, he taught the Dharma to the monks, saying:
"Venerable ones, do not utter harsh words toward your gurus, those who stand in the place of gurus, your mothers and fathers, or your teachers and preceptors."
Samsara is suffering;
samsara is supreme suffering.
The monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Venerable Sir, what actions were performed by Saṃśaya in his previous lives, as a result of which he emerged from his mother’s womb as a dead corpse for five hundred births? And how did he go forth [into the religious life]?"
"...and Arhatship was realized. The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it is by saṃsāra itself that actions were previously performed and accumulated in other births— actions whose conditions have been gathered, whose causal factors have ripened, which have arrived like a flood, and which are inevitable.
Since these actions were performed and accumulated within saṃsāra, who else shall experience their results?"
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.
Nor do they ripen in the element of wind;
rather, both wholesome and unwholesome actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases:
"Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons."
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Long ago, monks, in the past, during this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years,
there appeared in the world a Perfectly Enlightened One named Kāśyapa— one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,
an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

He dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. In the city of Vārāṇasī, a certain son of a guild-president went forth into homelessness in the presence of an elder; and that elder was an arhat.
He was free from passion.
Then, when a festival had arrived in that region,
the young bhikṣu raised the elder:
"Arise, let us go to the village for alms.
The Elder said,

"Go now and attend to the side of wholesome qualities.
A young bhikṣu rouses the elder a second and even a third time, saying: "Arise; we shall go to the village for alms."
A second and even a third time the Elder said:
"Child, it is still only morning; go now and attend to the side of wholesome qualities."
Then, that young monk, greedy for the flavor [of the food], uttered harsh words:
"May you not emerge from the sheath as a living being even for five hundred lifetimes!
Here I am, having emerged!"
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the young monk, is this very saṃsāra."
Because he uttered harsh words with a corrupted mind in the presence of an Arhat,
as the ripening of that karma, for five hundred births he emerged from his mother’s womb as nothing but a dead corpse.
After those five hundred births had passed, he has now attained human status.
Then, recollecting that, he says: "Samsara is suffering;

Because he, having become remorseful, confessed his transgression to the Elder and maintained the holy life, he has now realized arhatship.

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.

In the city of Saupāraka, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal status, and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born, and as soon as he was born, his entire body became covered with pustules.
When his testicles burst open, they became a single mass of flesh;
and as pus and blood flowed from his body, it produced a great stench.
Then his father, employing the power of his wealth and accompanied by medicines, mantras, and attendants, personally began to administer medical treatment;
yet that disease did not subside, because it was sustained by the force of karma.
Out of shame for his body being so mangled, he covered it with clothes and concealed it.
He was given the name Guptika.
When the boy Guptika had grown up, his playmates and companions arrived at the city of Saupāraka from Śrāvastī.
Then they said to his father:
"Father, if he were taken to Śrāvastī, it would be possible to free him from this illness, because there the physicians, medicines, and other necessities are easily available."
Then, having heard those words, his father gave him many jewels and attendants and sent him off to Śrāvastī.
Accompanied by his friends, he eventually arrived at Śrāvastī.
There, too, his disease born of karma could not be cured, despite the abundance of physicians, medicinal substances, drugs, and attendants.
Then, at another time, he went out to the Jeta Grove.
There he saw the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides,
his mind was filled with serene faith upon merely seeing the Blessed One. Having developed this faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One, having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, element, and nature, taught him that the five aggregates of clinging are a disease, an abscess, a thorn, a calamity, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Having realized the impermanence of conditioned phenomena, he went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, and having realized that this very fivefold wheel of saṃsāra is unstable and moving, he—
having struck down all conditioned states by virtue of their nature to decay, fall, scatter, and perish— realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights, turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
and became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods including Indra and Upendra.
His fellow-born companions also went forth into homelessness, moved by that very same sense of spiritual urgency.
They approached the venerable Guptika;
having approached, they said this to the venerable Guptika:
"Venerable Guptika, what is it that is subject to destruction?"
Or what in this world is of a nature not subject to destruction?
Form, venerable sirs, is of a nature subject to destruction;
through its cessation, Nirvana is of a nature not subject to destruction.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable friends, are subject to disintegration;
through their cessation, nirvana is the state beyond disintegration. What do you think, venerable friends?
"Is form permanent or impermanent?
"It is impermanent, Venerable Guptika.
"And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or not? "It is suffering."
"This is suffering, Venerable Guptika! Moreover, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—
would a learned noble disciple truly regard it as 'this is mine' from the standpoint of a self?"

"No, venerable Guptika."
"What do you think, venerable ones: are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?

"And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change..."

"No, Venerable Guptika.

or whether it is far—"
