Gaṅgika (ed. Speyer, vol. II)
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders; and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— thus the Buddha, the Blessed One, was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, renowned, and possessed of great merit.
Having obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he dwelt with the community of disciples near the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.

In Vārāṇasī there was a certain householder, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her;
yet, as he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself, neither a son nor a daughter was born to him.
Placing his cheek upon his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth, yet I have neither son nor daughter."
"Upon my passing, since all this property will be without an heir, it will fall under the jurisdiction of the king.
Then he was told by ascetics, brahmins, fortune-tellers, friends, relatives, and kinsmen:
"Perform propitiation of the deities."
Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other specific deities;
namely, he supplicated the deities of gardens, the deities of groves, the deities of crossroads, and the deities of street junctions;
he even supplicated those deities who are innate, those associated with his dharma, and those who are constantly attached to him.
There is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of prayers;
but that is not so.
If it were otherwise, every single person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Moreover, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three?
The mother and father are filled with passion and have come together; [the mother is in her fertile period]; and a gandharva is present.
When the mother is healthy and in her fertile period,
and a gandharva is present—
through the coming together of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.

While he remained thus intent on his petition, a certain being, having passed away from a certain class of beings, descended into the womb of that Prajāpati. There are five unique qualities found in some women who are of a wise nature. Which are they?
What are the five? She knows whether a man is impassioned or dispassionate;
she knows the proper time and she knows the season.
He knows when the embryo has entered;
he knows from whom the embryo has entered;
he knows whether it is a boy or a girl.
If it is a male child,
he remains resting against the right side of the womb;
if it is a female child, [she remains resting against the left].
She remained resting on her left side;
being exceedingly joyful, she announced it to her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, you prosper!"
"I have become pregnant;
and since he remains resting against my right side,
it is certain that it will be a boy."
He too, with a joyful heart, raised his upper body, extended his right arm, and uttered this exclamation:
"Perhaps I might behold the face of a son, long desired by me for so long;
may one be born to me who is not base-born,
and who shall perform my duties."
One who has been supported should support [the master] in return; one should accept what is inherited so that my family lineage may endure for a long time.
And when we have passed away, having given gifts, whether small or great, and performed meritorious deeds, they will dedicate the merit in my name, saying:
"May this follow those two wherever they go, whatever their rebirth.
And knowing her to be pregnant, he keeps her in the upper story of the palace, unconfined.

In the cold, she was provided with cold requisites; in the heat, with warm requisites; and with foods prescribed by physicians—neither too bitter, nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too sweet, nor too pungent, nor too astringent—but with foods free from bitterness, acidity, salinity, sweetness, pungency, and astringency.
Her body was adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, like an apsarā wandering in the Nandana grove, never descending from couch to couch or seat to seat to the ground below.
And for her, there was no hearing of any unpleasant sound whatsoever until the fetus reached full maturity.
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born who was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
When he was born, a birth festival was held and he was given the name Gaṅgika.
The boy Gaṅgika was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their hips, two to provide milk, two to clean his filth, and two to play with him.
He was reared and nourished by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various excellent provisions most refined;
he grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
Endowed with wholesome roots conducive to the state of non-differentiation, he finds no delight in the life of a householder.
He prostrates at the feet of his mother and father and makes this request: "Mother and father, please grant me your permission."
"I shall go forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
Then his parents, regarding him as their only son, did not grant him permission.
Thereupon, the thought occurred to Gaṅgika:
The attainment of human birth is difficult to find, the appearance of a Tathāgata is difficult to find,
and likewise, the perfection of the sense faculties is also difficult to find.
"What means might there be for me so that I may go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One?
It occurred to him:
"Suppose I were to make a vow and deprive myself of life by my own hand."
Thinking, "Having attained human status, may I go forth into the religious life as quickly as possible," he consumed poison with that very thought,
yet he did not die.
He fell into fire,
threw himself from a mountain,
and fell into a river or a pit.
Even there he did not die.
The thought occurred to him:
"What means might there be by which I could die?"
The thought occurred to him:
"In every respect, this King Ajātaśatru is fierce, impetuous, harsh, and reckless;
what if I were to break into his house at night?"
Having gone to the city of Rājagṛha, when night had fallen and his field of vision was obscured, he began to cut through a breach.
Then, being seized alive by the guards, he was brought before King Ajātaśatru:
"Your Majesty, this man is a thief, wicked and harmful."
"He who breaks into a breach in the royal palace at night"—
having thus deemed him a criminal, the king ordered that he be put to death.

Then, by executioners wearing blue garments, with garlands of *karavīra* flowers draped around their necks and weapons raised in their hands, having proclaimed [the sentence] at the openings of the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions at the beginning of the month of Śrāvaṇa, he is led out through the southern city gate and taken to the Śītavana cemetery.
As he was being led away, he said to those executioners:
"Go quickly, go quickly, sirs!
Lest there should ever be a change of heart on the part of the king."
Then this news was reported to the king by hunters who had killed wild animals.
Thereupon, the king turned him back and asked: "What is the reason that you wish to renounce your cherished life?"
He related that event in detail to the king.
Then King Ajātaśatru, with his hair standing on end like a kadamba flower and his throat choked with tears, weeping, uttered this inspired utterance:
"Oh, how perfectly matured is the continuity of his intellect!"
He has thoroughly understood the defects of cyclic existence and has perfectly attained the excellence of faith,
such that for the sake of the religious life, he is now determined to renounce this cherished life.
Then the king, having comforted him, said: "My son, I am the master of your life;
go now and go forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One."
Released by the king, he went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, having understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and shifting, and having struck down all conditioned states as being subject to decay, falling away, scattering, and destruction, [he realized the truth].

Through the abandonment of all afflictions, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward an axe or sandalwood paste, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights,
and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Upendra.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my monks, my disciples who have gone forth out of faith, namely Gaṅgika, the son of a guild-leader from Vārāṇasī."
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Gaṅgika, as a result of which fire finds no place in his body?"
He does not die by poison, nor by weapons, nor by water.
"And by him, Arhatship has been attained. The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Gaṅgika himself in previous births; their conditions have been met, their causal factors have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable."
Gangika himself has performed and accumulated these karmas;
who else shall experience them?
Monks, performed and accumulated karmas do not ripen in the external earth element.
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that performed actions—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen:
"Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (AVŚ 98.1)

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain Mātaṅga who was a scavenger at the cemetery. Once, having killed some travelers, he had acquired their goods. Then, thieves ran after him from behind.
Meanwhile, in a certain cemetery, a pratyekabuddha had entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Then, that cemetery-robber—
Mātaṅga, having cast down his goods before him, hid right there.
When those thieves saw the Pratyekabuddha, they began to hurl weapons and fire at him;
yet they were not even able to move a corner of his robe.
Because he had entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*),
when those thieves had departed, exhausted,
that Pratyekabuddha gradually emerged from his concentration.
Then that Mātaṅga, the scavenger of the cremation ground, having provided almsfood to that Pratyekabuddha, made this aspiration:
"May I too become a possessor of such qualities as these, and may I be free from harm by others, just as he is."
"In this way, wherever I may be born,
may I there be beyond the reach of harm from others,
and may I please, and never displease, a Teacher even more distinguished than this one."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the Mātaṅga cemetery-thief, he is this Gaṅgika."
Furthermore, he went forth as a monk under the Blessed One Kāśyapa;
there, he fully observed the life of celibacy,
and by that merit, he has now realized arhatship.

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for actions that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are exclusively white.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. [Avadānaśataka 99] Dīrghanakha.

(Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, citizens, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. (Speyer’s edition, vol. II)
Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One— honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit,
and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— together with the community of his disciples,
dwelt near Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Tiṣya in the village of Nālada. He had obtained a girl named Śārī from the house of Māṭhara. When Śāriputra descended into Śārī’s womb, [she conceived].
Then, while engaging in a debate with her brother Dīrghanakha, she brought him to a point of defeat.
Thereupon, Dīrghanakha went to the Southern Region (Dakṣiṇāpatha) and studied many treatises.
In due course, Śāriputra was born.
At the age of sixteen, he studied the Aindra grammar and defeated all the disputants;
subsequently, he went forth into homelessness within the teaching of the Blessed One.
Meanwhile, the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha heard that all those teachers had been defeated by his nephew and had now entered into discipleship under the ascetic Gautama.
Having heard this, a great sense of contempt arose within him,
and a realization that all treatises are incomplete arose within him.
Then, he gradually arrived at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion, was teaching the Dharma most sweetly to the fourfold assembly, like pure honey free from bees. Śāriputra also stood before the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One.
Then, the wandering ascetic Dīrghanakha saw the Blessed One seated in the shape of a half-moon, teaching the Dharma.
And seeing Śāriputra with a fan in his hand, fanning the Blessed One, he spoke this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Gautama, nothing at all is acceptable to me."
The Blessed One said:
"Aggivessana, even this view of yours is not tenable—
namely, this view:"
"I do not accept anything.
"Venerable Gautama, even this view of mine— that 'I do not accept anything'— is not acceptable to me."
"I do not tolerate all of this," [he said].
"But, Agnivaiśyāyana, for one who understands thus, will there not be the abandoning, the relinquishing, and the vomiting out of this view;
and the non-reconnection, the non-grasping, and the non-manifestation of another view?"

"Furthermore, Master Gautama, for one who knows thus and sees thus, will there be the abandoning, the relinquishing, the vomiting out of this view; and will there be the non-reconnection, the non-clinging, and the non-manifestation of another view?
You will not be in agreement with many people, Agnivaiśyāyana."
[He] will explain: these are called "thinner than the thin. O Agnivaiśyāyana, there are these three in the world that serve as bases for views.
Which three?
Here, Agnivaiśyāyana, one person holds such a view and speaks thus:
"Everything is acceptable to me."
Furthermore, here someone has such a view and speaks thus:
"Nothing is acceptable to me.
Furthermore, another has such a view and speaks thus:
"In this way, some things are acceptable to me, while one thing is not acceptable to me.
In that regard, Agnivaiśyāyana, as for this view: "Everything is acceptable to me," [it is thus].
This view leads to passion, not to the absence of passion;
it leads to hatred, not to the absence of hatred;
it leads to delusion, not to the absence of delusion.
for conjunction, not for non-conjunction;
for defilement, not for purification;
for accumulation, not for diminution.
It leads to delighting in, grasping at, and adhering to [existence].
In this regard, Agnivaiśyāyana, as for this view:
"Nothing is acceptable to me"—
This view leads to non-attachment, not to attachment;
to non-hatred, not to hatred;
to non-delusion, not to delusion.
For the sake of dissociation, not for conjunction;
for the sake of purification, not for defilement; for the sake of non-accumulation, not for accumulation.
It leads to non-delight, non-clinging, and non-attachment.
In this regard, as for this view:
"One thing is acceptable to me,
one thing is not acceptable to me"— that which is acceptable to him, first of all...
That leads to passion, to hatred, to delusion, to bondage, and to affliction;
it does not lead to purification, nor to diminution;
it conduces to delight, to grasping, and to attachment.
That which he does not tolerate leads to non-attachment, not to attachment; it leads to non-hatred, not to hatred.
For the sake of non-delusion, not for delusion; for the sake of non-attachment, not for attachment;
for the sake of purification, not for defilement.
It leads to diminution, not to accumulation;
to non-delight, non-clinging, and non-attachment.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
And I should hold such a view and speak thus: "Everything is acceptable to me;
with two [positions] there would be for me conflict and dispute."
And he who holds such a view and speaks thus:
"Nothing is acceptable to me";
and he who holds such a view and speaks thus: [nothing is acceptable to me].
"This one is acceptable to me, this one is not acceptable to me"—
when there is such contention, there is dispute;
when there is dispute, there is violence.
Thus, perceiving that [view] as involving conflict, dispute, and violence,
he abandons this view.
And one does not take up any other view. Thus, there occurs the abandonment, relinquishment, and vomiting away of this view;
and there is the non-reconnection, non-appropriation, and non-manifestation of another view.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
"If I were to hold such a view and speak thus:
'Nothing is acceptable to me,' [then I would be at fault]."
I would have a dispute and a contention with two [kinds of people]: namely,
those who hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:
"I forgive everything," says one who holds such a view and speaks thus; while another holds such a view and speaks thus:
"I forgive some things, but I do not forgive others."
When there is conflict, there is dispute;
when there is dispute, there is violence.
Thus, perceiving this [view] as accompanied by conflict, accompanied by dispute, and accompanied by violence, he relinquishes this view.
And one does not take up another view;
thus there occurs the abandoning, the relinquishing, and the vomiting out of this view,
as well as the non-reconnection, the non-appropriation, and the non-manifestation of another view.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
"If I were to hold such a view and speak thus: 'Nothing at all is acceptable to me,' [then I would be at fault]."
I would have a conflict and a dispute with two [types of people]: namely,
those who hold such a view and speak thus:
"I forgive everything," as well as one who holds such a view and speaks thus:
"I forgive some things, but I do not forgive others."
When there is contention, there is dispute;
when there is dispute, there is violence.
Thus, perceiving this [view] as accompanied by contention, accompanied by dispute, and accompanied by violence, he relinquishes this view.
And one does not take up another view;
thus there is the abandoning, the relinquishing, and the vomiting out of this view,
as well as the non-reconnection, the non-appropriation, and the non-manifestation of another view.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
"If I were to hold such a view and speak thus: 'One thing is acceptable to me...'"
"One thing is not pleasing to me; with two things there would be conflict for me, there would be dispute."
And he who has such a view and such a doctrine as: "Everything is acceptable to me," and he who has such a view and such a doctrine as: [everything is not acceptable to me].
"I do not tolerate anything"—
when there is such contention, there is dispute;
when there is dispute, there is violence.
Thus, perceiving that [view] as involving conflict, dispute, and violence, he relinquishes this view and does not take up another view.
In this way, there occurs the abandonment, the relinquishment, and the vomiting out of this view.
And for any other view, there is no reconnection, no grasping, and no manifestation.

Indeed, Agnivaiśyāyana, this body is material, gross, and composed of the four great elements; thus should a noble disciple dwell constantly observing its arising and passing away, dwelling observing dispassion toward it, and dwelling observing its relinquishment.
While the noble disciple dwells thus constantly observing its arising and passing away, [he attains liberation].

Whatever desire for the body, affection for the body, love for the body, attachment to the body, clinging to the body, or fixation on the body he may have toward it, that does not remain by completely overwhelming his mind.
"Agnivaiśyāyana, there are these three feelings.
Which three?
Pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant."
At whatever time a learned noble disciple experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time two feelings of his have ceased:
the painful and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
And at that time, the noble disciple experiences only pleasant feeling;
yet even pleasant feeling is impermanent and subject to cessation.
At whatever time the noble disciple experiences painful feeling, [he understands it as such].
At that time, two of his feelings have ceased:
the pleasant and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
At that time, the noble disciple experiences only painful feeling.
Even painful feeling is impermanent and subject to cessation.
At whatever time a noble disciple experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time two of his feelings have ceased.
At that time, the noble disciple experiences a feeling that is pleasant, painful, and indeed neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
even this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is impermanent and subject to cessation.
It occurs to him: "Of what cause are these feelings, of what origin, of what nature, and of what provenance?
These feelings have contact as their cause, contact as their origin, contact as their nature, and contact as their provenance.
From the arising of that contact, those various feelings arise;
from the cessation of that contact, those various feelings cease.
They become stilled, cooled, and come to an end.
Whatever feeling he experiences— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—
he understands, as it truly is, the arising and the passing away of those feelings, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them.

For him who understands, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feelings, he dwells observing impermanence in arisen feelings; he dwells observing their vanishing, observing their fading away, observing their cessation, and observing their relinquishment.
Experiencing a feeling that has the body as its limit, he understands, as it truly is, "I experience a feeling that has the body as its limit."
Experiencing a sensation that ends with life, he understands as it really is: "I am experiencing a sensation that ends with life.

And after the breaking up of the body, upon the exhaustion of life, all his sensations cease here and now without remainder; they go to their complete cessation, disappearance, destruction, and exhaustion.
To him, it occurs thus:
Even for one experiencing a pleasant feeling, there will be the dissolution of the body;
this indeed is the end of suffering.
Even for one experiencing a painful [feeling],...
Even when one experiences a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, the body will eventually break up;
this indeed is the end of suffering.
He experiences even a pleasant feeling...
Being dissociated, he experiences; he is not bound. He experiences even painful feeling and even neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
One who is dissociated experiences, not one who is associated.
Dissociated from what?
Detached from passion, hatred, and delusion;
detached from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair;
I say he is detached from suffering.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having been ordained for half a month, was standing behind the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One.
This thought occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"The Blessed One praises only the abandoning of those phenomena."
He describes only dispassion, only cessation, and only relinquishment:
"What if I were to dwell contemplating the abandonment of those various phenomena,
dwelling contemplating dispassion, and dwelling contemplating cessation?"
"May I dwell contemplating relinquishment. As the Venerable Śāriputra dwelt thus, contemplating the impermanence of these phenomena, contemplating their passing away,
contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment, his mind was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
And for the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dharma arose regarding all phenomena.

Then the wanderer Dīrghanakha, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma; having crossed over doubt and transcended uncertainty, no longer dependent on others and not led by another, having attained confidence in the Teacher’s instruction, in the Teacher’s dispensation, and in the teachings, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable sir, may I obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
may I lead the holy life under the Blessed One.
The wanderer Dīrghanakha obtained the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.

Having thus gone forth, that venerable one dwelt alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, he attained that goal for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with right faith go forth from the home to the homeless life.
Having realized for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, he attains it and declares:
"Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further state of existence beyond this."
The Venerable One, having understood, became an Arhat with a mind well-liberated.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my monks, my disciples who have attained analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid), namely, the monk Koṣṭhila."
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what actions were performed and accumulated by Mahākauṣṭhila, as a result of which he became a great debater?"
"Having gone forth, he realized arhatship.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Koṣṭhila in previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable."
Koṣṭhila performed and accumulated these karmas;
who else shall experience them?
Monks, karmas performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element.
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—reach their maturation:
"Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (AVŚ 99.1)

In the past, monks, in times gone by, in the city of Vārāṇasī, about five hundred bandits, led by their commander, set out on a robbery. While they were wandering about, they came upon a certain grove of acacia trees. Then the commander spoke to them:
"Look, do you see any other man here with eyes as broad as lotus petals, by whom we might offer a sacrifice to the yakṣas and then depart?
Now, a pratyekabuddha was dwelling there in that acacia forest.
Then, having been spotted by those wandering thieves, he was led into the presence of the army commander.
Thereupon, the leader of the bandits gave the order: "Let this man be executed!
Then that Pratyekabuddha, for the sake of showing them favor, rose into the sky like a king of swans with outspread wings and began to display various miraculous feats.
Then the general, like a tree cut down at its root, fell at his feet and confessed his transgression.
Having offered him alms-food, he made this aspiration:
"May I too become a possessor of such qualities as these."
And may I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and never displease him.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the leader of the band of thieves, is this very Koṣṭhila."
Furthermore, he went forth as a monk under the Blessed One Kāśyapa;
there, he maintained the life of celibacy for ten thousand years,
and by that merit, he has now realized arhatship.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, it is entirely white;
and for those that are mixed, it is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having set aside entirely black deeds and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white deeds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One spoke thus;
with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
AVŚ 100: Saṃgīti.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and citizens.

The Buddha, the Blessed One—honored by merchants, caravan leaders, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; thus revered by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; renowned, of great merit, and a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—together with his community of disciples.
He was staying at Kuśinagarī in the grove of twin śāla trees belonging to the Mallas.
Then, at that very time of his final nirvāṇa, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Prepare, Ānanda, a couch for the Tathāgata between the twin śāla trees, with its head toward the north."

"Today, in the middle watch of the night, the Tathāgata will pass into final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder. "So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having done so, he prepared a couch with its head toward the north between the twin śāla trees and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, a couch has been prepared for the Tathāgata between the twin śāla trees, with its head toward the north.
Then the Blessed One approached the couch.
Having approached, he prepares his bed on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and keeping the thought of Nirvana alone in mind.
There, during the middle watch of the night, the Blessed One passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Immediately upon the Buddha, the Blessed One’s final passing, at that very moment, a great earthquake occurred, meteors fell, and the quarters of the sky blazed;
in the atmosphere, the drums of the gods resounded.

Immediately after the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, both of the twin *śāla* trees in the grove—the most excellent of trees—covered the Tathāgata’s lion-bed with *śāla* flowers.
Immediately after the Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, a certain monk at that time spoke this verse:
"Truly beautiful are these two most excellent trees of this *śāla* grove."
They scattered flowers over the Teacher who had entered final nirvana.
Immediately after the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, Śakra, the lord of the gods, spoke this verse:
“Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent; their nature is to arise and pass away.
Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss. (AVŚ 100.2)
Immediately after the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, Brahmā Sahāmpati spoke this verse:
"All beings in this world will cast off their physical forms,
now that such a Teacher, a peerless person in all the worlds, has passed away."
Having attained the powers of a Tathāgata, the Visionary One has entered parinirvāṇa.

Immediately after the Buddha, the Blessed One, had attained final nirvāṇa, the Venerable Āniruddha spoke this verse: “The inhalations and exhalations have ceased for the Protector whose mind was steadfast; having attained the imperturbable peace, the Visionary has entered final nirvāṇa. (AVŚ 100.4)
At that time it became terrifying; at that time it caused the hair to stand on end, when the Teacher, endowed with all forms of power, met his death. (AVŚ 100.5)
"Enduring sensations with a mind that does not shrink back, his liberation of the mind is like the extinguishing of a lamp. Thus it was said.
When the Buddha, the Blessed One, had been in parinirvāṇa for seven days, the Venerable Ānanda, circumambulating the Blessed One’s funeral pyre, spoke this verse:
“By that same bodily form through which the Guide, possessed of great supernatural power, went to the Brahma-world,
he was now being consumed by a subtle heat, though encircled by five hundred yugas.”
Indeed, the body of the Buddha was enveloped by a thousand robes;
yet two robes there were not burned at all— the inner one and the second outer one.
One hundred years after the Buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka reigned in the city of Pāṭaliputra;

the realm was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo.
The righteous King of Dharma ruled the kingdom according to the Dharma. At another time, he sported, enjoyed himself, and dallied with his queen.
While he was thus sporting, enjoying himself, and dallying, after some time the queen became pregnant.
After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born who was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing, with eyes like those of a kunāla bird.
Upon his birth, a birth festival was performed and his name was established:
"What shall be the name of the boy?
The kinsmen said,
"Since his eyes, as soon as he was born, resemble those of a *kuṇāla* bird,"
"Therefore, let the boy's name be Kuṇāla.
The boy Kuṇāla was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide breast milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nurtured by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various excellent provisions most refined.
He grew quickly, like a lotus in a pond.
Then, having placed him—adorned with every ornament—upon his lap and gazing at him again and again, the king, thrilled by the perfection of his form, said:
"My son is peerless in the world in terms of beauty."
At that time, there was a village named Puṣpabherotsa in Gāndhāra.
There, a son was born to a certain householder; he surpassed human complexion yet had not yet attained divine complexion.
At his birth, [a vessel] filled with water scented with divine perfumes appeared.
A jewel-encrusted lotus pond appeared,
as did a vast, mobile garden filled with flowers.
Wherever the prince went, there a lotus pond and a garden appeared;
therefore, the name "Sundara" was established for him.
In due course, the prince grew up.
Then, at a later time, merchants from Puṣpabheruṭsa went to Pāṭaliputra on some business;
they approached the king bringing gifts.
Then, having prostrated at his feet and presented a gift to the king, they stood before him.
Thereupon, King Aśoka showed Kuṇāla to them, saying:
"O merchants!..."
"Have you ever, while wandering here or there, previously seen anyone endowed with such a distinction of form?
Then those merchants, joining their palms in reverence, prostrated at his feet, sought his protection, and said to the king:
"O Lord, in our territory there is a youth named Sundara, who has surpassed human appearance but has not yet attained divine appearance."
At his birth, a jewel-encrusted lotus pond filled with water scented with divine perfumes appeared, as did a vast, mobile garden abounding in flowers and fruits;
wherever the prince went, there a lotus pond and a garden would manifest.
Upon hearing this, King Aśoka was struck with great wonder;
filled with curiosity, he dispatched a messenger, saying:
"This King Aśoka desires to come for the purpose of seeing Prince Sundara."
"Whatever task you have to perform or whatever duty you must carry out, do that.
Then the great multitude of people became afraid, thinking: "If the king comes here with a great military force..."
"Lest he should cause some misfortune," [he thought].
Thereupon, the prince had a magnificent vehicle prepared, gave a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces as a gift, and sent him to Aśoka.
Traveling by stages, he reached the city of Pāṭaliputra.
Taking a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he arrived in the presence of King Aśoka.
Upon seeing Prince Sundara’s form, splendor, and excellence of complexion, as well as the divine lotus pond and the garden, King Aśoka was struck with great wonder.
Then, in order to produce further amazement in the Elder Upagupta, King Aśoka took Prince Sundara and went to Kukkuṭāgāra.
There, eighteen thousand arhats headed by Upagupta resided,
along with twice that number of trainees (śaikṣas) and virtuous ordinary persons (pṛthagjanakalyāṇaka).
Then, having prostrated at the feet of the Elder, he sat before him to listen to the Dharma.
The Elder Upagupta taught him the Dharma.
Thereupon, the prince, whose mental continuum was fully ripened, heard the Dharma and became desirous of going forth.
Having obtained permission from King Aśoka, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder Upagupta.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction,
he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to the axe or sandalwood, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the higher faculties; he turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor,
and became one to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods including Indra and Upendra.
Then King Aśoka, being in doubt, asked the Elder:
"Venerable sir, what deeds were performed by Sundara, by which he possesses such a form as this?"
"But what were the deeds by which this jewel-encrusted lotus pond, filled with divine fragrant water, and that great, mobile garden, abundant with flowers and fruits, came into being?
The Elder Upagupta replied:

"O Great King, by Sundara alone— in former births— actions were performed and accumulated which have reached their full measure, whose conditions have matured, which stand before him like a rushing torrent, and which are inevitable."
Sundara alone has performed and accumulated these actions;
who else shall experience them?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element.
not in the water element, not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
Moreover, it is precisely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—reach their maturation:
"Actions do not perish even after hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (AVŚ 100.1)

Long ago, Great King, when the Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, was wandering through the countryside of Magadha, desiring to perform the communal recitation of the Dharma (dharmasaṃgīti).
At that time, a certain poor farmer saw a great community of monks.
Afflicted with grief due to separation from his Teacher, exhausted by the journey, and his body covered in dust,
compassion arose within him. Thereupon, he invited five hundred monks, headed by Kāśyapa, to bathe in a steam-heated bathhouse.
Then, having prepared warm water infused with various fragrances, he bathed those monks and adorned them with robes.
Having satisfied them with excellent food and granted them the refuges and the precepts, he made this aspiration:
"May I go forth in this very teaching of Śākyamuni and attain arhatship."
What do you think, Great King? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the poor farmer, is this very monk Sundara.
Because he bathed those monks with the steam-bath (jentāka), [he has attained this fruit].
Because of that, such a distinction of form came to be for him:
he obtained a beautiful lotus pond filled with divine sandalwood water, and he acquired a great, moving garden abounding in flowers and fruits;
this was because he had received the precepts for taking refuge.
Therefore, in this very life, he realized arhatship.
Thus, O Great King, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, O Great King, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed,
you should apply yourself solely to actions that are exclusively white.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Then Rāhula Aśoka, having rejoiced and approved of what the Venerable Elder Upagupta had spoken, rose from his seat and departed.
